concepts.title: Terminal Velocity
concepts.one_liner: The velocity approaches a limit, called the "terminal velocity."
concepts.summary_md: Air resistance prevents the velocity of a skydiver from increasing indefinitely. The velocity approaches a limit, called the "terminal velocity."
concepts.motivation_md: This concept introduces the idea of a physical limit, demonstrating how real-world phenomena like air resistance can cap an object's speed, making the abstract concept of a limit more tangible.
concepts.recap_md: - Air resistance limits the speed of falling objects.- This limiting speed is known as "terminal velocity."
concepts.raw_body: Air resistance prevents the velocity of a skydiver from increasing indefinitely. The velocity approaches a limit, called the "terminal velocity."

concepts.title: Introduction to Calculus and Limits
concepts.one_liner: The fundamental building block on which rates of change rest is the concept of a "limit."
concepts.summary_md: Calculus, developed by Newton and Leibniz, provided the first real understanding of "instantaneous rate of change." The concept of a "limit" is the fundamental building block on which rates of change rest, and all other calculus concepts are now based on it.
concepts.motivation_md: Calculus was developed to understand "instantaneous rates of change" like velocity and acceleration. The concept of a "limit" is the foundational idea that underpins all of calculus, making it essential to grasp for further study.
concepts.recap_md: - Calculus, developed by Newton and Leibniz, clarified "instantaneous rate of change."- The "limit" is the fundamental building block for rates of change and all other calculus concepts.
concepts.raw_body: The development of calculus in the seventeenth century by Newton and Leibniz provided scientists with their first real understanding of what is meant by an "instantaneous rate of change" such as velocity and acceleration. Once the idea was understood conceptually, efficient computational methods followed, and science took a quantum leap forward. The fundamental building block on which rates of change rest is the concept of a "limit," an idea that is so important that all other calculus concepts are now based on it.

concepts.title: Chapter Overview: Developing the Concept of a Limit
concepts.one_liner: In this chapter we will develop the concept of a limit in stages, proceeding from an informal, intuitive notion to a precise mathematical definition.
concepts.summary_md: This chapter develops the concept of a limit in stages, moving from an informal, intuitive notion to a precise mathematical definition. It will also cover theorems and procedures for calculating limits, concluding with the use of limits to study "continuous" curves.
concepts.motivation_md: This chapter outlines the structured approach to understanding limits, starting with intuition and progressing to formal definitions and practical calculations. This staged development ensures a thorough grasp of this fundamental calculus concept.
concepts.recap_md: - The chapter develops limits from an intuitive notion to a precise mathematical definition.- It will cover theorems and procedures for calculating limits.- Limits will be used to study "continuous" curves.
concepts.raw_body: In this chapter we will develop the concept of a limit in stages, proceeding from an informal, intuitive notion to a precise mathematical definition. We will also develop theorems and procedures for calculating limits, and we will conclude the chapter by using the limits to study "continuous" curves.

concepts.title: Intuitive Approach to Limits
concepts.one_liner: The concept of a "limit" is the fundamental building block on which all calculus concepts are based.
concepts.summary_md: The concept of a "limit" is the fundamental building block on which all calculus concepts are based. This section studies limits informally, aiming to develop an intuitive feel for the basic ideas before moving to computational methods and precise definitions.
concepts.motivation_md: Understanding limits intuitively first helps build a strong conceptual foundation before diving into the more rigorous computational methods and precise definitions. This approach makes the abstract concept more accessible.
concepts.recap_md: - The "limit" is the fundamental building block for all calculus concepts.- This section focuses on an informal, intuitive understanding of limits.- Future sections will cover computational methods and precise definitions.
concepts.raw_body: The concept of a "limit" is the fundamental building block on which all calculus concepts are based. In this section we will study limits informally, with the goal of developing an intuitive feel for the basic ideas. In the next three sections we will focus on computational methods and precise definitions.

concepts.title: The Tangent Line Problem
concepts.one_liner: Given a function $f$ and a point $P\left(x_{0}, y_{0}\right)$ on its graph, find an equation of the line that is tangent to the graph at $P$.
concepts.summary_md: The Tangent Line Problem asks: Given a function $f$ and a point $P\left(x_{0}, y_{0}\right)$ on its graph, find an equation of the line that is tangent to the graph at $P$.
concepts.motivation_md: The tangent line problem is one of the two classical problems that led to the development of calculus. Its solution requires the concept of a limit and is fundamental to understanding instantaneous rates of change and derivatives.
concepts.recap_md: - The problem involves finding the equation of a line tangent to a function's graph at a specific point $P\left(x_{0}, y_{0}\right)$.- This problem is a foundational challenge that calculus addresses.
concepts.raw_body: > THE TANGENT LINE PROBLEM Given a function $f$ and a point $P\left(x_{0}, y_{0}\right)$ on its graph, find an equation of the line that is tangent to the graph at $P$ (Figure 1.1.1).

concepts.title: The Area Problem
concepts.one_liner: Given a function $f$, find the area between the graph of $f$ and an interval $[a, b]$ on the $x$-axis.
concepts.summary_md: The Area Problem asks: Given a function $f$, find the area between the graph of $f$ and an interval $[a, b]$ on the $x$-axis.
concepts.motivation_md: The area problem is the second classical problem that spurred the development of calculus. Its solution, involving the concept of limits and integrals, allows us to calculate areas of irregular shapes, which has wide applications in science and engineering.
concepts.recap_md: - The problem involves finding the area bounded by a function's graph and an interval $[a, b]$ on the $x$-axis.- This is a fundamental problem addressed by integral calculus.
concepts.raw_body: THE AREA PROBLEM Given a function $f$, find the area between the graph of $f$ and an interval $[a, b]$ on the $x$-axis (Figure 1.1.2).

concepts.title: Distinction Between Differential and Integral Calculus
concepts.one_liner: Traditionally, that portion of calculus arising from the tangent line problem is called differential calculus and that arising from the area problem is called integral calculus.
concepts.summary_md: Traditionally, differential calculus arises from the tangent line problem, while integral calculus arises from the area problem. However, these two problems are so closely related that the distinction between differential and integral calculus is somewhat artificial.
concepts.motivation_md: This concept clarifies the historical division of calculus into differential and integral branches based on the problems they address. It also hints at their deep underlying connection, preparing students for the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus.
concepts.recap_md: - Differential calculus traditionally addresses the tangent line problem.- Integral calculus traditionally addresses the area problem.- The distinction between them is somewhat artificial due to their close relationship.
concepts.raw_body: Traditionally, that portion of calculus arising from the tangent line problem is called differential calculus and that arising from the area problem is called integral calculus. However, we will see later that the tangent line and area problems are so closely related that the distinction between differential and integral calculus is somewhat artificial.

concepts.title: Tangent Line as a Limit of Secant Lines
concepts.one_liner: If we move the point $Q$ along the curve toward $P$, then the secant line will rotate toward a limiting position, which is the tangent line at $P$.
concepts.summary_md: To define a tangent line for general curves, consider a point $P$ on the curve and another point $Q$ on the curve. The line through $P$ and $Q$ is a secant line. As $Q$ moves along the curve toward $P$, the secant line rotates toward a limiting position, which is defined as the tangent line at $P$.
concepts.motivation_md: This definition generalizes the concept of a tangent line beyond circles, making it applicable to any curve. It introduces the crucial idea of a "limiting position," which is foundational for understanding derivatives and instantaneous rates of change in calculus.
concepts.recap_md: - A secant line connects two points, $P$ and $Q$, on a curve.- As point $Q$ approaches point $P$ along the curve, the secant line approaches a limiting position.- This limiting position of the secant line is defined as the tangent line at point $P$.
concepts.raw_body: To obtain a definition of a tangent line that applies to curves other than circles, we must view tangent lines another way. For this purpose, suppose that we are interested in the tangent line at a point $P$ on a curve in the $x y$-plane and that $Q$ is any point that lies on the curve and is different from $P$. The line through $P$ and $Q$ is called a secant line for the curve at $P$. Intuition suggests that if we move the point $Q$ along the curve toward $P$, then the secant line will rotate toward a limiting position. The line in this limiting position is what we will consider to be the tangent line at $P$ (Figure 1.1.4a). As suggested by Figure 1.1.4b, this new concept of a tangent line coincides with the traditional concept when applied to circles.

concepts.title: Area as a Limit of Approximations
concepts.one_liner: This suggests that we can define the area under the curve to be the limiting value of these approximations.
concepts.summary_md: For regions with curved boundaries, a general approach is to approximate the area by inscribing rectangles of equal width under the curve and adding their areas. Intuition suggests that using more and more rectangles will make approximations closer to the exact area. This defines area as the limiting value of these approximations.
concepts.motivation_md: This concept addresses the challenge of calculating areas for regions with curved boundaries, which cannot be solved by simple geometric subdivision. It introduces the idea of using limits to find exact areas by refining approximations.
concepts.recap_md: - Areas of regions with straight-line boundaries can be found by subdividing into basic shapes.- For curved boundaries, approximate area by summing areas of inscribed rectangles.- The exact area is defined as the limiting value of these approximations as the number of rectangles increases.
concepts.raw_body: Just as the general notion of a tangent line leads to the concept of limit, so does the general notion of area. For plane regions with straight-line boundaries, areas can often be calculated by subdividing the region into rectangles or triangles and adding the areas of the constituent parts (Figure 1.1.6). However, for regions with curved boundaries, such as that in Figure 1.1.7a, a more general approach is needed. One such approach is to begin by approximating the area of the region by inscribing a number of rectangles of equal width under the curve and adding the areas of these rectangles (Figure 1.1.7b). Intuition suggests that if we repeat that approximation process using more and more rectangles, then the rectangles will tend to fill in the gaps under the curve, and the approximations will get closer and closer to the exact area under the curve (Figure 1.1.7c). This suggests that we can define the area under the curve to be the limiting value of these approximations. This idea will be considered in detail later, but the point to note here is that once again the concept of a limit comes into play.

concepts.title: Decimals and Limits
concepts.one_liner: Thus, limits even occur in the familiar context of decimal representations of real numbers.
concepts.summary_md: The decimal expansion of a fraction like $\frac{1}{3} = 0.33333 \ldots$ can be written as an infinite sum: $0.3+0.03+0.003+\cdots$. This means the succession of finite sums gets closer and closer to a limiting value of $\frac{1}{3}$ as more terms are included.
concepts.motivation_md: This concept demonstrates that limits are not just an abstract mathematical idea but are implicitly present in familiar mathematical contexts, like decimal representations. It helps build intuition for infinite processes converging to a finite value.
concepts.recap_md: - Decimal expansions like $0.333\ldots$ represent infinite sums.- These infinite sums are interpreted as a succession of finite sums.- The value of the decimal is the limiting value that these finite sums approach.

concepts.title: Focus on the Limit Concept
concepts.one_liner: Now that we have seen how limits arise in various ways, let us focus on the limit concept itself.
concepts.summary_md: Having explored how the concept of limits emerges in diverse mathematical contexts, such as tangent lines, areas, and decimals, the next step is to concentrate on the formal definition and properties of the limit concept itself.
concepts.motivation_md: This concept serves as a transition, signaling a shift from illustrating the occurrence of limits to formally defining and understanding the limit concept in its own right. It sets the stage for deeper mathematical exploration.
concepts.recap_md: - Limits appear in various mathematical problems, including tangent lines and areas.- They also arise in familiar contexts like decimal representations.- The next step is to delve into the formal definition and understanding of limits.
concepts.raw_body: Now that we have seen how limits arise in various ways, let us focus on the limit concept itself.

concepts.title: Describing Function Behavior as Variable Approaches a Value
concepts.one_liner: The most basic use of limits is to describe how a function behaves as the independent variable approaches a given value.
concepts.summary_md: Limits are fundamentally used to describe a function's behavior as its independent variable approaches a specific value. For example, for $f(x)=x^{2}-x+1$, as $x$ gets closer to 2 from either side, the values of $f(x)$ get closer to 3. This is written as $\lim _{x \rightarrow 2}\left(x^{2}-x+1\right)=3$.
concepts.motivation_md: This concept introduces the primary application of limits: precisely quantifying how a function's output changes as its input gets arbitrarily close to a particular point. This is crucial for understanding continuity, derivatives, and integrals.
concepts.recap_md: - Limits describe how $f(x)$ behaves as $x$ approaches a specific value.- The notation $\lim _{x \rightarrow a} f(x)=L$ means $f(x)$ approaches $L$ as $x$ approaches $a$.- This behavior is observed as $x$ approaches from both the left and right sides.

concepts.title: Limit Independent of Function Value at 'a'
concepts.one_liner: The limit describes the behavior of $f$ close to $a$ but not at $a$.
concepts.summary_md: The value of $f$ at $a$, or even whether $f$ is defined at $a$, has no bearing on the limit $L$. This is because $x$ is required to be different from $a$ when considering the limit. The limit exclusively describes the behavior of the function in the immediate vicinity of $a$, rather than at the point $a$ itself.
concepts.motivation_md: This concept clarifies a critical distinction: limits are about tendencies as inputs get close to a point, not about the function's actual value at that point. This is essential for understanding concepts like removable discontinuities and derivatives.
concepts.recap_md: - When evaluating $\lim _{x \rightarrow a} f(x)$, $x$ is considered close to $a$ but not equal to $a$.- Therefore, the value of $f(a)$ does not affect the limit $L$.- A function does not even need to be defined at $a$ for its limit to exist there.
concepts.raw_body: Since $x$ is required to be different from $a$ in (6), the value of $f$ at $a$, or even whether $f$ is defined at $a$, has no bearing on the limit $L$. The limit describes the behavior of $f$ close to $a$ but not at $a$.

concepts.title: Limits (An Informal View)
concepts.one_liner: If the values of $f(x)$ can be made as close as we like to $L$ by taking values of $x$ sufficiently close to $a$ (but not equal to $a$), then we write $\lim _{x \rightarrow a} f(x)=L$.
concepts.summary_md: The informal definition of a limit states that if $f(x)$ can be made arbitrarily close to a value $L$ by choosing $x$ sufficiently close to $a$ (but not equal to $a$), then we write $\lim _{x \rightarrow a} f(x)=L$. This is read as 'the limit of $f(x)$ as $x$ approaches $a$ is $L$,' or ' $f(x)$ approaches $L$ as $x$ approaches $a$.'
concepts.motivation_md: This concept provides the foundational, intuitive definition of a limit, which is central to calculus. It allows us to precisely describe the behavior of functions near a point, even if the function is undefined or behaves unusually at that exact point.
concepts.recap_md: - The informal limit definition states $f(x)$ approaches $L$ as $x$ approaches $a$ (but $x \neq a$).- This means $f(x)$ can be made arbitrarily close to $L$ by making $x$ sufficiently close to $a$.- The notation is $\lim _{x \rightarrow a} f(x)=L$ or $f(x) \rightarrow L$ as $x \rightarrow a$.

concepts.title: Sampling Pitfalls in Determining Limits
concepts.one_liner: Numerical evidence can sometimes lead to incorrect conclusions about limits because of roundoff error or because the sample values chosen do not reveal the true limiting behavior.
concepts.summary_md: Numerical evidence, such as tables of values, can be misleading when determining limits due to roundoff error or unrepresentative sample values. For example, sampling $x$-intercepts for $\sin(\frac{\pi}{x})$ might incorrectly suggest a limit of 0 as $x \rightarrow 0$, when in reality the function oscillates between -1 and 1. This highlights the need for alternative methods to confirm limits.
concepts.motivation_md: This concept warns against the limitations of numerical and graphical methods for determining limits, emphasizing that they can be deceptive. It motivates the need for more rigorous, analytical techniques to confirm limiting behavior.
concepts.recap_md: - Numerical evidence can be misleading for limits due to roundoff error or poor sample choices.- A function might oscillate rapidly near a point, appearing to approach a limit numerically when it does not.- It is crucial to use alternative methods to corroborate limits conjectured from numerical data.
concepts.raw_body:
Numerical evidence can sometimes lead to incorrect conclusions about limits because of roundoff error or because the sample values chosen do not reveal the true limiting behavior. For example, one might incorrectly conclude from Table 1.1.3 that

$$
\lim _{x \rightarrow 0} \sin \left(\frac{\pi}{x}\right)=0
$$

The fact that this is not correct is evidenced by the graph of $f$ in Figure 1.1.11. The graph reveals that the values of $f$ oscillate between -1 and 1 with increasing rapidity as $x \rightarrow 0$ and hence do not approach a limit. The data in the table deceived us because the $x$-values selected all happened to be $x$-intercepts for $f(x)$. This points out the need for having alternative methods for corroborating limits conjectured from numerical evidence.

concepts.title: Introduction to One-Sided Limits
concepts.one_liner: However, some functions exhibit different behaviors on the two sides of an $x$-value $a$, in which case it is necessary to distinguish whether values of $x$ near $a$ are on the left side or on the right side of $a$ for purposes of investigating limiting behavior.
concepts.summary_md: While a two-sided limit requires $f(x)$ to approach $L$ as $x$ approaches $a$ from both sides, some functions behave differently on either side of $a$. In such cases, one-sided limits are used to distinguish behavior from the left or right. For example, for $f(x)=\frac{|x|}{x}$, as $x \rightarrow 0^{+}$, $f(x) \rightarrow 1$, and as $x \rightarrow 0^{-}$, $f(x) \rightarrow -1$.
concepts.motivation_md: This concept introduces one-sided limits to address situations where a function approaches different values from the left and right sides of a point. This is essential for a complete understanding of limits, continuity, and functions with sharp changes or discontinuities.
concepts.recap_md: - A two-sided limit requires $f(x)$ to approach $L$ from both the left and right of $a$.- One-sided limits describe behavior when $x$ approaches $a$ specifically from the left ($x \rightarrow a^{-}$) or from the right ($x \rightarrow a^{+}$).- Functions with different behaviors on either side of $a$ necessitate the use of one-sided limits.
concepts.raw_body:
The limit in (6) is called a two-sided limit because it requires the values of $f(x)$ to get closer and closer to $L$ as values of $x$ are taken from either side of $x=a$. However, some functions exhibit different behaviors on the two sides of an $x$-value $a$, in which case it is necessary to distinguish whether values of $x$ near $a$ are on the left side or on the right side of $a$ for purposes of investigating limiting behavior. For example, consider the function

$$
f(x)=\frac{|x|}{x}=\left\{\begin{align*}
1, & x>0  \tag{12}\\
-1, & x<0
\end{align*}\right.
$$

which is graphed in Figure 1.1.12. As $x$ approaches 0 from the right, the values of $f(x)$ approach a limit of 1 [in fact, the values of $f(x)$ are exactly 1 for all such $x$ ], and similarly, as $x$ approaches 0 from the left, the values of $f(x)$ approach a limit of -1 . We denote these limits by writing

$$
\begin{equation*}
\lim _{x \rightarrow 0^{+}} \frac{|x|}{x}=1 \quad \text { and } \quad \lim _{x \rightarrow 0^{-}} \frac{|x|}{x}=-1 \tag{13}
\end{equation*}
$$

With this notation, the superscript "+" indicates a limit from the right and the superscript "-" indicates a limit from the left.

concepts.title: One-Sided Limits (An Informal View)
concepts.one_liner: If $f(x)$ can be made as close as we like to $L$ by taking $x$ sufficiently close to $a$ (but greater than $a$), then $\lim _{x \rightarrow a^{+}} f(x)=L$.
concepts.summary_md: If the values of $f(x)$ can be made as close as we like to $L$ by taking values of $x$ sufficiently close to $a$ (but greater than $a$), then we write $\lim _{x \rightarrow a^{+}} f(x)=L$. Similarly, if $f(x)$ approaches $L$ as $x$ approaches $a$ (but less than $a$), we write $\lim _{x \rightarrow a^{-}} f(x)=L$.
concepts.motivation_md: One-sided limits are essential for describing function behavior near a point where a two-sided limit might not exist, such as at a discontinuity or endpoint. They allow us to analyze how a function approaches a specific value from either the left or the right, providing a more precise understanding of local behavior.
concepts.recap_md: - $\lim _{x \rightarrow a^{+}} f(x)=L$ means $f(x)$ approaches $L$ as $x$ approaches $a$ from values greater than $a$ (from the right). - $\lim _{x \rightarrow a^{-}} f(x)=L$ means $f(x)$ approaches $L$ as $x$ approaches $a$ from values less than $a$ (from the left).

concepts.title: When a Limit Does Not Exist
concepts.one_liner: There is no guarantee that a function $f$ will have a two-sided limit at a given point $a$; in this case, we say that $\lim _{x \rightarrow a} f(x)$ does not exist.
concepts.summary_md: In general, there is no guarantee that a function $f$ will have a two-sided limit at a given point $a$; that is, the values of $f(x)$ may not get closer and closer to any single real number $L$ as $x \rightarrow a$. In this case we say that $\lim _{x \rightarrow a} f(x)$ does not exist. Similarly, one-sided limits may also not exist if $f(x)$ does not approach a single real number $L$.
concepts.motivation_md: Understanding when a limit does not exist is crucial for identifying points of discontinuity or other complex behaviors in a function. It helps in analyzing the function's overall structure and predicting its behavior, especially in applications where continuity is assumed or required.
concepts.recap_md: - A two-sided limit $\lim _{x \rightarrow a} f(x)$ does not exist if $f(x)$ does not approach a single real number $L$ as $x \rightarrow a$. - One-sided limits $\lim _{x \rightarrow a^{+}} f(x)$ or $\lim _{x \rightarrow a^{-}} f(x)$ do not exist if $f(x)$ does not approach a single real number $L$ from the respective side.
concepts.raw_body:
In general, there is no guarantee that a function $f$ will have a two-sided limit at a given point $a$; that is, the values of $f(x)$ may not get closer and closer to any single real number $L$ as $x \rightarrow a$. In this case we say that

$$
\lim _{x \rightarrow a} f(x) \text { does not exist }
$$

Similarly, the values of $f(x)$ may not get closer and closer to a single real number $L$ as $x \rightarrow a^{+}$or as $x \rightarrow a^{-}$. In these cases we say that

$$
\lim _{x \rightarrow a^{+}} f(x) \text { does not exist }
$$

or that

$$
\lim _{x \rightarrow a^{-}} f(x) \text { does not exist }
$$

concepts.title: The Relationship Between One-Sided and Two-Sided Limits
concepts.one_liner: The two-sided limit of a function $f(x)$ exists at $a$ if and only if both of the one-sided limits exist at $a$ and have the same value.
concepts.summary_md: The two-sided limit of a function $f(x)$ exists at $a$ if and only if both of the one-sided limits exist at $a$ and have the same value. This means $\lim _{x \rightarrow a} f(x)=L$ if and only if $\lim _{x \rightarrow a^{-}} f(x)=L=\lim _{x \rightarrow a^{+}} f(x)$.
concepts.motivation_md: This theorem provides a fundamental link between one-sided and two-sided limits, offering a powerful tool for determining the existence and value of a two-sided limit. It is particularly useful when dealing with piecewise functions or functions with potential discontinuities, allowing for a systematic approach to limit evaluation.
concepts.recap_md: - For $\lim _{x \rightarrow a} f(x)$ to exist, both $\lim _{x \rightarrow a^{-}} f(x)$ and $\lim _{x \rightarrow a^{+}} f(x)$ must exist. - If the two-sided limit exists, then $\lim _{x \rightarrow a^{-}} f(x) = \lim _{x \rightarrow a^{+}} f(x)$. - If $\lim _{x \rightarrow a^{-}} f(x) = \lim _{x \rightarrow a^{+}} f(x) = L$, then $\lim _{x \rightarrow a} f(x) = L$.
concepts.raw_body:
1.1.3 THE RELATIONSHIP BETWEEN ONE-SIDED AND TWO-SIDED LIMITS The twosided limit of a function $f(x)$ exists at $a$ if and only if both of the one-sided limits exist at $a$ and have the same value; that is,

$$
\lim _{x \rightarrow a} f(x)=L \quad \text { if and only if } \quad \lim _{x \rightarrow a^{-}} f(x)=L=\lim _{x \rightarrow a^{+}} f(x)
$$

concepts.title: Infinite Limits
concepts.one_liner: Sometimes one-sided or two-sided limits fail to exist because the values of the function increase or decrease without bound.
concepts.summary_md: Sometimes one-sided or two-sided limits fail to exist because the values of the function increase or decrease without bound. For example, as $x \rightarrow 0^{+}$ for $f(x)=1/x$, $f(x)$ increases without bound, written as $\lim _{x \rightarrow 0^{+}} \frac{1}{x}=+\infty$. Similarly, as $x \rightarrow 0^{-}$ for $f(x)=1/x$, $f(x)$ decreases without bound, written as $\lim _{x \rightarrow 0^{-}} \frac{1}{x}=-\infty$.
concepts.motivation_md: Infinite limits provide a way to describe the behavior of functions that grow or shrink without bound near a certain point, even though a finite limit does not exist. This concept is crucial for identifying vertical asymptotes and understanding how functions behave at points of division by zero or other singularities.
concepts.recap_md: - Infinite limits describe cases where function values increase or decrease without bound near a point. - $\lim _{x \rightarrow a} f(x)=+\infty$ means $f(x)$ increases without bound as $x$ approaches $a$. - $\lim _{x \rightarrow a} f(x)=-\infty$ means $f(x)$ decreases without bound as $x$ approaches $a$.
concepts.raw_body:
## INFINITE LIMITS

Sometimes one-sided or two-sided limits fail to exist because the values of the function increase or decrease without bound. For example, consider the behavior of $f(x)=1 / x$ for values of $x$ near 0 . It is evident from the table and graph in Figure 1.1.15 that as $x$-values are taken closer and closer to 0 from the right, the values of $f(x)=1 / x$ are positive and increase without bound; and as $x$-values are taken closer and closer to 0 from the left, the values of $f(x)=1 / x$ are negative and decrease without bound. We describe these limiting behaviors by writing

$$
\lim _{x \rightarrow 0^{+}} \frac{1}{x}=+\infty \quad \text { and } \quad \lim _{x \rightarrow 0^{-}} \frac{1}{x}=-\infty
$$
