### 1.1.4 INFINITE LIMITS (AN INFORMAL VIEW) The expressions

$$
\lim _{x \rightarrow a^{-}} f(x)=+\infty \quad \text { and } \quad \lim _{x \rightarrow a^{+}} f(x)=+\infty
$$

denote that $f(x)$ increases without bound as $x$ approaches $a$ from the left and from the right, respectively. If both are true, then we write

$$
\lim _{x \rightarrow a} f(x)=+\infty
$$

Similarly, the expressions

$$
\lim _{x \rightarrow a^{-}} f(x)=-\infty \quad \text { and } \quad \lim _{x \rightarrow a^{+}} f(x)=-\infty
$$

denote that $f(x)$ decreases without bound as $x$ approaches $a$ from the left and from the right, respectively. If both are true, then we write

$$
\lim _{x \rightarrow a} f(x)=-\infty
$$

concepts.title: Infinite Limits (Informal View)
concepts.one_liner: The expressions $\lim _{x \rightarrow a^{-}} f(x)=+\infty$ and $\lim _{x \rightarrow a^{+}} f(x)=+\infty$ denote that $f(x)$ increases without bound as $x$ approaches $a$ from the left and from the right, respectively.
concepts.summary_md: The expressions $\lim _{x \rightarrow a^{-}} f(x)=+\infty$ and $\lim _{x \rightarrow a^{+}} f(x)=+\infty$ denote that $f(x)$ increases without bound as $x$ approaches $a$ from the left and from the right, respectively. If both are true, then we write $\lim _{x \rightarrow a} f(x)=+\infty$. Similarly, $\lim _{x \rightarrow a^{-}} f(x)=-\infty$ and $\lim _{x \rightarrow a^{+}} f(x)=-\infty$ denote that $f(x)$ decreases without bound.
concepts.motivation_md: This informal definition provides a concise notation to describe situations where a function's values grow or shrink indefinitely as the input approaches a specific point. It formalizes the concept of 'increasing/decreasing without bound,' which is crucial for understanding vertical asymptotes and the behavior of functions at singularities.
concepts.recap_md: - $\lim _{x \rightarrow a^{-}} f(x)=+\infty$ means $f(x)$ increases without bound as $x$ approaches $a$ from the left. - $\lim _{x \rightarrow a^{+}} f(x)=+\infty$ means $f(x)$ increases without bound as $x$ approaches $a$ from the right. - If both one-sided infinite limits are $+\infty$ (or $-\infty$), then the two-sided limit is also $+\infty$ (or $-\infty$).
concepts.raw_body:
### 1.1.4 INFINITE LIMITS (AN INFORMAL VIEW) The expressions

$$
\lim _{x \rightarrow a^{-}} f(x)=+\infty \quad \text { and } \quad \lim _{x \rightarrow a^{+}} f(x)=+\infty
$$

denote that $f(x)$ increases without bound as $x$ approaches $a$ from the left and from the right, respectively. If both are true, then we write

$$
\lim _{x \rightarrow a} f(x)=+\infty
$$

Similarly, the expressions

$$
\lim _{x \rightarrow a^{-}} f(x)=-\infty \quad \text { and } \quad \lim _{x \rightarrow a^{+}} f(x)=-\infty
$$

denote that $f(x)$ decreases without bound as $x$ approaches $a$ from the left and from the right, respectively. If both are true, then we write

$$
\lim _{x \rightarrow a} f(x)=-\infty
$$

concepts.title: Vertical Asymptotes
concepts.one_liner: The line $x=a$ is called a vertical asymptote of the curve $y=f(x)$ if the graph of $y=f(x)$ either rises or falls without bound, squeezing closer and closer to $x=a$.
concepts.summary_md: The line $x=a$ is called a vertical asymptote of the curve $y=f(x)$ if the graph of $y=f(x)$ either rises or falls without bound, squeezing closer and closer to the vertical line $x=a$ as $x$ approaches $a$ from the side indicated in the limit. This occurs when any of $\lim _{x \rightarrow a^{-}} f(x)=+\infty$, $\lim _{x \rightarrow a^{+}} f(x)=+\infty$, $\lim _{x \rightarrow a^{-}} f(x)=-\infty$, or $\lim _{x \rightarrow a^{+}} f(x)=-\infty$ are true.
concepts.motivation_md: Vertical asymptotes are crucial for understanding the global behavior of functions, especially rational functions, and for sketching their graphs accurately. They indicate points where a function's output becomes infinitely large or small, often corresponding to inputs where the function is undefined, such as division by zero.
concepts.recap_md: - A vertical line $x=a$ is a vertical asymptote if $f(x)$ approaches $\pm\infty$ as $x$ approaches $a$ from the left or right. - This means $\lim _{x \rightarrow a^{-}} f(x)=\pm\infty$ or $\lim _{x \rightarrow a^{+}} f(x)=\pm\infty$. - The graph of $y=f(x)$ gets arbitrarily close to the line $x=a$ but never touches it.
concepts.raw_body:
## VERTICAL ASYMPTOTES

Figure 1.1.17 illustrates geometrically what happens when any of the following situations occur:

$$
\lim _{x \rightarrow a^{-}} f(x)=+\infty, \quad \lim _{x \rightarrow a^{+}} f(x)=+\infty, \quad \lim _{x \rightarrow a^{-}} f(x)=-\infty, \quad \lim _{x \rightarrow a^{+}} f(x)=-\infty
$$

In each case the graph of $y=f(x)$ either rises or falls without bound, squeezing closer and closer to the vertical line $x=a$ as $x$ approaches $a$ from the side indicated in the limit. The line $x=a$ is called a vertical asymptote of the curve $y=f(x)$ (from the Greek word asymptotos, meaning "nonintersecting").

concepts.title: Computing Limits
concepts.one_liner: This section will discuss techniques for computing limits of many functions, based on the informal development of the limit concept.
concepts.summary_md: This section will discuss techniques for computing limits of many functions. These results are based on the informal development of the limit concept discussed in the preceding section. A more formal derivation of these results is possible after Section 1.4.
concepts.motivation_md: While the informal definition of a limit provides intuition, computing limits directly from it can be cumbersome. Learning algebraic techniques allows for efficient and precise calculation of limits for a wide range of functions, which is essential for further calculus topics like continuity and derivatives.
concepts.recap_md: - This section focuses on practical techniques for calculating limits. - The methods build upon the informal understanding of limits. - Formal proofs for these techniques will come later.
concepts.raw_body:
### 1.2 COMPUTING LIMITS

In this section we will discuss techniques for computing limits of many functions. We base these results on the informal development of the limit concept discussed in the preceding section. A more formal derivation of these results is possible after Section 1.4.

concepts.title: Some Basic Limits
concepts.one_liner: Our strategy for finding limits algebraically has two parts: first, obtaining limits of simple functions, then developing theorems to use them as building blocks.
concepts.summary_md: Our strategy for finding limits algebraically has two parts. First, we will obtain the limits of some simple functions. Then, we will develop a repertoire of theorems that will enable us to use the limits of those simple functions as building blocks for finding limits of more complicated functions.
concepts.motivation_md: Beginning with basic limits establishes foundational knowledge and simple cases that can be easily understood. These basic limits then serve as essential building blocks, allowing the development of more complex theorems and techniques to evaluate limits for a wider variety of functions systematically.
concepts.recap_md: - The strategy involves first finding limits of simple functions. - Then, theorems will be developed to use these simple limits as building blocks. - This approach allows for computing limits of more complex functions.
concepts.raw_body:
## SOME BASIC LIMITS

Our strategy for finding limits algebraically has two parts:

- First we will obtain the limits of some simple functions.
- Then we will develop a repertoire of theorems that will enable us to use the limits of those simple functions as building blocks for finding limits of more complicated functions.

concepts.title: Basic Limits
concepts.one_liner: The limits of a constant and of $x$ as $x$ approaches $a$ are $k$ and $a$ respectively, along with one-sided limits of $1/x$ as $x$ approaches 0.
concepts.summary_md: Theorem 1.2.1 states that for any real numbers $a$ and $k$: $\lim _{x \rightarrow a} k=k$ and $\lim _{x \rightarrow a} x=a$. It also defines one-sided limits for $1/x$ as $x$ approaches 0: $\lim _{x \rightarrow 0^{-}} \frac{1}{x}=-\infty$ and $\lim _{x \rightarrow 0^{+}} \frac{1}{x}=+\infty$.
concepts.motivation_md: These basic limits serve as the building blocks for evaluating more complex limits. They establish the fundamental behavior of constant and identity functions, and the inverse function near zero, which are crucial for applying limit properties.
concepts.recap_md: - The limit of a constant function is the constant itself: $\lim _{x \rightarrow a} k=k$. - The limit of $x$ as $x$ approaches $a$ is $a$: $\lim _{x \rightarrow a} x=a$. - One-sided limits of $1/x$ as $x \rightarrow 0$ are $\pm\infty$.
concepts.raw_body:
### 1.2.1 Theorem Let $a$ and $k$ be real numbers.

(a) $\lim _{x \rightarrow a} k=k$
(b) $\lim _{x \rightarrow a} x=a$
(c) $\lim _{x \rightarrow 0^{-}} \frac{1}{x}=-\infty$
(d) $\lim _{x \rightarrow 0^{+}} \frac{1}{x}=+\infty$

concepts.title: Properties of Limits
concepts.one_liner: The limit of a sum is the sum of the limits, the limit of a difference is the difference of the limits, the limit of a product is the product of the limits, and the limit of a quotient is the quotient of the limits, provided the limit of the denominator is not zero.
concepts.summary_md: Theorem 1.2.2 states that if $\lim _{x \rightarrow a} f(x)=L_{1}$ and $\lim _{x \rightarrow a} g(x)=L_{2}$ exist, then limits of sums, differences, products, and quotients (if $L_2 \neq 0$) can be found by performing the operation on the individual limits. For example, $\lim _{x \rightarrow a}[f(x)+g(x)]=L_{1}+L_{2}$. The theorem also applies to the limit of an $n$th root, $\lim _{x \rightarrow a} \sqrt[n]{f(x)}=\sqrt[n]{L_{1}}$, with conditions for even $n$.
concepts.motivation_md: These properties allow us to break down complex limit problems into simpler ones. Instead of evaluating a limit for an entire expression, we can evaluate limits for individual components and then combine them using these rules, simplifying the calculation process.
concepts.recap_md: - The limit of a sum, difference, product, or quotient (denominator non-zero) of functions is the sum, difference, product, or quotient of their individual limits. - The limit of an $n$th root of a function is the $n$th root of its limit, with conditions for even roots. - These properties also hold for one-sided limits.
concepts.raw_body:
1.2.2 THEOREM Let a be a real number, and suppose that

$$
\lim _{x \rightarrow a} f(x)=L_{1} \quad \text { and } \quad \lim _{x \rightarrow a} g(x)=L_{2}
$$

That is, the limits exist and have values $L_{1}$ and $L_{2}$, respectively. Then:
(a) $\lim _{x \rightarrow a}[f(x)+g(x)]=\lim _{x \rightarrow a} f(x)+\lim _{x \rightarrow a} g(x)=L_{1}+L_{2}$
(b) $\lim _{x \rightarrow a}[f(x)-g(x)]=\lim _{x \rightarrow a} f(x)-\lim _{x \rightarrow a} g(x)=L_{1}-L_{2}$
(c) $\lim _{x \rightarrow a}[f(x) g(x)]=\left(\lim _{x \rightarrow a} f(x)\right)\left(\lim _{x \rightarrow a} g(x)\right)=L_{1} L_{2}$
(d) $\lim _{x \rightarrow a} \frac{f(x)}{g(x)}=\frac{\lim _{x \rightarrow a} f(x)}{\lim _{x \rightarrow a} g(x)}=\frac{L_{1}}{L_{2}}, \quad$ provided $L_{2} \neq 0$
(e) $\lim _{x \rightarrow a} \sqrt[n]{f(x)}=\sqrt[n]{\lim _{x \rightarrow a} f(x)}=\sqrt[n]{L_{1}}$, provided $L_{1}>0$ if $n$ is even.

Moreover, these statements are also true for the one-sided limits as $x \rightarrow a^{-}$or as $x \rightarrow a^{+}$.

This theorem can be stated informally as follows:
(a) The limit of a sum is the sum of the limits.
(b) The limit of a difference is the difference of the limits.
(c) The limit of a product is the product of the limits.
(d) The limit of a quotient is the quotient of the limits, provided the limit of the denominator is not zero.
(e) The limit of an $n$th root is the $n$th root of the limit.

concepts.title: Limits of Polynomials and Rational Functions
concepts.one_liner: This section discusses the evaluation of limits for polynomial and rational functions as $x$ approaches a specific value $a$.
concepts.summary_md: This concept introduces the specific methods and theorems used to evaluate limits of polynomial and rational functions as the variable $x$ approaches a real number $a$. It sets the stage for understanding how to apply general limit properties to these common function types.
concepts.motivation_md: Polynomials and rational functions are fundamental in calculus. Understanding how to find their limits as $x \rightarrow a$ is crucial because these functions appear frequently in applications and form the basis for more advanced topics like continuity and derivatives.
concepts.recap_md: - Focuses on evaluating limits for polynomial functions. - Focuses on evaluating limits for rational functions. - Applies when $x$ approaches a specific real number $a$.
concepts.raw_body: ## LIMITS OF POLYNOMIALS AND RATIONAL FUNCTIONS AS $\boldsymbol{x} \rightarrow \boldsymbol{a}$

concepts.title: Limit of a Polynomial
concepts.one_liner: For any polynomial $p(x)$ and any real number $a$, $\lim _{x \rightarrow a} p(x)=p(a)$.
concepts.summary_md: Theorem 1.2.3 states that to find the limit of a polynomial function $p(x)=c_{0}+c_{1} x+\cdots+c_{n} x^{n}$ as $x$ approaches a real number $a$, one can simply substitute $a$ into the polynomial. That is, $\lim _{x \rightarrow a} p(x)=c_{0}+c_{1} a+\cdots+c_{n} a^{n}=p(a)$.
concepts.motivation_md: This theorem provides a straightforward method for evaluating limits of polynomials. It simplifies the process by allowing direct substitution, which is a direct consequence of polynomials being continuous functions, making limit calculations much easier.
concepts.recap_md: - For a polynomial $p(x)$, $\lim _{x \rightarrow a} p(x)$ is found by direct substitution. - The limit value is simply $p(a)$.
concepts.raw_body:
### 1.2.3 THEOREM For any polynomial

$$
p(x)=c_{0}+c_{1} x+\cdots+c_{n} x^{n}
$$

and any real number $a$,

$$
\lim _{x \rightarrow a} p(x)=c_{0}+c_{1} a+\cdots+c_{n} a^{n}=p(a)
$$

concepts.title: Limits of Rational Functions with Zero Denominator
concepts.one_liner: The method of Theorem 1.2.2(d) is not applicable for rational functions where the limit of the denominator is zero.
concepts.summary_md: When evaluating limits of rational functions, if the limit of the denominator is zero, Theorem 1.2.2(d) cannot be used. This situation leads to two main cases: either the limit of the numerator is not zero, or both the numerator and denominator limits are zero. If the denominator limit is zero but the numerator limit is not, the limit of the rational function does not exist, potentially resulting in limits of $-\infty$, $+\infty$, or different infinities from each side.
concepts.motivation_md: Understanding these cases is crucial because direct substitution fails when the denominator approaches zero. This concept highlights scenarios where limits might not exist or might tend towards infinity, requiring different analytical techniques beyond simple algebraic properties.
concepts.recap_md: - Theorem 1.2.2(d) is invalid if the denominator's limit is zero. - If the denominator limit is zero but the numerator limit is not, the rational function's limit does not exist. - Such limits can be $-\infty$, $+\infty$, or different infinities from each side.
concepts.raw_body:
The method used in the last example will not work for rational functions in which the limit of the denominator is zero because Theorem 1.2.2(d) is not applicable. There are two cases of this type to be considered-the case where the limit of the denominator is zero and the limit of the numerator is not, and the case where the limits of the numerator and denominator are both zero. If the limit of the denominator is zero but the limit of the numerator is not, then one can prove that the limit of the rational function does not exist and that one of the following situations occurs:

- The limit may be $-\infty$ from one side and $+\infty$ from the other.
- The limit may be $+\infty$.
- The limit may be $-\infty$.

concepts.title: Computing Limits by Canceling Common Factors
concepts.one_liner: When $p(a)=0$ and $q(a)=0$ for a rational function $p(x)/q(x)$, the limit as $x \rightarrow a$ can be found by canceling common factors of $x-a$.
concepts.summary_md: For a rational function $p(x)/q(x)$ where both $p(a)=0$ and $q(a)=0$, the numerator and denominator must share one or more common factors of $(x-a)$. In such cases, the limit of $p(x)/q(x)$ as $x \rightarrow a$ can be determined by algebraically canceling all common factors of $(x-a)$ and then evaluating the limit of the resulting simplified function using previously learned methods.
concepts.motivation_md: This technique provides a way to resolve indeterminate forms of type $0/0$ for rational functions. By canceling common factors, we remove the discontinuity at $x=a$, allowing us to evaluate the limit, which often corresponds to a 'hole' in the graph rather than an asymptote.
concepts.recap_md: - Applicable when $p(a)=0$ and $q(a)=0$ for $p(x)/q(x)$. - Factor out and cancel common factors of $(x-a)$ from numerator and denominator. - Evaluate the limit of the simplified rational function.
concepts.raw_body: In the case where $p(x) / q(x)$ is a rational function for which $p(a)=0$ and $q(a)=0$, the numerator and denominator must have one or more common factors of $x-a$. In this case the limit of $p(x) / q(x)$ as $x \rightarrow a$ can be found by canceling all common factors of $x-a$ and using one of the methods already considered to find the limit of the simplified function. Here is an example.

concepts.title: Indeterminate Form of Type 0/0
concepts.one_liner: A quotient $f(x) / g(x)$ in which the numerator and denominator both have a limit of zero as $x \rightarrow a$ is called an indeterminate form of type $\mathbf{0} / \mathbf{0}$.
concepts.summary_md: An indeterminate form of type $\mathbf{0} / \mathbf{0}$ occurs when evaluating a limit of a quotient $f(x) / g(x)$ as $x \rightarrow a$, and both $\lim _{x \rightarrow a} f(x)=0$ and $\lim _{x \rightarrow a} g(x)=0$. This form is 'indeterminate' because it's difficult to predict the limit's existence or value by inspection, as two conflicting influences (numerator tending to zero, denominator tending to zero) are at play.
concepts.motivation_md: Recognizing an indeterminate form of type $0/0$ is crucial because it signals that direct substitution or simple limit properties are insufficient. It indicates that further algebraic manipulation or advanced techniques (like L'Hôpital's Rule later on) are required to determine the true behavior of the function near the point.
concepts.recap_md: - Occurs when $\lim f(x)=0$ and $\lim g(x)=0$ for a quotient $f(x)/g(x)$. - The limit's value cannot be determined by simple inspection due to conflicting tendencies. - Requires further algebraic or analytical techniques to evaluate.
concepts.raw_body: A quotient $f(x) / g(x)$ in which the numerator and denominator both have a limit of zero as $x \rightarrow a$ is called an indeterminate form of type $\mathbf{0} / \mathbf{0}$. The problem with such limits is that it is difficult to tell by inspection whether the limit exists, and, if so, its value. Informally stated, this is because there are two conflicting influences at work. The value of $f(x) / g(x)$ would tend to zero as $f(x)$ approached zero if $g(x)$ were to remain at some fixed nonzero value, whereas the value of this ratio would tend to increase or decrease without bound as $g(x)$ approached zero if $f(x)$ were to remain at some fixed nonzero value. But with both $f(x)$ and $g(x)$ approaching zero, the behavior of the ratio depends on precisely how these conflicting tendencies offset one another for the particular $f$ and $g$.

concepts.title: Limits of Rational Functions
concepts.one_liner: For a rational function $f(x)=p(x)/q(x)$, if $q(a) \neq 0$, then $\lim _{x \rightarrow a} f(x)=f(a)$.
concepts.summary_md: Theorem 1.2.4 provides rules for evaluating limits of rational functions $f(x)=p(x)/q(x)$ as $x \rightarrow a$. If the denominator $q(a) \neq 0$, then the limit can be found by direct substitution, so $\lim _{x \rightarrow a} f(x)=f(a)$. However, if $q(a)=0$ but $p(a) \neq 0$, then the limit $\lim _{x \rightarrow a} f(x)$ does not exist.
concepts.motivation_md: This theorem consolidates the primary cases for evaluating limits of rational functions. It clarifies when direct substitution is valid and when a limit will definitively not exist, guiding students on when to apply different techniques or conclude non-existence without further calculation.
concepts.recap_md: - If $q(a) \neq 0$, the limit of a rational function $p(x)/q(x)$ as $x \rightarrow a$ is $f(a)$ (direct substitution). - If $q(a)=0$ but $p(a) \neq 0$, the limit of the rational function as $x \rightarrow a$ does not exist.
concepts.raw_body:
### 1.2.4 THEOREM Let

$$
f(x)=\frac{p(x)}{q(x)}
$$

be a rational function, and let a be any real number.
(a) If $q(a) \neq 0$, then $\lim _{x \rightarrow a} f(x)=f(a)$.
(b) If $q(a)=0$ but $p(a) \neq 0$, then $\lim _{x \rightarrow a} f(x)$ does not exist.

concepts.title: Limits Involving Radicals
concepts.one_liner: Limits Involving Radicals
concepts.summary_md: When evaluating limits that involve radical expressions, algebraic techniques such as rationalizing the numerator or denominator can often simplify the expression, making it possible to apply limit laws or direct substitution.
concepts.motivation_md: Radical expressions can sometimes lead to indeterminate forms (like 0/0 or infinity/infinity) when evaluating limits directly. Special algebraic techniques are needed to transform these expressions into a form where the limit can be found.
concepts.recap_md: - Use algebraic manipulation to simplify expressions with radicals before evaluating the limit. - Rationalizing the numerator or denominator by multiplying by the conjugate is a common technique. - This helps to eliminate indeterminate forms and apply standard limit properties.
concepts.raw_body: ## LIMITS INVOLVING RADICALS

concepts.title: Limits of Piecewise-Defined Functions
concepts.one_liner: Limits of Piecewise-Defined Functions
concepts.summary_md: To find the limit of a piecewise-defined function as $x$ approaches a point, it is crucial to consider the function's definition on each side of that point. This often involves evaluating one-sided limits.
concepts.motivation_md: Piecewise functions behave differently across their domain, especially at the points where their definition changes. Understanding limits for these functions is essential for determining continuity and differentiability at these critical points.
concepts.recap_md: - To evaluate a limit at a point where the function definition changes, compute the left-hand and right-hand limits. - If the left-hand and right-hand limits are equal, the overall limit exists. - If the limit is at a point within a single piece's domain, evaluate it using that piece's definition.
concepts.raw_body: ## LIMITS OF PIECEWISE-DEFINED FUNCTIONS

concepts.title: Introduction to Limits at Infinity and End Behavior
concepts.one_liner: We will be concerned with the behavior of $f(x)$ as $x$ increases or decreases without bound.
concepts.summary_md: This section introduces limits that describe the behavior of a function $f(x)$ as $x$ increases without bound ($x \rightarrow+\infty$) or decreases without bound ($x \rightarrow-\infty$). This behavior is sometimes called the end behavior of the function.
concepts.motivation_md: Up to now we have been concerned with limits that describe the behavior of a function $f(x)$ as $x$ approaches some real number $a$. Now, we extend this concept to understand how functions behave at the extreme ends of their domain.
concepts.recap_md: - Limits at infinity describe function behavior as $x$ gets very large positively or negatively. - $x \rightarrow+\infty$ means $x$ increases without bound. - $x \rightarrow-\infty$ means $x$ decreases without bound.
concepts.raw_body:
Up to now we have been concerned with limits that describe the behavior of a function $f(x)$ as $x$ approaches some real number $a$. In this section we will be concerned with the behavior of $f(x)$ as $x$ increases or decreases without bound.

## LIMITS AT INFINITY AND HORIZONTAL ASYMPTOTES

If the values of a variable $x$ increase without bound, then we write $x \rightarrow+\infty$, and if the values of $x$ decrease without bound, then we write $x \rightarrow-\infty$. The behavior of a function $f(x)$ as $x$ increases without bound or decreases without bound is sometimes called the end behavior of the function. For example,
concepts.section_title: LIMITS AT INFINITY; END BEHAVIOR OF A FUNCTION

concepts.title: Limits at Infinity (Informal View)
concepts.one_liner: If the values of $f(x)$ eventually get as close as we like to a number $L$ as $x$ increases without bound, then we write $\lim _{x \rightarrow+\infty} f(x)=L$.
concepts.summary_md: If the values of $f(x)$ eventually get as close as we like to a number $L$ as $x$ increases without bound, we write $\lim _{x \rightarrow+\infty} f(x)=L$. Similarly, if $f(x)$ approaches $L$ as $x$ decreases without bound, we write $\lim _{x \rightarrow-\infty} f(x)=L$.
concepts.motivation_md: This informal definition provides a foundational understanding for describing the long-term behavior of functions. It allows us to precisely state when a function's output stabilizes around a specific value as its input grows or shrinks indefinitely.
concepts.recap_md: - $\lim _{x \rightarrow+\infty} f(x)=L$ means $f(x)$ approaches $L$ as $x$ increases indefinitely. - $\lim _{x \rightarrow-\infty} f(x)=L$ means $f(x)$ approaches $L$ as $x$ decreases indefinitely. - Both describe the function's output getting arbitrarily close to $L$.
concepts.section_title: LIMITS AT INFINITY; END BEHAVIOR OF A FUNCTION

concepts.title: Horizontal Asymptote
concepts.one_liner: If either limit holds, we call the line $y=L$ a horizontal asymptote for the graph of $f$.
concepts.summary_md: If $\lim _{x \rightarrow+\infty} f(x)=L$ or $\lim _{x \rightarrow-\infty} f(x)=L$, the graph of $f$ eventually comes as close as we like to the line $y=L$. In such cases, the line $y=L$ is defined as a horizontal asymptote for the graph of $f$.
concepts.motivation_md: Horizontal asymptotes provide critical information about the end behavior of a function's graph. They help visualize how a function's values stabilize or approach a constant as the input becomes extremely large or small.
concepts.recap_md: - A horizontal asymptote is a line $y=L$ that the graph of $f$ approaches. - This occurs if $\lim _{x \rightarrow+\infty} f(x)=L$. - It also occurs if $\lim _{x \rightarrow-\infty} f(x)=L$.
concepts.raw_body: In the first case the graph of $f$ eventually comes as close as we like to the line $y=L$ as $x$ increases without bound, and in the second case it eventually comes as close as we like to the line $y=L$ as $x$ decreases without bound. If either limit holds, we call the line $y=L$ a horizontal asymptote for the graph of $f$.
concepts.section_title: LIMITS AT INFINITY; END BEHAVIOR OF A FUNCTION

concepts.title: Limit Laws for Limits at Infinity
concepts.one_liner: The limit laws in Theorem 1.2.2 carry over without change to limits at $+\infty$ and $-\infty$.
concepts.summary_md: The standard limit laws apply to limits at $+\infty$ and $-\infty$. Specifically, for a positive integer $n$, $\lim _{x \rightarrow\pm\infty}(f(x))^{n}=\left(\lim _{x \rightarrow\pm\infty} f(x)\right)^{n}$. Constants can be moved through the limit symbol, $\lim _{x \rightarrow\pm\infty} k f(x)=k \lim _{x \rightarrow\pm\infty} f(x)$. For a constant function $f(x)=k$, $\lim _{x \rightarrow\pm\infty} k=k$.
concepts.motivation_md: These laws simplify the process of evaluating limits of complex functions at infinity. By breaking down complicated expressions into simpler parts, we can apply known rules to find the overall limit, making calculations more manageable.
concepts.recap_md: - Basic limit laws from Theorem 1.2.2 apply to limits at infinity. - The power rule states $\lim _{x \rightarrow\pm\infty}(f(x))^{n}=\left(\lim _{x \rightarrow\pm\infty} f(x)\right)^{n}$. - Constants can be factored out: $\lim _{x \rightarrow\pm\infty} k f(x)=k \lim _{x \rightarrow\pm\infty} f(x)$. - The limit of a constant function is the constant itself: $\lim _{x \rightarrow\pm\infty} k=k$.
concepts.section_title: LIMITS AT INFINITY; END BEHAVIOR OF A FUNCTION

concepts.title: Infinite Limits at Infinity (Informal View)
concepts.one_liner: If the values of $f(x)$ increase without bound as $x \rightarrow+\infty$ or as $x \rightarrow-\infty$, then we write $\lim _{x \rightarrow+\infty} f(x)=+\infty$ or $\lim _{x \rightarrow-\infty} f(x)=+\infty$ as appropriate.
concepts.summary_md: Infinite limits at infinity describe situations where $f(x)$ increases or decreases without bound as $x$ approaches $+\infty$ or $-\infty$. We write $\lim _{x \rightarrow+\infty} f(x)=+\infty$ or $\lim _{x \rightarrow-\infty} f(x)=+\infty$ if $f(x)$ increases without bound. If $f(x)$ decreases without bound, we write $\lim _{x \rightarrow+\infty} f(x)=-\infty$ or $\lim _{x \rightarrow-\infty} f(x)=-\infty$.
concepts.motivation_md: This notation allows us to describe the end behavior of functions that do not approach a finite number but instead grow or shrink indefinitely. It's crucial for understanding the overall shape and behavior of graphs, especially for polynomials and rational functions.
concepts.recap_md: - $\lim _{x \rightarrow+\infty} f(x)=+\infty$ means $f(x)$ grows indefinitely as $x$ grows indefinitely. - $\lim _{x \rightarrow-\infty} f(x)=+\infty$ means $f(x)$ grows indefinitely as $x$ shrinks indefinitely. - $\lim _{x \rightarrow+\infty} f(x)=-\infty$ means $f(x)$ shrinks indefinitely as $x$ grows indefinitely. - $\lim _{x \rightarrow-\infty} f(x)=-\infty$ means $f(x)$ shrinks indefinitely as $x$ shrinks indefinitely.
concepts.raw_body:
Limits at infinity, like limits at a real number $a$, can fail to exist for various reasons. One such possibility is that the values of $f(x)$ increase or decrease without bound as $x \rightarrow+\infty$ or as $x \rightarrow-\infty$. We will use the following notation to describe this situation.
1.3.2 INFINITE LIMITS AT INFINITY (AN INFORMAL VIEW) If the values of $f(x)$ increase without bound as $x \rightarrow+\infty$ or as $x \rightarrow-\infty$, then we write

$$
\lim _{x \rightarrow+\infty} f(x)=+\infty \quad \text { or } \quad \lim _{x \rightarrow-\infty} f(x)=+\infty
$$

as appropriate; and if the values of $f(x)$ decrease without bound as $x \rightarrow+\infty$ or as $x \rightarrow-\infty$, then we write

$$
\lim _{x \rightarrow+\infty} f(x)=-\infty \quad \text { or } \quad \lim _{x \rightarrow-\infty} f(x)=-\infty
$$

as appropriate.
concepts.section_title: LIMITS AT INFINITY; END BEHAVIOR OF A FUNCTION

concepts.title: Limits of x^n as x approaches infinity
concepts.one_liner: The end behavior of polynomials $x^{n}$ for $n=1,2,3, \ldots$ are special cases of general results for limits at infinity.
concepts.summary_md: For positive integers $n$, the limits of $x^n$ as $x$ approaches infinity are given by: $\lim _{x \rightarrow+\infty} x^{n}=+\infty$. For $x \rightarrow-\infty$, $\lim _{x \rightarrow-\infty} x^{n}=-\infty$ if $n$ is odd ($n=1,3,5, \ldots$), and $\lim _{x \rightarrow-\infty} x^{n}=+\infty$ if $n$ is even ($n=2,4,6, \ldots$).
concepts.motivation_md: These fundamental limits for power functions ($x^n$) serve as building blocks for evaluating limits of more complex polynomial and rational functions at infinity. Understanding these basic cases is crucial for analyzing end behavior.
concepts.recap_md: - As $x \rightarrow+\infty$, $x^n \rightarrow+\infty$ for any positive integer $n$. - As $x \rightarrow-\infty$, $x^n \rightarrow-\infty$ if $n$ is odd. - As $x \rightarrow-\infty$, $x^n \rightarrow+\infty$ if $n$ is even.
concepts.section_title: LIMITS AT INFINITY; END BEHAVIOR OF A FUNCTION

concepts.title: End Behavior of Polynomials Principle
concepts.one_liner: The end behavior of a polynomial matches the end behavior of its highest degree term.
concepts.summary_md: The end behavior of a polynomial matches the end behavior of its highest degree term. This is a useful principle about polynomials, expressed informally.
concepts.motivation_md: This principle simplifies the analysis of polynomial behavior as x approaches infinity. Instead of evaluating the entire polynomial, one only needs to consider the dominant term, making limit calculations much more straightforward.
concepts.recap_md: - The end behavior of a polynomial is determined by its highest degree term.- This principle simplifies analyzing polynomial limits at infinity.
concepts.raw_body:
There is a useful principle about polynomials which, expressed informally, states:

The end behavior of a polynomial matches the end behavior of its highest degree term.
concepts.section_title: LIMITS AT INFINITY; END BEHAVIOR OF A FUNCTION

concepts.title: Limits of Polynomials at Infinity
concepts.one_liner: If $c_{n} \neq 0$, then the limit of a polynomial as $x \rightarrow \pm\infty$ equals the limit of its highest degree term $c_n x^n$ as $x \rightarrow \pm\infty$.
concepts.summary_md: More precisely, if $c_{n} \neq 0$, then the limit of a polynomial $(c_{0}+c_{1} x+\cdots+c_{n} x^{n})$ as $x \rightarrow-\infty$ is equal to the limit of its highest degree term $c_{n} x^{n}$ as $x \rightarrow-\infty$. The same holds true for limits as $x \rightarrow+\infty$.
concepts.motivation_md: This theorem provides a formal mathematical statement for the informal "End Behavior of Polynomials Principle." It allows for rigorous calculation of limits of polynomials at infinity by simplifying the expression to only consider the highest degree term.
concepts.recap_md: - For a polynomial, $\lim _{x \rightarrow-\infty}\left(c_{0}+\cdots+c_{n} x^{n}\right) = \lim _{x \rightarrow-\infty} c_{n} x^{n}$.- Similarly, $\lim _{x \rightarrow+\infty}\left(c_{0}+\cdots+c_{n} x^{n}\right) = \lim _{x \rightarrow+\infty} c_{n} x^{n}$.- This applies when $c_n \neq 0$.
concepts.section_title: LIMITS AT INFINITY; END BEHAVIOR OF A FUNCTION

concepts.title: Computing Limits of Rational Functions by Division
concepts.one_liner: One technique for determining the end behavior of a rational function is to divide each term in the numerator and denominator by the highest power of $x$ that occurs in the denominator.
concepts.summary_md: To determine the end behavior of a rational function, a technique involves dividing every term in both the numerator and the denominator by the highest power of $x$ found in the denominator. This process simplifies the expression, allowing the limiting behavior to be determined using previously established results.
concepts.motivation_md: This technique transforms complex rational functions into a form where individual terms approach zero or a constant as x approaches infinity. This simplifies the limit calculation, making it easier to apply known limit properties to find the overall end behavior.
concepts.recap_md: - Divide all terms in the numerator and denominator by the highest power of $x$ in the denominator.- This simplifies the rational function, making its limiting behavior easier to determine.
concepts.raw_body: One technique for determining the end behavior of a rational function is to divide each term in the numerator and denominator by the highest power of $x$ that occurs in the denominator, after which the limiting behavior can be determined using results we have already established. Here are some examples.
concepts.section_title: LIMITS AT INFINITY; END BEHAVIOR OF A FUNCTION

concepts.title: Quick Method for Limits of Rational Functions at Infinity
concepts.one_liner: The end behavior of a rational function matches the end behavior of the quotient of the highest degree term in the numerator divided by the highest degree term in the denominator.
concepts.summary_md: Building on the principle that a polynomial's end behavior is determined by its highest degree term, a quick method for rational functions concludes that their end behavior matches the end behavior of the quotient formed by dividing the highest degree term of the numerator by that of the denominator.
concepts.motivation_md: This "quick method" provides a shortcut for finding limits of rational functions at infinity, bypassing the more involved division technique. It leverages the dominance of highest degree terms in both numerator and denominator to rapidly determine the function's end behavior.
concepts.recap_md: - Identify the highest degree term in the numerator and the denominator.- The rational function's end behavior is the same as the limit of the ratio of these two highest degree terms.
concepts.raw_body:
Since the end behavior of a polynomial matches the end behavior of its highest degree term, one can reasonably conclude:

The end behavior of a rational function matches the end behavior of the quotient of the highest degree term in the numerator divided by the highest degree term in the denominator.
concepts.section_title: LIMITS AT INFINITY; END BEHAVIOR OF A FUNCTION

concepts.title: End Behavior of Trigonometric, Exponential, and Logarithmic Functions
concepts.one_liner: Trigonometric functions generally fail to have limits as $x \rightarrow \pm\infty$ due to periodicity, while exponential and logarithmic functions have specific, well-defined end behaviors.
concepts.summary_md: Trigonometric functions like $f(x)=\sin x$ do not have limits as $x \rightarrow \pm\infty$ because their values oscillate without approaching a specific number. In contrast, exponential functions like $e^x$ and logarithmic functions like $\ln x$ have defined end behaviors. For example, $\lim _{x \rightarrow+\infty} e^{x}=+\infty$ and $\lim _{x \rightarrow-\infty} e^{x}=0$. Also, $\lim _{x \rightarrow+\infty} \ln x=+\infty$ and $\lim _{x \rightarrow 0^{+}} \ln x=-\infty$.
concepts.motivation_md: Understanding the end behavior of these fundamental functions is crucial for analyzing more complex functions involving them. It helps predict long-term trends, identify asymptotes, and solve problems in various scientific and engineering applications where these functions model real-world phenomena.
concepts.recap_md: - Trigonometric functions typically do not have limits at $\pm\infty$ due to their periodic nature.- Exponential functions have distinct end behaviors: $\lim _{x \rightarrow+\infty} e^{x}=+\infty$ and $\lim _{x \rightarrow-\infty} e^{x}=0$.- Logarithmic functions also have specific limits, such as $\lim _{x \rightarrow+\infty} \ln x=+\infty$ and $\lim _{x \rightarrow 0^{+}} \ln x=-\infty$.
concepts.section_title: LIMITS AT INFINITY; END BEHAVIOR OF A FUNCTION

concepts.title: Asymptotic Curves
concepts.one_liner: Curves $y=f(x)$ and $y=g(x)$ are asymptotic as $x \rightarrow+\infty$ if $\lim _{x \rightarrow+\infty}[f(x)-g(x)]=0$, and similarly for $x \rightarrow-\infty$.
concepts.summary_md: The concept of an asymptote can be broadened beyond lines to include curves. Two curves, $y=f(x)$ and $y=g(x)$, are defined as asymptotic as $x \rightarrow+\infty$ if the limit of their difference, $\lim _{x \rightarrow+\infty}[f(x)-g(x)]$, equals zero. The same definition applies for curves asymptotic as $x \rightarrow-\infty$.
concepts.motivation_md: This extended definition of asymptotes allows for a more nuanced description of how functions behave at their extremes. It helps identify complex relationships where one curve approaches another curve, not just a straight line, providing a powerful tool for analyzing function behavior.
concepts.recap_md: - Asymptotic curves extend the idea of asymptotes beyond just lines.- Two curves $y=f(x)$ and $y=g(x)$ are asymptotic as $x \rightarrow+\infty$ if $\lim _{x \rightarrow+\infty}[f(x)-g(x)]=0$.- The same condition applies for $x \rightarrow-\infty$.
concepts.raw_body:
69-73 The notion of an asymptote can be extended to include curves as well as lines. Specifically, we say that curves $y=f(x)$ and $y=g(x)$ are asymptotic as $\boldsymbol{x} \rightarrow+\infty$ provided

$$
\lim _{x \rightarrow+\infty}[f(x)-g(x)]=0
$$

and are asymptotic as $\boldsymbol{x} \rightarrow-\infty$ provided

$$
\lim _{x \rightarrow-\infty}[f(x)-g(x)]=0
$$
concepts.section_title: LIMITS AT INFINITY; END BEHAVIOR OF A FUNCTION

concepts.title: Limits (Discussed More Rigorously)
concepts.one_liner: This section provides a more rigorous discussion of limits.
concepts.summary_md: This section, titled 'LIMITS (DISCUSSED MORE RIGOROUSLY)', indicates a deeper and more formal exploration of the concept of limits, moving beyond informal definitions.
concepts.motivation_md: An informal understanding of limits is useful for intuition, but a rigorous definition is essential for proving theorems and handling more complex cases where intuition might fail. This rigorous discussion lays the groundwork for advanced calculus concepts.
concepts.recap_md: - This section introduces a formal, rigorous treatment of limits.- It builds upon previous informal discussions of limits.
concepts.raw_body: ### 1.4 LIMITS (DISCUSSED MORE RIGOROUSLY)

concepts.title: Motivation for the Definition of a Two-Sided Limit
concepts.one_liner: This section provides the motivation for the formal definition of a two-sided limit.
concepts.summary_md: This section focuses on the 'MOTIVATION FOR THE DEFINITION OF A TWO-SIDED LIMIT', aiming to explain the rationale and necessity behind its formal mathematical construction.
concepts.motivation_md: Understanding the motivation behind the formal definition of a two-sided limit helps students grasp *why* it's defined the way it is. It addresses the need for a precise way to describe a function's behavior as it approaches a point from both sides, which is fundamental to continuity and differentiability.
concepts.recap_md: - This section explains the reasons for defining a two-sided limit.- It highlights the importance of a formal definition for understanding limits.
concepts.raw_body: ## MOTIVATION FOR THE DEFINITION OF A TWO-SIDED LIMIT

concepts.title: Epsilon-Delta Definition of a Two-Sided Limit
concepts.one_liner: We will write $\lim _{x \rightarrow a} f(x)=L$ if given any number $\epsilon>0$ we can find a number $\delta>0$ such that $|f(x)-L|<\epsilon \quad \text { if } \quad 0<|x-a|<\delta$.
concepts.summary_md: Let $f(x)$ be defined for all $x$ in some open interval containing the number $a$, with the possible exception that $f(x)$ need not be defined at $a$. We write $\lim _{x \rightarrow a} f(x)=L$ if given any number $\epsilon>0$, we can find a number $\delta>0$ such that $|f(x)-L|<\epsilon$ whenever $0<|x-a|<\delta$.
concepts.motivation_md: This definition provides a precise and unambiguous way to define the intuitive idea of a limit. It allows mathematicians to formally prove properties of limits and build the foundations of calculus without relying on vague graphical or numerical approximations.
concepts.recap_md: - The limit $\lim _{x \rightarrow a} f(x)=L$ means $f(x)$ gets arbitrarily close to $L$ as $x$ gets arbitrarily close to $a$ (but not equal to $a$).- For any $\epsilon>0$ (how close $f(x)$ must be to $L$), there must exist a $\delta>0$ (how close $x$ must be to $a$).- The condition is $|f(x)-L|<\epsilon$ whenever $0<|x-a|<\delta$.
concepts.raw_body:
1.4.1 LIMIT DEFINITION Let $f(x)$ be defined for all $x$ in some open interval containing the number $a$, with the possible exception that $f(x)$ need not be defined at $a$. We will write

$$
\lim _{x \rightarrow a} f(x)=L
$$

if given any number $\epsilon>0$ we can find a number $\delta>0$ such that

$$
|f(x)-L|<\epsilon \quad \text { if } \quad 0<|x-a|<\delta
$$

concepts.title: General Form of an Epsilon-Delta Limit Proof
concepts.one_liner: This example illustrates the general form of a limit proof: We assume that we are given a positive number $\epsilon$, and we try to prove that we can find a positive number $\delta$ such that $|f(x)-L|<\epsilon \text { if } 0<|x-a|<\delta$.
concepts.summary_md: The general form of a limit proof involves assuming a positive number $\epsilon$ is given, and then proving that a positive number $\delta$ can be found such that $|f(x)-L|<\epsilon$ if $0<|x-a|<\delta$. This is achieved by first discovering $\delta$, often expressed as a function of $\epsilon$, and then formally proving that the discovered $\delta$ works.
concepts.motivation_md: This concept provides a structured approach to constructing rigorous limit proofs using the epsilon-delta definition. It outlines the steps and logical flow required to formally demonstrate that a limit exists, moving beyond intuitive understanding to a precise mathematical argument.
concepts.recap_md: - A limit proof begins by assuming an arbitrary positive $\epsilon$ is given.- The goal is to find a positive $\delta$ (typically in terms of $\epsilon$) that satisfies the limit condition.- The proof involves two main steps: discovering $\delta$ through algebraic manipulation, then formally showing it works.
aliases: How to write an epsilon-delta proof

concepts.title: The Value of Delta is Not Unique
concepts.one_liner: The value of $\delta$ in the epsilon-delta definition is not unique.
concepts.summary_md: The value of $\delta$ found for a given $\epsilon$ in the epsilon-delta definition of a limit is not unique. If a particular $\delta$ works to satisfy the limit condition, then any smaller positive $\delta'$ will also work, as it imposes an even stricter condition on how close $x$ must be to $a$.
concepts.motivation_md: Understanding that $\delta$ is not unique clarifies the 'existence' clause in the epsilon-delta definition ('we can find a number $\delta>0$'). It emphasizes that any sufficiently small positive $\delta$ will satisfy the condition, not just one specific value, which is important for constructing proofs.
concepts.recap_md: - For a given $\epsilon$, if a $\delta$ satisfies the limit condition, then any $\delta'$ such that $0 < \delta' < \delta$ will also satisfy it.- This means there isn't a single 'correct' $\delta$, but rather an infinite range of valid $\delta$ values.
concepts.raw_body: ## THE VALUE OF $\boldsymbol{\delta}$ IS NOT UNIQUE

concepts.title: Limits as x approaches plus or minus infinity (rigorous)
concepts.one_liner: This concept introduces the rigorous definitions for limits as $x$ approaches positive or negative infinity.
concepts.summary_md: This section rigorously defines limits as the independent variable $x$ approaches positive or negative infinity. Unlike limits at a finite point $a$, these definitions involve finding a number $N$ (instead of $\delta$) to control the behavior of $f(x)$ as $x$ becomes very large or very small, ensuring $f(x)$ is arbitrarily close to $L$.
concepts.motivation_md: The intuitive understanding of limits at infinity needs a precise mathematical formulation, similar to how epsilon-delta defines limits at a finite point. This rigorous approach allows for formal proofs and a deeper understanding of asymptotic behavior, which is crucial for analyzing function graphs and real-world phenomena.
concepts.recap_md: - Rigorous definitions are needed for limits as $x \rightarrow \pm \infty$ to provide mathematical precision.- These definitions use a number $N$ to specify how far $x$ must extend for $f(x)$ to be within $\epsilon$ of the limit $L$.
concepts.raw_body: ## LIMITS AS $\boldsymbol{x} \rightarrow \pm \infty$

concepts.title: Epsilon-N Definition of Limit as x approaches +infinity
concepts.one_liner: We will write $\lim _{x \rightarrow+\infty} f(x)=L$ if given any number $\epsilon>0$, there corresponds a positive number $N$ such that $|f(x)-L|<\epsilon \quad \text { if } \quad x>N$.
concepts.summary_md: Let $f(x)$ be defined for all $x$ in some infinite open interval extending in the positive $x$-direction. We write $\lim _{x \rightarrow+\infty} f(x)=L$ if given any number $\epsilon>0$, there corresponds a positive number $N$ such that $|f(x)-L|<\epsilon$ whenever $x>N$.
concepts.motivation_md: This definition provides a precise way to express the idea that a function's value approaches a specific number $L$ as $x$ grows without bound. It is crucial for formally analyzing the end behavior of functions, proving the existence of horizontal asymptotes, and understanding limits in advanced calculus.
concepts.recap_md: - The limit $\lim _{x \rightarrow+\infty} f(x)=L$ means $f(x)$ approaches $L$ as $x$ gets infinitely large.- For any $\epsilon>0$ (how close $f(x)$ must be to $L$), there must exist a positive number $N$ (how large $x$ must be).- The condition is $|f(x)-L|<\epsilon$ whenever $x>N$.
concepts.raw_body:
1.4.2 DEFINITION Let $f(x)$ be defined for all $x$ in some infinite open interval extending in the positive $x$-direction. We will write

$$
\lim _{x \rightarrow+\infty} f(x)=L
$$

if given any number $\epsilon>0$, there corresponds a positive number $N$ such that

$$
|f(x)-L|<\epsilon \quad \text { if } \quad x>N
$$

concepts.title: Epsilon-N Definition of Limit as x approaches -infinity
concepts.one_liner: We will write $\lim _{x \rightarrow-\infty} f(x)=L$ if given any number $\epsilon>0$, there corresponds a negative number $N$ such that $|f(x)-L|<\epsilon \quad \text { if } \quad x<N$.
concepts.summary_md: Let $f(x)$ be defined for all $x$ in some infinite open interval extending in the negative $x$-direction. We write $\lim _{x \rightarrow-\infty} f(x)=L$ if given any number $\epsilon>0$, there corresponds a negative number $N$ such that $|f(x)-L|<\epsilon$ whenever $x<N$.
concepts.motivation_md: This definition formally describes the behavior of a function as $x$ decreases without bound, approaching negative infinity. It is essential for analyzing the left-hand end behavior of functions, proving the existence of horizontal asymptotes on the left side, and providing a complete rigorous framework for limits.
concepts.recap_md: - The limit $\lim _{x \rightarrow-\infty} f(x)=L$ means $f(x)$ approaches $L$ as $x$ gets infinitely negative.- For any $\epsilon>0$ (how close $f(x)$ must be to $L$), there must exist a negative number $N$ (how small $x$ must be).- The condition is $|f(x)-L|<\epsilon$ whenever $x<N$.
concepts.raw_body:
1.4.3 DEFINITION Let $f(x)$ be defined for all $x$ in some infinite open interval extending in the negative $x$-direction. We will write

$$
\lim _{x \rightarrow-\infty} f(x)=L
$$

if given any number $\epsilon>0$, there corresponds a negative number $N$ such that

$$
|f(x)-L|<\epsilon \quad \text { if } \quad x<N
$$

concepts.title: Prompt to Define Various Infinite Limits
concepts.one_liner: This concept prompts the learner to define various types of infinite limits, including one-sided limits approaching infinity and limits at infinity that are infinite.
concepts.summary_md: The concept presents a series of limit expressions, such as $\lim _{x \rightarrow a^{+}} f(x)=+\infty$ and $\lim _{x \rightarrow+\infty} f(x)=-\infty$, and asks the learner to formulate their rigorous definitions. This encourages applying the principles of epsilon-delta and epsilon-N definitions to scenarios where either $x$ or $f(x)$ (or both) approach infinity.
concepts.motivation_md: This prompt encourages active learning and deeper understanding by challenging students to extend known limit definitions to new scenarios involving infinity. It helps solidify their grasp of the underlying principles by requiring them to construct definitions themselves, rather than just memorizing them.
concepts.recap_md: - Consider how to define limits where $f(x)$ approaches $\pm\infty$ as $x \rightarrow a$ (one-sided or two-sided).- Consider how to define limits where $f(x)$ approaches $\pm\infty$ as $x \rightarrow \pm\infty$.- Think about how to adapt $\epsilon-\delta$ or $\epsilon-N$ logic to these "infinite" outcomes, possibly using a large number $M$ instead of $\epsilon$.
concepts.raw_body:
How would you define these limits?

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \lim _{x \rightarrow a^{+}} f(x)=+\infty \\
& \lim _{x \rightarrow a^{-}} f(x)=+\infty \\
& \lim _{x \rightarrow a^{+}} f(x)=-\infty \\
& \lim _{x \rightarrow+\infty} f(x)=+\infty \\
& \lim _{x \rightarrow-\infty} f(x)=-\infty \\
& \lim _{x \rightarrow+\infty} f(x)=-\infty \\
& \lim _{x \rightarrow-\infty} f(x)=-\infty
\end{aligned}
$$

concepts.title: Infinite Limits (rigorous)
concepts.one_liner: This concept introduces the rigorous definitions for infinite limits, where the function's value approaches positive or negative infinity.
concepts.summary_md: This section rigorously defines infinite limits, which occur when the value of $f(x)$ grows without bound (approaches $+\infty$) or decreases without bound (approaches $-\infty$) as $x$ approaches a finite number $a$ or infinity. These definitions use a large number $M$ (or $N$) to ensure $f(x)$ exceeds (or falls below) any given bound.
concepts.motivation_md: Just as finite limits require rigorous definitions, so do infinite limits. This formalization allows for precise analysis of vertical asymptotes and other unbounded behaviors of functions, moving beyond intuitive graphical understanding to formal proof and a deeper mathematical foundation.
concepts.recap_md: - Infinite limits describe when $f(x)$ approaches $+\infty$ or $-\infty$.- These limits can occur as $x$ approaches a finite number $a$ (vertical asymptotes) or as $x$ approaches $\pm\infty$.- Rigorous definitions involve finding a number $M$ (for $f(x)$) or $N$ (for $x$) to satisfy the conditions, ensuring $f(x)$ can be made arbitrarily large or small.
concepts.raw_body: ## INFINITE LIMITS

concepts.title: M-Delta Definition of Limit as x approaches a is +infinity
concepts.one_liner: We will write $\lim _{x \rightarrow a} f(x)=+\infty$ if given any positive number $M$, we can find a number $\delta>0$ such that $f(x)>M$ if $0<|x-a|<\delta$.
concepts.summary_md: A function $f(x)$ has a limit of $+\infty$ as $x$ approaches $a$ if, for any positive number $M$, we can find a $\delta>0$ such that $f(x)>M$ whenever $x$ is within $\delta$ distance of $a$ (but not equal to $a$). This means $f(x)$ can be made arbitrarily large by taking $x$ sufficiently close to $a$.
concepts.motivation_md: The standard epsilon-delta definition of a limit applies when the limit is a finite number. This definition extends the rigorous framework to describe the behavior of functions that grow without bound as $x$ approaches a specific value, providing a precise way to express 'approaching infinity'.
concepts.recap_md:
- The limit of $f(x)$ as $x \rightarrow a$ is $+\infty$.
- For any $M>0$, there exists $\delta>0$.
- If $0<|x-a|<\delta$, then $f(x)>M$.
concepts.raw_body:
1.4.4 DEFINITION Let $f(x)$ be defined for all $x$ in some open interval containing $a$, except that $f(x)$ need not be defined at $a$. We will write

$$
\lim _{x \rightarrow a} f(x)=+\infty
$$

if given any positive number $M$, we can find a number $\delta>0$ such that $f(x)$ satisfies

$$
f(x)>M \quad \text { if } \quad 0<|x-a|<\delta
$$

concepts.title: M-Delta Definition of Limit as x approaches a is -infinity
concepts.one_liner: We will write $\lim _{x \rightarrow a} f(x)=-\infty$ if given any negative number $M$, we can find a number $\delta>0$ such that $f(x)<M$ if $0<|x-a|<\delta$.
concepts.summary_md: A function $f(x)$ has a limit of $-\infty$ as $x$ approaches $a$ if, for any negative number $M$, we can find a $\delta>0$ such that $f(x)<M$ whenever $x$ is within $\delta$ distance of $a$ (but not equal to $a$). This means $f(x)$ can be made arbitrarily large in the negative direction by taking $x$ sufficiently close to $a$.
concepts.motivation_md: Just as functions can increase without bound, they can also decrease without bound. This definition provides a precise way to describe functions that approach negative infinity as $x$ approaches a specific value, complementing the definition for positive infinite limits.
concepts.recap_md:
- The limit of $f(x)$ as $x \rightarrow a$ is $-\infty$.
- For any $M<0$, there exists $\delta>0$.
- If $0<|x-a|<\delta$, then $f(x)<M$.
concepts.raw_body:
1.4.5 DEFINITION Let $f(x)$ be defined for all $x$ in some open interval containing $a$, except that $f(x)$ need not be defined at $a$. We will write

$$
\lim _{x \rightarrow a} f(x)=-\infty
$$

if given any negative number $M$, we can find a number $\delta>0$ such that $f(x)$ satisfies

$$
f(x)<M \quad \text { if } \quad 0<|x-a|<\delta
$$

concepts.title: Rigorous definition of right-sided limit
concepts.one_liner: A rigorous definition of $\lim _{x \rightarrow a^{+}} f(x)=L$ describes the behavior of $f(x)$ as $x$ approaches $a$ from values greater than $a$.
concepts.summary_md: The rigorous definition of a right-sided limit, $\lim _{x \rightarrow a^{+}} f(x)=L$, states that for every $\epsilon>0$, there exists a $\delta>0$ such that if $a < x < a+\delta$, then $|f(x)-L|<\epsilon$. This means $f(x)$ gets arbitrarily close to $L$ as $x$ approaches $a$ only from the right side.
concepts.motivation_md: One-sided limits are crucial for analyzing function behavior at points where the overall limit might not exist, such as at endpoints of domains or at jump discontinuities. They allow us to describe how a function approaches a point from a specific direction.
concepts.recap_md:
- The limit of $f(x)$ as $x$ approaches $a$ from the right is $L$.
- For every $\epsilon>0$, there exists $\delta>0$.
- If $a < x < a+\delta$, then $|f(x)-L|<\epsilon$.
concepts.raw_body: 27. Give rigorous definitions of $\lim _{x \rightarrow a^{+}} f(x)=L$ and $\lim _{x \rightarrow a^{-}} f(x)=L$.

concepts.title: Rigorous definition of left-sided limit
concepts.one_liner: A rigorous definition of $\lim _{x ightarrow a^{-}} f(x)=L$ describes the behavior of $f(x)$ as $x$ approaches $a$ from values less than $a$.
concepts.summary_md: The rigorous definition of a left-sided limit, $\lim _{x \rightarrow a^{-}} f(x)=L$, states that for every $\epsilon>0$, there exists a $\delta>0$ such that if $a-\delta < x < a$, then $|f(x)-L|<\epsilon$. This means $f(x)$ gets arbitrarily close to $L$ as $x$ approaches $a$ only from the left side.
concepts.motivation_md: One-sided limits are essential for understanding function behavior at points where the overall limit may not exist, such as at endpoints of intervals or where a function has a sudden 'jump'. They provide a precise way to analyze approach from a specific direction.
concepts.recap_md:
- The limit of $f(x)$ as $x$ approaches $a$ from the left is $L$.
- For every $\epsilon>0$, there exists $\delta>0$.
- If $a-\delta < x < a$, then $|f(x)-L|<\epsilon$.

concepts.title: Intuitive understanding of continuity
concepts.one_liner: We perceive the path of a thrown baseball as an unbroken curve, which translates into a precise mathematical formulation called continuity.
concepts.summary_md: The intuitive understanding of continuity comes from observing phenomena like a thrown baseball, whose path is an "unbroken curve." This concept of an "unbroken curve" is translated into a precise mathematical formulation, allowing us to describe functions that do not have sudden jumps or breaks.
concepts.motivation_md: Before diving into the formal definition, it's helpful to build an intuitive understanding of what continuity means. This analogy helps connect the abstract mathematical concept to a tangible real-world experience, making the formal definition more accessible and meaningful.
concepts.recap_md:
- Continuity is intuitively understood as an "unbroken curve."
- A thrown baseball's path is an example of continuous motion.
- This intuition is formalized mathematically.
concepts.raw_body: A thrown baseball cannot vanish at some point and reappear someplace else to continue its motion. Thus, we perceive the path of the ball as an unbroken curve. In this section, we translate "unbroken curve" into a precise mathematical formulation called continuity, translate "unbroken curve" into a precise mathematical formulation called continuity,

concepts.title: Continuity at a point
concepts.one_liner: A function $f$ is said to be continuous at $x=c$ provided three specific conditions are satisfied.
concepts.summary_md: A function $f$ is continuous at $x=c$ if three conditions hold: 1. $f(c)$ is defined. 2. $\lim _{x \rightarrow c} f(x)$ exists. 3. $\lim _{x \rightarrow c} f(x)=f(c)$. All three must be true for continuity at that point.
concepts.motivation_md: The concept of continuity is fundamental in calculus, allowing us to analyze functions that behave 'nicely' without sudden jumps or breaks. This precise definition provides a rigorous framework for identifying such functions, which are essential for theorems like the Intermediate Value Theorem and the Extreme Value Theorem.
concepts.recap_md:
- $f(c)$ must be defined.
- $\lim _{x \rightarrow c} f(x)$ must exist.
- $\lim _{x \rightarrow c} f(x)$ must equal $f(c)$.
concepts.raw_body:

1. $f(c)$ is defined.
2. $\lim _{x \rightarrow c} f(x)$ exists.
3. $\lim _{x \rightarrow c} f(x)=f(c)$.

concepts.title: Discontinuity at a point
concepts.one_liner: If one or more of the conditions for continuity at a point fails to hold, then $f$ has a discontinuity at $x=c$.
concepts.summary_md: A function $f$ has a discontinuity at $x=c$ if any of the three conditions for continuity at that point are not met. This can occur if $f(c)$ is undefined, if $\lim _{x \rightarrow c} f(x)$ does not exist (e.g., due to unequal one-sided limits or infinite limits), or if $\lim _{x \rightarrow c} f(x)$ exists but is not equal to $f(c)$.
concepts.motivation_md: Understanding discontinuities is as important as understanding continuity. By classifying how continuity fails, we can better analyze the behavior of functions, identify problematic points, and apply appropriate mathematical tools or theorems.
concepts.recap_md:
- Discontinuity occurs if $f(c)$ is undefined.
- Discontinuity occurs if $\lim _{x \rightarrow c} f(x)$ does not exist.
- Discontinuity occurs if $\lim _{x \rightarrow c} f(x) \neq f(c)$.

concepts.title: Jump discontinuity
concepts.one_liner: A function has a jump discontinuity at $c$ if the one-sided limits of $f(x)$ as $x$ approaches $c$ both exist but are not equal.
concepts.summary_md: A jump discontinuity occurs at $x=c$ when the limit of $f(x)$ as $x$ approaches $c$ does not exist because the one-sided limits, $\lim _{x \rightarrow c^{+}} f(x)$ and $\lim _{x \rightarrow c^{-}} f(x)$, both exist but have different values. This violates the second condition of continuity, where the overall limit must exist.
concepts.motivation_md: Identifying specific types of discontinuities helps in understanding the nature of a function's 'break'. A jump discontinuity indicates a sudden, finite change in function value, which is distinct from a hole or an infinite break, and often arises in piecewise functions or step functions.
concepts.recap_md:
- One-sided limits at $c$ both exist.
- The left-hand limit does not equal the right-hand limit.
- This causes the overall limit at $c$ to not exist.

concepts.title: Discontinuities in applications
concepts.one_liner: In applications, discontinuities often signal the occurrence of important physical events.
concepts.summary_md: In applications, discontinuities often signal the occurrence of important physical events. For example, a graph of voltage versus time for an an underground cable cut at $t=t_{0}$ shows a discontinuity as voltage drops to zero. Another example is inventory versus time for a company that restocks its warehouse, where discontinuities occur at restocking times.
concepts.motivation_md: This concept highlights the practical relevance of understanding discontinuities. It shows that these mathematical features are not just abstract ideas but represent real-world phenomena like sudden changes or events in physical systems or business processes.
concepts.recap_md: - Discontinuities in applications often indicate significant physical events. - Examples include voltage drops when a cable is cut or inventory jumps when a warehouse is restocked. - These real-world scenarios help illustrate the practical meaning of a function being discontinuous.
concepts.raw_body: In applications, discontinuities often signal the occurrence of important physical events. For example, Figure 1.5.3a is a graph of voltage versus time for an underground cable that is accidentally cut by a work crew at time $t=t_{0}$ (the voltage drops to zero when the line is cut). Figure 1.5.3b shows the graph of inventory versus time for a company that restocks its warehouse to $y_{1}$ units when the inventory falls to $y_{0}$ units. The discontinuities occur at those times when restocking occurs.

concepts.title: Continuity on an open interval
concepts.one_liner: If a function $f$ is continuous at each number in an open interval $(a, b)$, then we say that $f$ is continuous on $(a, b)$.
concepts.summary_md: If a function $f$ is continuous at each number in an open interval $(a, b)$, then we say that $f$ is continuous on $(a, b)$. This definition applies to infinite open intervals of the form $(a,+\infty)$, $(-\infty, b)$, and $(-\infty,+\infty)$. In the case where $f$ is continuous on $(-\infty,+\infty)$, we will say that $f$ is continuous everywhere.
concepts.motivation_md: This definition extends the concept of continuity from a single point to an entire interval. It provides a way to describe the behavior of functions over a range of values, which is fundamental for understanding their overall properties and for later concepts like differentiability and integrability.
concepts.recap_md: - A function $f$ is continuous on an open interval $(a, b)$ if it is continuous at every number within that interval. - This definition also applies to infinite open intervals such as $(a,+\infty)$ and $(-\infty,+\infty)$. - If $f$ is continuous on $(-\infty,+\infty)$, it is said to be continuous everywhere.
concepts.raw_body: If a function $f$ is continuous at each number in an open interval $(a, b)$, then we say that $f$ is continuous on ( $\boldsymbol{a}, \boldsymbol{b}$ ). This definition applies to infinite open intervals of the form ( $a,+\infty$ ), $(-\infty, b)$, and $(-\infty,+\infty)$. In the case where $f$ is continuous on $(-\infty,+\infty)$, we will say that $f$ is continuous everywhere.

concepts.title: Continuous from the left
concepts.one_liner: A function $f$ is continuous from the left at $c$ if $\lim _{x \rightarrow c^{-}} f(x)=f(c)$.
concepts.summary_md: A function $f$ is continuous from the left at $c$ if the limit of $f(x)$ as $x$ approaches $c$ from the left is equal to the function's value at $c$. This is expressed as $\lim _{x \rightarrow c^{-}} f(x)=f(c)$.
concepts.motivation_md: This definition is crucial for analyzing continuity at the endpoints of closed intervals or at points where a function might have a "jump." It allows for a precise description of continuity when approaching a point from only one direction.
concepts.recap_md: - A function $f$ is continuous from the left at $c$ if $\lim _{x \rightarrow c^{-}} f(x)=f(c)$. - This condition ensures that the function's value matches the limit as $x$ approaches $c$ from values less than $c$.
concepts.raw_body:
In general, we will say a function $f$ is continuous from the left at $c$ if

$$
\lim _{x \rightarrow c^{-}} f(x)=f(c)

concepts.title: Continuous from the right
concepts.one_liner: A function $f$ is continuous from the right at $c$ if $\lim _{x \rightarrow c^{+}} f(x)=f(c)$.
concepts.summary_md: A function $f$ is continuous from the right at $c$ if the limit of $f(x)$ as $x$ approaches $c$ from the right is equal to the function's value at $c$. This is expressed as $\lim _{x \rightarrow c^{+}} f(x)=f(c)$.
concepts.motivation_md: Similar to continuity from the left, this definition is essential for describing function behavior at interval endpoints or at points where a function might change abruptly. It provides a specific condition for continuity when approaching a point from values greater than it.
concepts.recap_md: - A function $f$ is continuous from the right at $c$ if $\lim _{x \rightarrow c^{+}} f(x)=f(c)$. - This condition ensures that the function's value matches the limit as $x$ approaches $c$ from values greater than $c$.
concepts.raw_body:
and is continuous from the right at $c$ if

\lim _{x \rightarrow c^{+}} f(x)=f(c)

concepts.title: Continuity on a closed interval
concepts.one_liner: A function $f$ is said to be continuous on a closed interval $[a, b]$ if three specific conditions are satisfied.
concepts.summary_md: A function $f$ is said to be continuous on a closed interval $[a, b]$ if the following conditions are satisfied: 1. $f$ is continuous on $(a, b)$. 2. $f$ is continuous from the right at $a$. 3. $f$ is continuous from the left at $b$.
concepts.motivation_md: This definition extends the idea of continuity to include the endpoints of an interval. It's crucial for functions defined over finite, bounded domains, allowing for a complete analysis of their behavior across the entire interval, including its boundaries.
concepts.recap_md: - For continuity on $[a, b]$, the function must be continuous on the open interval $(a, b)$. - The function must also be continuous from the right at the left endpoint $a$. - Finally, the function must be continuous from the left at the right endpoint $b$.
concepts.raw_body:
1.5.2 Definition A function $f$ is said to be continuous on a closed interval $[\boldsymbol{a}, \boldsymbol{b}]$ if the following conditions are satisfied:

1. $f$ is continuous on $(a, b)$.
2. $f$ is continuous from the right at $a$.
3. $f$ is continuous from the left at $b$.

concepts.title: Properties of continuous functions
concepts.one_liner: If functions $f$ and $g$ are continuous at $c$, then their sum, difference, product, and quotient (if denominator is nonzero) are also continuous at $c$.
concepts.summary_md: If the functions $f$ and $g$ are continuous at $c$, then: (a) $f+g$ is continuous at $c$. (b) $f-g$ is continuous at $c$. (c) $f g$ is continuous at $c$. (d) $f / g$ is continuous at $c$ if $g(c) \neq 0$ and has a discontinuity at $c$ if $g(c)=0$.
concepts.motivation_md: This theorem provides fundamental rules for combining continuous functions. It simplifies the process of determining the continuity of complex functions by breaking them down into simpler, known continuous components, without needing to re-evaluate limits for each combination.
concepts.recap_md: - The sum, difference, and product of two functions continuous at $c$ are also continuous at $c$. - The quotient of two functions continuous at $c$ is continuous at $c$, provided the denominator is not zero at $c$. - If the denominator is zero at $c$, the quotient has a discontinuity at $c$.
concepts.raw_body:
### 1.5.3 THEOREM If the functions $f$ and $g$ are continuous at $c$, then

(a) $f+g$ is continuous at $c$.
(b) $f-g$ is continuous at $c$.
(c) $f g$ is continuous at $c$.
(d) $f / g$ is continuous at $c$ if $g(c) \neq 0$ and has a discontinuity at $c$ if $g(c)=0$.

concepts.title: Continuity of polynomials and rational functions
concepts.one_liner: Polynomials are continuous everywhere, and rational functions are continuous where their denominator is nonzero.
concepts.summary_md: A polynomial is continuous everywhere. A rational function is continuous at every point where the denominator is nonzero, and has discontinuities at the points where the denominator is zero.
concepts.motivation_md: This theorem provides powerful shortcuts for determining the continuity of two common classes of functions: polynomials and rational functions. It eliminates the need to apply the formal definition of continuity for these functions, making continuity analysis much more efficient.
concepts.recap_md: - All polynomial functions are continuous for all real numbers. - Rational functions are continuous at every point where their denominator is not equal to zero. - Rational functions have discontinuities at points where their denominator is zero.
concepts.raw_body:
### 1.5.4 THEOREM

(a) A polynomial is continuous everywhere.
(b) A rational function is continuous at every point where the denominator is nonzero, and has discontinuities at the points where the denominator is zero.

concepts.title: Limit of a composite function
concepts.one_liner: If $\lim _{x \rightarrow c} g(x)=L$ and if the function $f$ is continuous at $L$, then $\lim _{x \rightarrow c} f(g(x))=f(L)$.
concepts.summary_md: If $\lim _{x \rightarrow c} g(x)=L$ and if the function $f$ is continuous at $L$, then $\lim _{x \rightarrow c} f(g(x))=f(L)$. This means the limit of a composite function can be found by applying the outer function to the limit of the inner function: $\lim _{x \rightarrow c} f(g(x))=f\left(\lim _{x \rightarrow c} g(x)\right)$. This theorem holds for various types of limits, including one-sided and infinite limits.
concepts.motivation_md: This theorem provides a powerful tool for evaluating limits of complex functions by breaking them down into simpler parts. It allows us to "pass the limit inside" a continuous function, simplifying calculations and extending the applicability of limit properties to composite functions.
concepts.recap_md: - If $\lim _{x \rightarrow c} g(x)=L$ and $f$ is continuous at $L$, then $\lim _{x \rightarrow c} f(g(x))=f(L)$.- The limit can be written as $\lim _{x \rightarrow c} f(g(x))=f\left(\lim _{x \rightarrow c} g(x)\right)$.- This theorem applies to one-sided and infinite limits as well.
concepts.raw_body:
### 1.5.5 THEOREM If $\lim _{x \rightarrow c} g(x)=L$ and if the function $f$ is continuous at $L$, then $\lim _{x \rightarrow c} f(g(x))=f(L)$. That is,
$$ \lim _{x \rightarrow c} f(g(x))=f\left(\lim _{x \rightarrow c} g(x)\right) $$
This equality remains valid if $\lim _{x \rightarrow c}$ is replaced everywhere by one of $\lim _{x \rightarrow c^{+}}$, $\lim _{x \rightarrow c^{-}}, \lim _{x \rightarrow+\infty}$, or $\lim _{x \rightarrow-\infty}$.

concepts.title: Continuity of composite functions
concepts.one_liner: If the function $g$ is continuous at $c$, and the function $f$ is continuous at $g(c)$, then the composition $f \circ g$ is continuous at $c$.
concepts.summary_md: This theorem states two conditions for the continuity of composite functions. (a) If the inner function $g$ is continuous at $c$, and the outer function $f$ is continuous at $g(c)$, then the composite function $f \circ g$ is continuous at $c$. (b) Furthermore, if both $g$ and $f$ are continuous everywhere, then their composition $f \circ g$ is also continuous everywhere.
concepts.motivation_md: Understanding the continuity of composite functions is crucial for analyzing more complex functions built from simpler ones. This theorem allows us to determine the continuity of a combined function without having to check the formal definition of continuity, simplifying analysis in calculus.
concepts.recap_md: - If $g$ is continuous at $c$ and $f$ is continuous at $g(c)$, then $f \circ g$ is continuous at $c$.- If both $g$ and $f$ are continuous everywhere, then $f \circ g$ is continuous everywhere.
concepts.raw_body:
### 1.5.6 THEOREM

(a) If the function $g$ is continuous at $c$, and the function $f$ is continuous at $g(c)$, then the composition $f \circ g$ is continuous at $c$.
(b) If the function $g$ is continuous everywhere and the function $f$ is continuous everywhere, then the composition $f \circ g$ is continuous everywhere.

concepts.title: The absolute value of a continuous function is continuous
concepts.one_liner: The absolute value of a continuous function is continuous.
concepts.summary_md: This idea states that if you have a function that is continuous, taking its absolute value will result in another function that is also continuous. This property is useful when dealing with transformations of continuous functions.
concepts.motivation_md: This property is a direct consequence of the continuity of the absolute value function itself and the theorem on the continuity of composite functions. It simplifies the analysis of functions involving absolute values, as we don't need to re-prove continuity from scratch.
concepts.recap_md: - If $f(x)$ is continuous, then $|f(x)|$ is also continuous.
concepts.raw_body: The absolute value of a continuous function is continuous.

concepts.title: Intermediate-Value Theorem
concepts.one_liner: If $f$ is continuous on a closed interval $[a, b]$ and $k$ is any number between $f(a)$ and $f(b)$, inclusive, then there is at least one number $x$ in the interval $[a, b]$ such that $f(x)=k$.
concepts.summary_md: The Intermediate-Value Theorem states that for a function $f$ that is continuous on a closed interval $[a, b]$, if $k$ is any value between $f(a)$ and $f(b)$ (inclusive), then there must exist at least one number $x$ within the interval $[a, b]$ such that $f(x)=k$. This means a continuous function takes on every intermediate value between its values at the endpoints.
concepts.motivation_md: The Intermediate-Value Theorem is fundamental because it guarantees the existence of certain function values. It's particularly useful for proving the existence of roots or solutions to equations, even when finding the exact values is difficult or impossible. It underpins many numerical methods.
concepts.recap_md: - If $f$ is continuous on $[a, b]$, and $k$ is between $f(a)$ and $f(b)$, then $f(x)=k$ for some $x$ in $[a, b]$.- This theorem guarantees that a continuous function hits all values between its endpoints.
concepts.raw_body: ### 1.5.7 THEOREM (Intermediate-Value Theorem) If $f$ is continuous on a closed interval $[a, b]$ and $k$ is any number between $f(a)$ and $f(b)$, inclusive, then there is at least one number $x$ in the interval $[a, b]$ such that $f(x)=k$.

concepts.title: Approximating roots using the Intermediate-Value Theorem
concepts.one_liner: One procedure for approximating roots is based on the consequence of the Intermediate-Value Theorem: If $f$ is continuous on $[a, b]$, and if $f(a)$ and $f(b)$ are nonzero and have opposite signs, then there is at least one solution of the equation $f(x)=0$ in the interval ( $a, b$ ).
concepts.summary_md: Many problems require solving $f(x)=0$ for its roots, which are often difficult to find exactly. The Intermediate-Value Theorem provides a method for approximating these roots. Specifically, if a function $f$ is continuous on $[a, b]$ and $f(a)$ and $f(b)$ have opposite signs, then there must be at least one root $x$ in the interval $(a, b)$ where $f(x)=0$.
concepts.motivation_md: This technique is essential for finding approximate solutions to equations that cannot be solved algebraically. By leveraging the IVT, we can narrow down intervals where roots exist, providing a practical method for numerical approximation in real-world applications and further mathematical analysis.
concepts.recap_md: - To approximate roots, use the IVT's consequence: if $f$ is continuous on $[a, b]$ and $f(a)$, $f(b)$ have opposite signs, a root exists in $(a, b)$.- This allows for narrowing down the interval containing a root.
