A variety of problems can be reduced to solving an equation $f(x)=0$ for its roots. Sometimes it is possible to solve for the roots exactly using algebra, but often this is not possible and one must settle for decimal approximations of the roots. One procedure for approximating roots is based on the following consequence of the Intermediate-Value Theorem.

### 1.5.8 THEOREM If $f$ is continuous on $[a, b]$, and if $f(a)$ and $f(b)$ are nonzero and have opposite signs, then there is at least one solution of the equation $f(x)=0$ in the interval ( $a, b$ ).

concepts.title: Existence of a root using Intermediate-Value Theorem
concepts.one_liner: If $f$ is continuous on $[a, b]$, and if $f(a)$ and $f(b)$ are nonzero and have opposite signs, then there is at least one solution of the equation $f(x)=0$ in the interval ( $a, b$ ).
concepts.summary_md: This theorem, a direct consequence of the Intermediate-Value Theorem, guarantees the existence of a root. It states that if a function $f$ is continuous on a closed interval $[a, b]$, and if the function values $f(a)$ and $f(b)$ are nonzero and have opposite signs, then there must be at least one solution to the equation $f(x)=0$ within the open interval $(a, b)$.
concepts.motivation_md: This theorem provides a powerful existence guarantee for roots of continuous functions. It's the theoretical basis for numerical methods like the bisection method, allowing us to confidently search for roots within specific intervals, even if we can't find them analytically.
concepts.recap_md: - If $f$ is continuous on $[a, b]$, and $f(a)$ and $f(b)$ have opposite signs, then a root exists.- This root, where $f(x)=0$, is guaranteed to be in the open interval $(a, b)$.
concepts.raw_body: ### 1.5.8 THEOREM If $f$ is continuous on $[a, b]$, and if $f(a)$ and $f(b)$ are nonzero and have opposite signs, then there is at least one solution of the equation $f(x)=0$ in the interval ( $a, b$ ).

concepts.title: Absolute error in approximation
concepts.one_liner: If $x$ is an approximation to a quantity $x_{0}$, then the absolute error $\epsilon$ is defined as $\epsilon=\left|x-x_{0}\right|$.
concepts.summary_md: When approximating a quantity $x_{0}$ with an approximate value $x$, it is important to describe the error. The absolute error, denoted by $\epsilon$, quantifies the magnitude of this error and is defined as the absolute difference between the approximation and the true value: $\epsilon=\left|x-x_{0}\right|$.
concepts.motivation_md: In numerical methods and practical applications, exact values are often unattainable. Defining absolute error provides a standard, quantifiable way to measure the accuracy of an approximation, which is crucial for determining if an approximation is "good enough" for a given purpose.
concepts.recap_md: - Absolute error $\epsilon$ measures the difference between an approximation $x$ and the true value $x_0$.- It is defined as $\epsilon=\left|x-x_{0}\right|$.
concepts.raw_body:
Before we illustrate how this theorem can be used to approximate roots, it will be helpful to discuss some standard terminology for describing errors in approximations. If $x$ is an approximation to a quantity $x_{0}$, then we call

$$
\epsilon=\left|x-x_{0}\right|
$$

concepts.title: Approximating roots using a graphing or calculating utility
concepts.one_liner: Use a graphing or calculating utility to approximate roots, such as $x_{0} \approx 1.3245$ to three decimal-place accuracy.
concepts.summary_md: This technique involves using a graphing or calculating utility to find approximate values for roots of an equation. Such tools can quickly provide high-precision decimal approximations, like $x_{0} \approx 1.3245$, often to a specified level of decimal-place accuracy, which is useful when exact algebraic solutions are not feasible.
concepts.motivation_md: Modern graphing and calculating utilities offer efficient and precise ways to find numerical approximations of roots, especially for complex functions where analytical solutions are impossible. This technique complements theoretical methods by providing practical, readily available solutions.
concepts.recap_md: - Graphing or calculating utilities can approximate roots of equations.- These tools provide decimal approximations, often to a specified accuracy.- This is a practical method when exact solutions are hard to find.
concepts.raw_body: Use a graphing or calculating utility to show that the root $x_{0}$ in Example 5 can be approximated as $x_{0} \approx 1.3245$ to three decimal-place accuracy.

concepts.title: Understanding decimal place accuracy in approximations
concepts.one_liner: To say that $x$ approximates $x_{0}$ to $n$ decimal places does not mean that the first $n$ decimal places of $x$ and $x_{0}$ will be the same when the numbers are rounded to $n$ decimal places.
concepts.summary_md: To say that $x$ approximates $x_{0}$ to $n$ decimal places does not mean that the first $n$ decimal places of $x$ and $x_{0}$ will be the same when the numbers are rounded to $n$ decimal places. For example, $x=1.084$ approximates $x_{0}=1.087$ to two decimal places because $\left|x-x_{0}\right|=0.003$ (< 0.005 ). Thus, if you approximate a number to $n$ decimal places, then you should display that approximation to at least $n+1$ decimal places to preserve the accuracy.
concepts.motivation_md: This concept clarifies a common misconception about decimal place accuracy. It highlights that simply rounding to `n` decimal places might not reflect the true approximation, providing a more robust understanding of numerical precision.
concepts.recap_md: - Approximating $x_0$ to $n$ decimal places means $|x - x_0| < 0.5 \times 10^{-n}$.- This does not guarantee that the first $n$ decimal places of $x$ and $x_0$ will be the same after rounding.- To preserve accuracy, display an approximation to $n$ decimal places with at least $n+1$ decimal places.
concepts.raw_body: To say that $x$ approximates $x_{0}$ to $n$ decimal places does not mean that the first $n$ decimal places of $x$ and $x_{0}$ will be the same when the numbers are rounded to $n$ decimal places. For example, $x=1.084$ approximates $x_{0}=1.087$ to two decimal places because $\left|x-x_{0}\right|=0.003$ (< 0.005 ). However, if we round these values to two decimal places, then we obtain $x \approx 1.08$ and $x_{0} \approx 1.09$. Thus, if you approximate a number to $n$ decimal places, then you should display that approximation to at least $n+1$ decimal places to preserve the accuracy.

concepts.title: Removable discontinuity
concepts.one_liner: A function $f$ is said to have a removable discontinuity at $x=c$ if $\lim _{x \rightarrow c} f(x)$ exists but $f$ is not continuous at $x=c$.
concepts.summary_md: A function $f$ is said to have a removable discontinuity at $x=c$ if $\lim _{x \rightarrow c} f(x)$ exists but $f$ is not continuous at $x=c$. This occurs either because $f$ is not defined at $c$ or because the definition for $f(c)$ differs from the value of the limit.
concepts.motivation_md: This definition provides a specific classification for a type of discontinuity where the "hole" or "jump" in the graph can be "removed" by redefining or defining the function at a single point, making it continuous.
concepts.recap_md: - A removable discontinuity occurs at $x=c$ if $\lim _{x \rightarrow c} f(x)$ exists.- The function $f$ is not continuous at $x=c$ because $f(c)$ is undefined or $f(c) \neq \lim _{x \rightarrow c} f(x)$.- This type of discontinuity can be "removed" by redefining $f(c)$ to be equal to the limit.
concepts.raw_body: 33-36 A function $f$ is said to have a removable discontinuity at $x=c$ if $\lim _{x \rightarrow c} f(x)$ exists but $f$ is not continuous at $x=c$, either because $f$ is not defined at $c$ or because the definition for $f(c)$ differs from the value of the limit. This terminology will be needed in these exercises.

concepts.title: Continuity of trigonometric functions
concepts.one_liner: The graphs of $\sin x$ and $\cos x$ are drawn as continuous curves, implying that $\lim _{x \rightarrow c} \sin x=\sin c$ and $\lim _{x \rightarrow c} \cos x=\cos c$.
concepts.summary_md: The graphs of $\sin x$ and $\cos x$ are drawn as continuous curves. If the angle $x$ approaches the angle $c$, then the point $P(\cos x, \sin x)$ moves along the unit circle toward $Q(\cos c, \sin c)$, and the coordinates of $P$ approach the corresponding coordinates of $Q$. This implies $\lim _{x \rightarrow c} \sin x=\sin c$ and $\lim _{x \rightarrow c} \cos x=\cos c$, showing these functions are continuous everywhere. Other trigonometric functions can be shown continuous by expressing them in terms of $\sin x$ and $\cos x$.
concepts.motivation_md: Understanding the continuity of trigonometric functions is fundamental for calculus. It allows us to directly substitute values to find limits for these functions, simplifying calculations and enabling the application of continuity theorems to more complex expressions involving trigonometry.
concepts.recap_md: - The graphs of $\sin x$ and $\cos x$ are continuous curves.- As $x \rightarrow c$, $\sin x \rightarrow \sin c$ and $\cos x \rightarrow \cos c$, demonstrating continuity everywhere.- Continuity of other trig functions (e.g., $\tan x$) can be derived from $\sin x$ and $\cos x$.
concepts.raw_body:
Recall from trigonometry that the graphs of $\sin x$ and $\cos x$ are drawn as continuous curves. We will not formally prove that these functions are continuous, but we can motivate this fact by letting $c$ be a fixed angle in radian measure and $x$ a variable angle in radian measure. If, as illustrated in Figure 1.6.1, the angle $x$ approaches the angle $c$, then the point $P(\cos x, \sin x)$ moves along the unit circle toward $Q(\cos c, \sin c)$, and the coordinates of $P$ approach the corresponding coordinates of $Q$. This implies that

$$
\begin{equation*}
\lim _{x \rightarrow c} \sin x=\sin c \quad \text { and } \quad \lim _{x \rightarrow c} \cos x=\cos c \tag{1}
\end{equation*}
$$

Thus, $\sin x$ and $\cos x$ are continuous at the arbitrary point $c$; that is, these functions are continuous everywhere.

The formulas in (1) can be used to find limits of the remaining trigonometric functions by expressing them in terms of $\sin x$ and $\cos x$; for example, if $\cos c \neq 0$, then

$$
\lim _{x \rightarrow c} \tan x=\lim _{x \rightarrow c} \frac{\sin x}{\cos x}=\frac{\sin c}{\cos c}=\tan c
$$
concepts.section_title: CONTINUITY OF TRIGONOMETRIC, EXPONENTIAL, AND INVERSE FUNCTIONS

concepts.title: Continuity of trigonometric functions
concepts.one_liner: If $c$ is any number in the natural domain of a trigonometric function, then its limit as $x$ approaches $c$ is equal to the function evaluated at $c$.
concepts.summary_md: Theorem 1.6.1 states that if $c$ is any number in the natural domain of a trigonometric function, then the limit of that function as $x$ approaches $c$ is equal to the function evaluated at $c$. This applies to all six trigonometric functions: $\sin x, \cos x, \tan x, \csc x, \sec x$, and $\cot x$.
concepts.motivation_md: This theorem formalizes the intuitive understanding that trigonometric functions are continuous on their domains. It provides a powerful tool for evaluating limits of these functions by direct substitution, simplifying many calculus problems.
concepts.recap_md: - For any trigonometric function, if $c$ is in its natural domain, $\lim _{x \rightarrow c} f(x)=f(c)$.- This means all six trigonometric functions are continuous on their respective domains.- Limits of trig functions can be found by direct substitution where the function is defined.
concepts.raw_body:
1.6.1 THEOREM If $c$ is any number in the natural domain of the stated trigonometric function, then

$$
\begin{array}{lll}
\lim _{x \rightarrow c} \sin x=\sin c & \lim _{x \rightarrow c} \cos x=\cos c & \lim _{x \rightarrow c} \tan x=\tan c \\
\lim _{x \rightarrow c} \csc x=\csc c & \lim _{x \rightarrow c} \sec x=\sec c & \lim _{x \rightarrow c} \cot x=\cot c
\end{array}
$$
concepts.section_title: CONTINUITY OF TRIGONOMETRIC, EXPONENTIAL, AND INVERSE FUNCTIONS

concepts.title: Continuity of inverse functions
concepts.one_liner: Geometrically, if a one-to-one function $f$ is continuous, its inverse $f^{-1}$ is also continuous, as their graphs are reflections about $y=x$.
concepts.summary_md: The graphs of a one-to-one function $f$ and its inverse $f^{-1}$ are reflections of one another about the line $y=x$. Geometrically, if the graph of $f$ has no breaks or holes in it, then neither does the graph of $f^{-1}$. This, and the fact that the range of $f$ is the domain of $f^{-1}$, suggests that the inverse of a continuous function is continuous.
concepts.motivation_md: This idea provides an intuitive understanding of why the continuity property is preserved when finding the inverse of a function. It allows us to infer the continuity of inverse functions (like inverse trigonometric or logarithmic functions) without needing separate, complex proofs.
concepts.recap_md: - Graphs of $f$ and $f^{-1}$ are reflections across $y=x$.- If $f$ is continuous (no breaks/holes), then its reflection $f^{-1}$ will also be continuous.- The domain of $f^{-1}$ is the range of $f$.
concepts.raw_body:
Since the graphs of a one-to-one function $f$ and its inverse $f^{-1}$ are reflections of one another about the line $y=x$, it is clear geometrically that if the graph of $f$ has no breaks or holes in it, then neither does the graph of $f^{-1}$. This, and the fact that the range of $f$ is the domain of $f^{-1}$, suggests the following result, which we state without formal proof.

To paraphrase Theorem 1.6.2, the inverse of a continuous function is continuous.
concepts.section_title: CONTINUITY OF TRIGONOMETRIC, EXPONENTIAL, AND INVERSE FUNCTIONS

concepts.title: Continuity of inverse functions
concepts.one_liner: If a one-to-one function $f$ is continuous at each point of its domain, then its inverse function $f^{-1}$ is continuous at each point of its domain.
concepts.summary_md: Theorem 1.6.2 states that if $f$ is a one-to-one function and is continuous at every point in its domain, then its inverse function, $f^{-1}$, is also continuous at every point in its domain. This means $f^{-1}$ is continuous at each point in the range of $f$.
concepts.motivation_md: This theorem formally establishes the continuity of inverse functions, which is crucial for understanding and working with functions like inverse trigonometric functions and logarithmic functions. It allows us to apply continuity properties to these important classes of functions.
concepts.recap_md: - If $f$ is one-to-one and continuous on its domain, then $f^{-1}$ is continuous.- The domain of $f^{-1}$ is the range of $f$.- This theorem ensures continuity for inverse functions like $\arcsin x$ or $\ln x$ on their respective domains.
concepts.raw_body: 1.6.2 THEOREM If $f$ is a one-to-one function that is continuous at each point of its domain, then $f^{-1}$ is continuous at each point of its domain; that is, $f^{-1}$ is continuous at each point in the range of $f$.
concepts.section_title: CONTINUITY OF TRIGONOMETRIC, EXPONENTIAL, AND INVERSE FUNCTIONS

concepts.title: Continuity of exponential and logarithmic functions
concepts.one_liner: For $b>0, b \neq 1$, the exponential function $b^{x}$ is continuous on $(-\infty,+\infty)$ and the logarithmic function $\log _{b} x$ is continuous on $(0,+\infty)$.
concepts.summary_md: Theorem 1.6.3 states that for any base $b>0$ and $b \neq 1$, the exponential function $b^{x}$ is continuous over its entire domain, which is $(-\infty,+\infty)$. Additionally, the logarithmic function $\log _{b} x$ is continuous over its domain, $(0,+\infty)$.
concepts.motivation_md: This theorem provides foundational knowledge about the continuity of exponential and logarithmic functions. These functions are ubiquitous in science and engineering, and knowing they are continuous on their domains allows for direct substitution when evaluating limits and applying calculus techniques.
concepts.recap_md: - For $b>0, b \neq 1$, the exponential function $b^{x}$ is continuous on $(-\infty,+\infty)$.- For $b>0, b \neq 1$, the logarithmic function $\log _{b} x$ is continuous on $(0,+\infty)$.- This means limits of these functions can be found by direct substitution within their domains.
concepts.raw_body:
### 1.6.3 THEOREM Let $b>0, b \neq 1$.

(a) The function $b^{x}$ is continuous on $(-\infty,+\infty)$.
(b) The function $\log _{b} x$ is continuous on ( $0,+\infty$ ).
concepts.section_title: CONTINUITY OF TRIGONOMETRIC, EXPONENTIAL, AND INVERSE FUNCTIONS

concepts.title: Obtaining limits by squeezing
concepts.one_liner: The method of squeezing proves that $f(x) \rightarrow L$ as $x \rightarrow c$ by 'trapping' $f$ between two functions, $g$ and $h$, whose limits are known to be $L$.
concepts.summary_md: The technique of squeezing is used to prove limits that are not easily established by algebraic manipulation, such as $\lim _{x \rightarrow 0} \frac{\sin x}{x}=1$. This method involves 'trapping' or 'squeezing' a function $f(x)$ between two other functions, $g(x)$ and $h(x)$. If the limits of both $g(x)$ and $h(x)$ as $x \rightarrow c$ are known to be $L$, then $f(x)$ is forced to also have a limit of $L$ as $x \rightarrow c$.
concepts.motivation_md: Some limits, like $\lim _{x \rightarrow 0} \frac{\sin x}{x}$, are indeterminate forms that cannot be solved by simple algebraic methods. The squeezing technique provides a powerful, rigorous way to determine such limits by bounding the function between two others whose limits are known.
concepts.recap_md: - The squeezing method proves $\lim _{x \rightarrow c} f(x)=L$.- It works by "trapping" $f(x)$ between two functions, $g(x)$ and $h(x)$, such that $g(x) \le f(x) \le h(x)$.- If $\lim _{x \rightarrow c} g(x)=L$ and $\lim _{x \rightarrow c} h(x)=L$, then $\lim _{x \rightarrow c} f(x)$ must also be $L$.
concepts.section_title: CONTINUITY OF TRIGONOMETRIC, EXPONENTIAL, AND INVERSE FUNCTIONS

concepts.title: The Squeezing Theorem
concepts.one_liner: If $f, g$, and $h$ are functions satisfying $g(x) \leq f(x) \leq h(x)$ and $g$ and $h$ have the same limit $L$ as $x$ approaches $c$, then $f$ also has this limit $L$.
concepts.summary_md: Let $f, g$, and $h$ be functions satisfying $g(x) \leq f(x) \leq h(x)$ for all $x$ in some open interval containing the number $c$, with the possible exception that the inequalities need not hold at $c$. If $\lim _{x \rightarrow c} g(x)=\lim _{x \rightarrow c} h(x)=L$, then $f$ also has this limit as $x$ approaches $c$, that is, $\lim _{x \rightarrow c} f(x)=L$.
concepts.motivation_md: This theorem provides a powerful method for finding the limit of a function that is difficult to evaluate directly, by "squeezing" it between two other functions whose limits are known and equal. It's particularly useful for functions involving trigonometric expressions or those with complex behavior near a point.
concepts.recap_md:
- If $g(x) \leq f(x) \leq h(x)$ for $x$ near $c$.
- If $\lim _{x \rightarrow c} g(x)=L$ and $\lim _{x \rightarrow c} h(x)=L$.
- Then $\lim _{x \rightarrow c} f(x)=L$.
concepts.raw_body:
### 1.6.4 THEOREM (The Squeezing Theorem) Let $f, g$, and $h$ be functions satisfying

$$
g(x) \leq f(x) \leq h(x)
$$

for all $x$ in some open interval containing the number $c$, with the possible exception that the inequalities need not hold at $c$. If $g$ and $h$ have the same limit as $x$ approaches $c$, say

$$
\lim _{x \rightarrow c} g(x)=\lim _{x \rightarrow c} h(x)=L
$$

then $f$ also has this limit as $x$ approaches $c$, that is,

$$
\lim _{x \rightarrow c} f(x)=L
$$
concepts.section_title: CONTINUITY OF TRIGONOMETRIC, EXPONENTIAL, AND INVERSE FUNCTIONS

concepts.title: Special trigonometric limits
concepts.one_liner: The special trigonometric limits state that $\lim _{x \rightarrow 0} \frac{\sin x}{x}=1$ and $\lim _{x \rightarrow 0} \frac{1-\cos x}{x}=0$.
concepts.summary_md: The theorem presents two special trigonometric limits: (a) $\lim _{x \rightarrow 0} \frac{\sin x}{x}=1$ and (b) $\lim _{x \rightarrow 0} \frac{1-\cos x}{x}=0$.
concepts.motivation_md: These limits are fundamental for evaluating more complex limits involving trigonometric functions, especially when direct substitution results in an indeterminate form like $0/0$. They are crucial for deriving the derivatives of trigonometric functions.
concepts.recap_md:
- $\lim _{x \rightarrow 0} \frac{\sin x}{x}=1$.
- $\lim _{x \rightarrow 0} \frac{1-\cos x}{x}=0$.
concepts.raw_body:
### 1.6.5 THEOREM

(a) $\lim _{x \rightarrow 0} \frac{\sin x}{x}=1$
(b) $\lim _{x \rightarrow 0} \frac{1-\cos x}{x}=0$
concepts.section_title: CONTINUITY OF TRIGONOMETRIC, EXPONENTIAL, AND INVERSE FUNCTIONS

concepts.title: Area of a sector
concepts.one_liner: The area $A$ of a sector of radius $r$ and central angle $\theta$ is given by the formula $A=\frac{1}{2} r^{2} \theta$.
concepts.summary_md: The area $A$ of a sector with radius $r$ and central angle $\theta$ is $A=\frac{1}{2} r^{2} \theta$. This formula can be derived from the relationship $\frac{A}{\pi r^{2}}=\frac{\theta}{2 \pi}$, which states that the area of the sector is to the area of the circle as the central angle of the sector is to the central angle of the circle.
concepts.motivation_md: Understanding the area of a sector is essential for various geometric and calculus applications, particularly when dealing with polar coordinates, arc length, and later, integration in circular regions. It provides a foundational geometric concept.
concepts.recap_md:
- The area $A$ of a sector is $A=\frac{1}{2} r^{2} \theta$.
- This formula relates the sector's area to the circle's area proportionally to their angles.
concepts.raw_body:
Recall that the area $A$ of a sector of radius $r$ and central angle $\theta$ is

$$
A=\frac{1}{2} r^{2} \theta
$$

This can be derived from the relationship

$$
\frac{A}{\pi r^{2}}=\frac{\theta}{2 \pi}
$$

which states that the area of the sector is to the area of the circle as the central angle of the sector is to the central angle of the circle.
concepts.section_title: CONTINUITY OF TRIGONOMETRIC, EXPONENTIAL, AND INVERSE FUNCTIONS

concepts.title: Tangent circle (osculating circle) as a limit of secant circles
concepts.one_liner: This idea develops an analogous concept to tangent lines, replacing secant lines with 'secant circles' and the tangent line with a 'tangent circle' (osculating circle).
concepts.summary_md: In Section 1.1, the notion of a tangent line was developed by considering it as a limiting position of secant lines. This concept extends that idea, replacing secant lines with "secant circles" and the tangent line with a "tangent circle," also known as the osculating circle. The discussion begins with the graph of $y=x^{2}$.
concepts.motivation_md: This concept introduces a more advanced geometric idea, extending the familiar concept of a tangent line to a "tangent circle." It helps build intuition for how limits can define complex geometric objects and is a stepping stone to understanding curvature.
concepts.recap_md:
- Tangent lines are limits of secant lines.
- Tangent circles (osculating circles) are limits of "secant circles."
- This idea explores the concept using the graph of $y=x^{2}$.
concepts.raw_body: In Section 1.1 we developed the notion of a tangent line to a graph at a given point by considering it as a limiting position of secant lines through that point (Figure 1.1.4a). In these exercises we will develop an analogous idea in which secant lines are replaced by "secant circles" and the tangent line is replaced by a "tangent circle" (called the osculating circle). We begin with the graph of $y=x^{2}$.
concepts.section_title: CONTINUITY OF TRIGONOMETRIC, EXPONENTIAL, AND INVERSE FUNCTIONS

concepts.title: The derivative as a tool for studying rates of change and continuous motion
concepts.one_liner: Calculus's ability to capture continuous motion mathematically allows for instant-by-instant analysis of changing quantities.
concepts.summary_md: One of calculus's main achievements is its capacity to mathematically model continuous motion, enabling analysis at any given instant. Many real-world phenomena involve changing quantities, such as rocket speed or currency inflation. This chapter introduces the "derivative," a mathematical tool for studying the rate at which one quantity changes relative to another, connecting it to the geometric concept of a tangent line.
concepts.motivation_md: This concept highlights the practical utility of calculus in understanding dynamic systems. It sets the stage for the derivative by linking it to the intuitive idea of rates of change and continuous motion, showing its relevance beyond abstract mathematics.
concepts.recap_md:
- Calculus can analyze continuous motion instant by instant.
- The derivative is a mathematical tool for studying rates of change.
- Rates of change are closely related to the geometric concept of a tangent line.
concepts.raw_body:
One of the crowning achievements of calculus is its ability to capture continuous motion mathematically, allowing that motion to be analyzed instant by instant.

Many real-world phenomena involve changing quantities-the speed of a rocket, the inflation of currency, the number of bacteria in a culture, the shock intensity of an earthquake, the voltage of an electrical signal, and so forth. In this chapter we will develop the concept of a "derivative," which is the mathematical tool for studying the rate at which one quantity changes relative to another. The study of rates of change is closely related to the geometric concept of a tangent line to a curve, so we will also be discussing the general definition of a tangent line and methods for finding its slope and equation.

concepts.title: Overview of Tangent Lines and Rates of Change
concepts.one_liner: This section discusses tangent lines to curves, the velocity of an object, and the rate at which one variable changes relative to another, showing their close links.
concepts.summary_md: This section will discuss three key ideas: tangent lines to curves, the velocity of an object moving along a line, and the rate at which one variable changes relative to another. The primary goal is to demonstrate how these seemingly unrelated concepts are, in fact, closely interconnected.
concepts.motivation_md: This overview prepares the learner by outlining the core topics of the section and emphasizing the unifying theme: how tangent lines, velocity, and rates of change are fundamentally linked. It provides a roadmap for the upcoming material.
concepts.recap_md:
- The section covers tangent lines to curves.
- It also addresses the velocity of an object moving along a line.
- The goal is to link these ideas with the rate of change of variables.
concepts.raw_body: > In this section we will discuss three ideas: tangent lines to curves, the velocity of an object moving along a line, and the rate at which one variable changes relative to another. Our goal is to show how these seemingly unrelated ideas are, in actuality, closely linked.
concepts.section_title: TANGENT LINES AND RATES OF CHANGE

concepts.title: Tangent Line to a Curve
concepts.one_liner: The tangent line to the curve $y=f(x)$ at $P\left(x_{0}, f\left(x_{0}\right)\right)$ is defined by the equation $y-f\left(x_{0}\right)=m_{\tan }\left(x-x_{0}\right)$, where $m_{\tan }=\lim _{x \rightarrow x_{0}} \frac{f(x)-f\left(x_{0}\right)}{x-x_{0}}$.
concepts.summary_md: The tangent line to the curve $y=f(x)$ at a point $P\left(x_{0}, f\left(x_{0}\right)\right)$ is defined by the equation $y-f\left(x_{0}\right)=m_{\tan }\left(x-x_{0}\right)$. The slope of this tangent line, $m_{\tan }$, is given by the limit $m_{\tan }=\lim _{x \rightarrow x_{0}} \frac{f(x)-f\left(x_{0}\right)}{x-x_{0}}$, provided this limit exists.
concepts.motivation_md: This definition provides a precise mathematical way to define the slope of a curve at a single point, which is crucial for understanding instantaneous rates of change, optimization, and the behavior of functions. It formalizes the intuitive idea of a line "just touching" a curve.
concepts.recap_md:
- The tangent line equation is $y-f\left(x_{0}\right)=m_{\tan }\left(x-x_{0}\right)$.
- The slope $m_{\tan }$ is defined as $\lim _{x \rightarrow x_{0}} \frac{f(x)-f\left(x_{0}\right)}{x-x_{0}}$.
- The limit must exist for the tangent line to be defined.
concepts.raw_body:
2.1.1 DEFINITION Suppose that $x_{0}$ is in the domain of the function $f$. The tangent line to the curve $y=f(x)$ at the point $P\left(x_{0}, f\left(x_{0}\right)\right)$ is the line with equation

$$
y-f\left(x_{0}\right)=m_{\tan }\left(x-x_{0}\right)
$$

where

$$
\begin{equation*}
m_{\tan }=\lim _{x \rightarrow x_{0}} \frac{f(x)-f\left(x_{0}\right)}{x-x_{0}} \tag{1}
\end{equation*}
$$

provided the limit exists. For simplicity, we will also call this the tangent line to $y=f(x)$ at $x_{0}$.
concepts.section_title: TANGENT LINES AND RATES OF CHANGE

concepts.title: Alternative Formula for Slope of Tangent Line
concepts.one_liner: An alternative formula for the tangent slope $m_{\tan }$ is $\lim _{h \rightarrow 0} \frac{f\left(x_{0}+h\right)-f\left(x_{0}\right)}{h}$, derived by letting $h=x-x_{0}$.
concepts.summary_md: An alternative way to express the formula for $m_{\tan }$ is by letting $h=x-x_{0}$. This substitution means that as $x \rightarrow x_{0}$, $h \rightarrow 0$. The formula then becomes $m_{\tan }=\lim _{h \rightarrow 0} \frac{f\left(x_{0}+h\right)-f\left(x_{0}\right)}{h}$. Both formulas typically lead to indeterminate forms of type $0/0$, requiring algebraic simplification.
concepts.motivation_md: This alternative formula is often more convenient for algebraic manipulation when calculating derivatives from the definition. It provides flexibility and a different perspective on the same concept, which can simplify problem-solving in various contexts.
concepts.recap_md:
- The alternative formula for $m_{\tan }$ uses $h=x-x_{0}$.
- It is expressed as $m_{\tan }=\lim _{h \rightarrow 0} \frac{f\left(x_{0}+h\right)-f\left(x_{0}\right)}{h}$.
- Both formulas for $m_{\tan }$ often result in $0/0$ indeterminate forms.
concepts.section_title: TANGENT LINES AND RATES OF CHANGE

concepts.title: Introduction to Velocity
concepts.one_liner: The speed and the direction of motion together comprise what is called the velocity of the object.
concepts.summary_md: One of the important themes in calculus is the study of motion. To describe the motion of an object completely, one must specify its speed (how fast it is going) and the direction in which it is moving. The speed and the direction of motion together comprise what is called the velocity of the object.
concepts.motivation_md: Calculus provides tools to analyze motion, and understanding velocity is fundamental to describing how objects move, including both their speed and direction.
concepts.recap_md: - Velocity describes both speed and direction of motion. - Speed tells how fast an object is going, but not its direction. - Knowing velocity, e.g., "500 mi/h due south," specifies both speed and direction.
concepts.raw_body: One of the important themes in calculus is the study of motion. To describe the motion of an object completely, one must specify its speed (how fast it is going) and the direction in which it is moving. The speed and the direction of motion together comprise what is called the velocity of the object. For example, knowing that the speed of an aircraft is 500 $\mathrm{mi} / \mathrm{h}$ tells us how fast it is going, but not which way it is moving. In contrast, knowing that the velocity of the aircraft is $500 \mathrm{mi} / \mathrm{h}$ due south pins down the speed and the direction of motion.
concepts.section_title: TANGENT LINES AND RATES OF CHANGE

concepts.title: Rectilinear Motion
concepts.one_liner: Rectilinear motion refers to motion along a line.
concepts.summary_md: Rectilinear motion is motion along a line. Examples include a piston moving up and down in a cylinder, a race car moving along a straight track, or an object falling straight down. Later, we will study motion along curves, but for now, we focus only on motion along a line.
concepts.motivation_md: Focusing on rectilinear motion simplifies the initial study of motion in calculus, allowing students to grasp fundamental concepts before moving to more complex two- or three-dimensional curved paths.
concepts.recap_md: - Rectilinear motion is defined as motion along a single line. - Examples include objects moving vertically or horizontally in a straight path. - This concept simplifies the initial study of motion in calculus.
concepts.raw_body:
Later, we will study the motion of objects that move along curves in two- or threedimensional space, but for now we will only consider motion along a line; this is called rectilinear motion. Some examples are a piston moving up and down in a cylinder, a race
car moving along a straight track, an object dropped from the top of a building and falling straight down, a ball thrown straight up and then falling down along the same line, and so forth.
concepts.section_title: TANGENT LINES AND RATES OF CHANGE

concepts.title: Position versus Time Curve
concepts.one_liner: A graphical description of rectilinear motion along an $s$-axis can be obtained by making a plot of the $s$-coordinate of the particle versus the elapsed time $t$.
concepts.summary_md: For computational purposes, a particle in rectilinear motion moves along an $s$-axis. A graphical description, called the position versus time curve, is obtained by plotting the $s$-coordinate of the particle against the elapsed time $t$. For example, if a car moves in the positive direction, $s$ increases as $t$ increases.
concepts.motivation_md: Visualizing motion helps understand how an object's position changes over time. The position versus time curve provides a clear graphical representation, making it easier to analyze movement patterns like increasing or decreasing position.
concepts.recap_md: - The $s$-axis represents the coordinate line for rectilinear motion. - A position versus time curve plots the $s$-coordinate of a particle against elapsed time $t$. - This curve visually describes how a particle's position changes over time.
concepts.raw_body: For computational purposes, we will assume that a particle in rectilinear motion moves along a coordinate line, which we will call the $s$-axis. A graphical description of rectilinear motion along an $s$-axis can be obtained by making a plot of the $s$-coordinate of the particle versus the elapsed time $t$ from starting time $t=0$. This is called the position versus time curve for the particle. Figure 2.1.5 shows two typical position versus time curves. The first is for a car that starts at the origin and moves only in the positive direction of the $s$-axis. In this case $s$ increases as $t$ increases. The second is for a ball that is thrown straight up in the positive direction of an $s$-axis from some initial height $s_{0}$ and then falls straight down in the negative direction. In this case $s$ increases as the ball moves up and decreases as it moves down.
concepts.section_title: TANGENT LINES AND RATES OF CHANGE

concepts.title: Displacement
concepts.one_liner: The change in position $f(t_{0}+h)-f(t_{0})$ is also called the displacement of the particle over the time interval between $t_{0}$ and $t_{0}+h$.
concepts.summary_md: The change in position, expressed as $f(t_{0}+h)-f(t_{0})$, is defined as the displacement of a particle. This value represents the net change in the particle's position over a specific time interval, from $t_{0}$ to $t_{0}+h$.
concepts.motivation_md: Displacement is a crucial concept for understanding motion because it quantifies the net change in an object's position, regardless of the path taken. It's a foundational component for calculating velocity.
concepts.recap_md: - Displacement is the change in position of a particle. - It is calculated as $f(t_{0}+h)-f(t_{0})$. - This value represents the net movement over a time interval $[t_{0}, t_{0}+h]$.
concepts.raw_body:
The change in position

$$
f\left(t_{0}+h\right)-f\left(t_{0}\right)
$$

is also called the displacement of the particle over the time interval between $t_{0}$ and $t_{0}+h$.
concepts.section_title: TANGENT LINES AND RATES OF CHANGE

concepts.title: Position Function
concepts.one_liner: If a particle's position coordinate $s$ is a function of elapsed time $t$, $s=f(t)$, then $f$ is called the position function of the particle.
concepts.summary_md: For a particle in rectilinear motion, its position coordinate $s$ is a function of the elapsed time $t$, denoted as $s=f(t)$. This function $f$ is called the position function of the particle. The graph of $s=f(t)$ is known as the position versus time curve.
concepts.motivation_md: The position function provides a mathematical model for an object's location at any given time. This allows for precise calculations and predictions about its movement, forming the basis for understanding velocity and acceleration.
concepts.recap_md: - A position function, $s=f(t)$, describes a particle's position $s$ at any given time $t$. - This function is used for particles in rectilinear motion along an $s$-axis. - The graph of the position function is the position versus time curve.
concepts.section_title: TANGENT LINES AND RATES OF CHANGE

concepts.title: Average Velocity
concepts.one_liner: The average velocity of the particle over a time interval $[t_{0}, t_{0}+h], h>0$, is defined to be $v_{	ext {ave }}=\frac{\text { change in position }}{\text { time elapsed }}=\frac{f\left(t_{0}+h\right)-f\left(t_{0}\right)}{h}$.
concepts.summary_md: The average velocity of a particle over a time interval $[t_{0}, t_{0}+h]$ is defined as the ratio of the change in position to the time elapsed. Mathematically, it is given by the formula $v_{	ext {ave }}=\frac{f\left(t_{0}+h\right)-f\left(t_{0}\right)}{h}$, where $f(t)$ is the position function.
concepts.motivation_md: Average velocity provides a way to quantify how fast an object is moving over a period. It's a practical measure for many real-world scenarios and serves as a crucial stepping stone towards understanding instantaneous velocity.
concepts.recap_md: - Average velocity is the ratio of change in position to the time elapsed. - The formula is $v_{	ext {ave }}=\frac{f\left(t_{0}+h\right)-f\left(t_{0}\right)}{h}$. - It describes the overall rate of change of position over a given time interval.
concepts.section_title: TANGENT LINES AND RATES OF CHANGE

concepts.title: Motivation for Instantaneous Velocity
concepts.one_liner: Formula (4) is not directly applicable for computing instantaneous velocity because the "time elapsed" at a specific instant is zero, so (4) is undefined.
concepts.summary_md: The formula for average velocity (4) cannot directly compute instantaneous velocity because 'time elapsed' at a specific instant is zero, making the expression undefined. To circumvent this, we compute average velocities over small time intervals. These approximations can lead to the instantaneous velocity if they have a limit as the time interval approaches zero.
concepts.motivation_md: While average velocity is useful, it doesn't describe motion at a precise moment. Instantaneous velocity is needed to understand the exact speed and direction of an object at a single point in time, which is critical for analyzing dynamic systems.
concepts.recap_md: - Average velocity formula (4) fails for instantaneous velocity because time elapsed is zero. - Average velocities over small time intervals can approximate instantaneous velocity. - The concept of a limit is introduced to define instantaneous velocity precisely.
concepts.raw_body: its behavior at a specific instant in time. Formula (4) is not directly applicable for computing instantaneous velocity because the "time elapsed" at a specific instant is zero, so (4) is undefined. One way to circumvent this problem is to compute average velocities for small time intervals between $t=t_{0}$ and $t=t_{0}+h$. These average velocities may be viewed as approximations to the "instantaneous velocity" of the particle at time $t_{0}$. If these average velocities have a limit as $h$ approaches zero, then we can take that limit to be the instantaneous velocity of the particle at time $t_{0}$. Here is an example.
concepts.section_title: TANGENT LINES AND RATES OF CHANGE

concepts.title: Instantaneous Velocity
concepts.one_liner: The instantaneous velocity $v_{\text {inst }}$ of a particle at time $t_{0}$ is defined to be the limit as $h \rightarrow 0$ of its average velocities $v_{\text {ave }}$ over time intervals between $t=t_{0}$ and $t=t_{0}+h$.
concepts.summary_md: For a particle with position function $s=f(t)$, the instantaneous velocity $v_{\text {inst }}$ at time $t_{0}$ is defined as the limit of its average velocities as the time interval $h$ approaches zero. This is expressed by the formula $v_{\mathrm{inst}}=\lim _{h \rightarrow 0} \frac{f\left(t_{0}+h\right)-f\left(t_{0}\right)}{h}$.
concepts.motivation_md: Instantaneous velocity provides a precise measure of an object's speed and direction at a single moment. This concept is fundamental to calculus, as it introduces the idea of a derivative, which is essential for analyzing rates of change in countless applications.
concepts.recap_md: - Instantaneous velocity is the limit of average velocities as the time interval approaches zero. - The formula is $v_{\mathrm{inst}}=\lim _{h \rightarrow 0} \frac{f\left(t_{0}+h\right)-f\left(t_{0}\right)}{h}$. - This definition is crucial for understanding the precise rate of change of position at a specific instant.
concepts.section_title: TANGENT LINES AND RATES OF CHANGE

concepts.title: Geometric Interpretation of Velocity
concepts.one_liner: Geometrically, average velocity is the slope of a secant line, and instantaneous velocity is the slope of a tangent line on a position-time curve.
concepts.summary_md: Geometrically, the average velocity $v_{	ext {ave }}$ between $t=t_{0}$ and $t=t_{0}+h$ is the slope of the secant line through points $P ig(t_{0}, f(t_{0}) ig)$ and $Q ig(t_{0}+h, f(t_{0}+h) ig)$ on the position versus time curve. The instantaneous velocity $v_{	ext {inst }}$ at time $t_{0}$ is the slope of the tangent line to the position versus time curve at the point $P ig(t_{0}, f(t_{0}) ig)$.
concepts.motivation_md: This concept helps visualize abstract velocity calculations. By relating average and instantaneous velocities to secant and tangent lines, it provides a concrete geometric understanding of how these rates of change are derived from a position-time graph.
concepts.recap_md: - Average velocity is the slope of the secant line between two points on a position-time curve. - Instantaneous velocity is the slope of the tangent line at a single point on the position-time curve.
concepts.raw_body: Geometrically, the average velocity $v_{\text {ave }}$ between $t=t_{0}$ and $t=t_{0}+h$ is the slope of the secant line through points $P\left(t_{0}, f\left(t_{0}\right)\right)$ and $Q\left(t_{0}+h, f\left(t_{0}+h\right)\right)$ on the position versus time curve, and the instantaneous velocity $v_{\text {inst }}$ at time $t_{0}$ is the slope of the tangent line to the position versus time curve at the point $P\left(t_{0}, f\left(t_{0}\right)\right)$ (Figure 2.1.7).
concepts.section_title: TANGENT LINES AND RATES OF CHANGE

concepts.title: Introduction to Rates of Change
concepts.one_liner: Velocity can be viewed as a rate of change, and rates of change occur in many applications beyond just position with respect to time.
concepts.summary_md: Velocity is the rate of change of position with respect to time. Rates of change are fundamental in many fields, such as microbiology (bacteria growth), engineering (rod length with temperature), and economics (production cost with quantity). For a linear function $y=mx+b$, the slope $m$ naturally measures the constant rate of change of $y$ with respect to $x$.
concepts.motivation_md: This concept introduces the broad applicability of "rates of change" beyond just velocity. It establishes that understanding how one quantity changes in relation to another is a core mathematical idea relevant across various disciplines, setting the stage for a formal definition.
concepts.recap_md: - Velocity is a specific example of a rate of change (position with respect to time). - Rates of change are crucial in diverse fields like biology, engineering, and economics. - For linear functions $y=mx+b$, the slope $m$ represents a constant rate of change.
concepts.raw_body:
Velocity can be viewed as rate of change-the rate of change of position with respect to time. Rates of change occur in other applications as well. For example:

- A microbiologist might be interested in the rate at which the number of bacteria in a colony changes with time.
- An engineer might be interested in the rate at which the length of a metal rod changes with temperature.
- An economist might be interested in the rate at which production cost changes with the quantity of a product that is manufactured.
- A medical researcher might be interested in the rate at which the radius of an artery changes with the concentration of alcohol in the bloodstream.

Our next objective is to define precisely what is meant by the "rate of change of $y$ with respect to $x$ " when $y$ is a function of $x$. In the case where $y$ is a linear function of $x$, say $y=m x+b$, the slope $m$ is the natural measure of the rate of change of $y$ with respect to $x$. As illustrated in Figure 2.1.8, each 1-unit increase in $x$ anywhere along the line produces an $m$-unit change in $y$, so we see that $y$ changes at a constant rate with respect to $x$ along the line and that $m$ measures this rate of change.
concepts.section_title: TANGENT LINES AND RATES OF CHANGE

concepts.title: Importance of Units in Rates of Change
concepts.one_liner: It is essential to include units when calculating slope and describing rates of change, as changing units can alter the slope.
concepts.summary_md: In applied problems, changing the units of measurement can change the slope of a line. Therefore, it is essential to include the units when calculating the slope and describing rates of change.
concepts.motivation_md: This concept highlights a practical consideration in applied mathematics. Understanding the impact of units ensures that calculations and interpretations of rates of change are physically meaningful and accurate, preventing common errors in real-world applications.
concepts.recap_md: - Units of measurement can affect the numerical value of a slope. - Always include units when calculating and stating rates of change in applied problems.
concepts.raw_body: In applied problems, changing the units of measurement can change the slope of a line, so it is essential to include the units when calculating the slope and describing rates of change. The following example illustrates this.
concepts.section_title: TANGENT LINES AND RATES OF CHANGE

concepts.title: Average vs. Instantaneous Rate of Change
concepts.one_liner: For a general curve $y=f(x)$, the rate of change is not constant, requiring a distinction between average and instantaneous rates of change.
concepts.summary_md: Unlike linear functions where the rate of change is constant, for a general curve $y=f(x)$, the rate of change varies. The change in $y$ for a 1-unit increase in $x$ is greater where the curve rises or falls rapidly. Therefore, we distinguish between the average rate of change over an interval and the instantaneous rate of change at a specific point.
concepts.motivation_md: This concept addresses the limitation of linear models for describing change. It introduces the necessity of differentiating between average and instantaneous rates to accurately describe how quantities change over intervals versus at precise moments, which is crucial for understanding non-linear phenomena.
concepts.recap_md: - The rate of change is constant for linear functions but varies for general curves. - Curves show greater change in $y$ where they rise or fall rapidly. - We must distinguish between average rate of change over an interval and instantaneous rate of change at a point.
concepts.raw_body: Although the rate of change of $y$ with respect to $x$ is constant along a nonvertical line $y=m x+b$, this is not true for a general curve $y=f(x)$. For example, in Figure 2.1.10 the change in $y$ that results from a 1 -unit increase in $x$ tends to have greater magnitude in regions where the curve rises or falls rapidly than in regions where it rises or falls slowly. As with velocity, we will distinguish between the average rate of change over an interval and the instantaneous rate of change at a specific point.
aliases: Difference between average and instantaneous rates of change
concepts.section_title: TANGENT LINES AND RATES OF CHANGE

concepts.title: Average Rate of Change
concepts.one_liner: The average rate of change of $y$ with respect to $x$ over an interval $ ig[x_{0}, x_{1} ig]$ is defined as $r_{	ext{ave}}= rac{f ig(x_{1} ig)-f ig(x_{0} ig)}{x_{1}-x_{0}}$.
concepts.summary_md: If $y=f(x)$, the average rate of change of $y$ with respect to $x$ over the interval $ ig[x_{0}, x_{1} ig]$ is defined by the formula: $$r_{	ext{ave}}= rac{f ig(x_{1} ig)-f ig(x_{0} ig)}{x_{1}-x_{0}}$$ (8)
concepts.motivation_md: This definition provides a precise mathematical way to quantify how much a function's output changes on average over a given input interval. It is a foundational concept for understanding how to measure change when the rate is not constant, leading to the more complex idea of instantaneous change.
concepts.recap_md: - The average rate of change measures how $y$ changes relative to $x$ over an interval. - It is calculated as the "rise over run" between two points on the function's graph. - The formula is $r_{	ext{ave}}= rac{f ig(x_{1} ig)-f ig(x_{0} ig)}{x_{1}-x_{0}}$.
concepts.section_title: TANGENT LINES AND RATES OF CHANGE

concepts.title: Instantaneous Rate of Change
concepts.one_liner: The instantaneous rate of change of $y$ with respect to $x$ at $x_0$ is defined as $r_{	ext{inst}}=	ext{lim}_{x_{1} ightarrow x_{0}}  rac{f ig(x_{1} ig)-f ig(x_{0} ig)}{x_{1}-x_{0}}$.
concepts.summary_md: The instantaneous rate of change of $y$ with respect to $x$ at a specific point $x_0$ is defined as the limit of the average rate of change as the interval shrinks to that point: $$r_{	ext{inst}}=	ext{lim}_{x_{1} ightarrow x_{0}}  rac{f ig(x_{1} ig)-f ig(x_{0} ig)}{x_{1}-x_{0}}$$ (9)
concepts.motivation_md: This definition is central to calculus, providing a way to measure the rate of change at a single, precise moment or point, rather than over an interval. It allows for the analysis of dynamic systems where rates are constantly changing, forming the basis for the concept of the derivative.
concepts.recap_md: - Instantaneous rate of change measures how $y$ changes relative to $x$ at a single point $x_0$. - It is defined using a limit of the average rate of change formula. - The formula is $r_{	ext{inst}}=	ext{lim}_{x_{1} ightarrow x_{0}}  rac{f ig(x_{1} ig)-f ig(x_{0} ig)}{x_{1}-x_{0}}$.
concepts.section_title: TANGENT LINES AND RATES OF CHANGE

concepts.title: Geometric Interpretation of Rate of Change
concepts.one_liner: Geometrically, the average rate of change is the slope of a secant line, and the instantaneous rate of change is the slope of a tangent line.
concepts.summary_md: Geometrically, the average rate of change of $y$ with respect to $x$ over the interval $ ig[x_{0}, x_{1} ig]$ is the slope of the secant line through the points $P ig(x_{0}, f(x_{0}) ig)$ and $Q ig(x_{1}, f(x_{1}) ig)$. The instantaneous rate of change of $y$ with respect to $x$ at $x_{0}$ is the slope of the tangent line at the point $P ig(x_{0}, f(x_{0}) ig)$, since it is the limit of the slopes of the secant lines through $P$.
concepts.motivation_md: This concept provides a visual framework for understanding rates of change. By linking abstract formulas to concrete geometric shapes (secant and tangent lines), it helps learners build intuition about how average and instantaneous changes relate to the shape of a function's graph.
concepts.recap_md: - Average rate of change is geometrically represented by the slope of a secant line. - Instantaneous rate of change is geometrically represented by the slope of a tangent line. - The tangent line's slope is the limit of secant line slopes.
concepts.raw_body: Geometrically, the average rate of change of $y$ with respect to $x$ over the interval $\left[x_{0}, x_{1}\right]$ is the slope of the secant line through the points $P\left(x_{0}, f\left(x_{0}\right)\right)$ and $Q\left(x_{1}, f\left(x_{1}\right)\right)$ (Figure 2.1.11), and the instantaneous rate of change of $y$ with respect to $x$ at $x_{0}$ is the slope of the tangent line at the point $P\left(x_{0}, f\left(x_{0}\right)\right)$ (since it is the limit of the slopes of the secant lines through $P$ ).

concepts.title: Alternative Formulas for Rates of Change
concepts.one_liner: By setting $h=x_{1}-x_{0}$, the formulas for average and instantaneous rates of change can be rewritten using $h$.
concepts.summary_md: By introducing the variable $h = x_1 - x_0$, the formulas for average and instantaneous rates of change can be expressed in an alternative form. The average rate of change becomes $r_{	ext{ave}}= rac{f ig(x_{0}+h ig)-f ig(x_{0} ig)}{h}$, and the instantaneous rate of change becomes $r_{	ext{inst}}=	ext{lim}_{h ightarrow 0}  rac{f ig(x_{0}+h ig)-f ig(x_{0} ig)}{h}$.
concepts.motivation_md: This concept provides an alternative, often more convenient, formulation for rates of change. The $h$-form is particularly useful for algebraic manipulation and is the standard form used in the definition of the derivative, simplifying calculations and theoretical proofs.
concepts.recap_md: - By letting $h=x_{1}-x_{0}$, the rate of change formulas can be rewritten. - The average rate of change is $r_{	ext{ave}}= rac{f ig(x_{0}+h ig)-f ig(x_{0} ig)}{h}$. - The instantaneous rate of change is $r_{	ext{inst}}=	ext{lim}_{h ightarrow 0}  rac{f ig(x_{0}+h ig)-f ig(x_{0} ig)}{h}$.

concepts.title: Rates of Change in Applications
concepts.one_liner: In applied problems, average and instantaneous rates of change must be accompanied by appropriate units.
concepts.summary_md: In applied problems, average and instantaneous rates of change must be accompanied by appropriate units. The units for a rate of change of $y$ with respect to $x$ are obtained by "dividing" the units of $y$ by the units of $x$ and then simplifying. For example, if $y$ is in degrees Fahrenheit and $x$ is in inches, the rate of change has units of degrees Fahrenheit per inch (${ }^{\circ} \mathrm{F} / \mathrm{in}$).
concepts.motivation_md: Understanding the units of rates of change is crucial for interpreting their meaning in real-world applications. Correct units ensure that the calculated rates accurately reflect physical or practical phenomena, allowing for proper analysis and communication of results.
concepts.recap_md:
- Units for a rate of change are obtained by "dividing" the units of $y$ by the units of $x$.
- Simplify units according to standard rules of algebra, e.g., $\mathrm{ft} / \mathrm{s} / \mathrm{s}$ becomes $\mathrm{ft} / \mathrm{s}^{2}$.
concepts.raw_body:
## RATES OF CHANGE IN APPLICATIONS

In applied problems, average and instantaneous rates of change must be accompanied by appropriate units. In general, the units for a rate of change of $y$ with respect to $x$ are obtained by "dividing" the units of $y$ by the units of $x$ and then simplifying according to the standard rules of algebra. Here are some examples:

- If $y$ is in degrees Fahrenheit ( ${ }^{\circ} \mathrm{F}$ ) and $x$ is in inches (in), then a rate of change of $y$ with respect to $x$ has units of degrees Fahrenheit per inch ( ${ }^{\circ} \mathrm{F} / \mathrm{in}$ ).
- If $y$ is in feet per second ( $\mathrm{ft} / \mathrm{s}$ ) and $x$ is in seconds (s), then a rate of change of $y$ with respect to $x$ has units of feet per second per second ( $\mathrm{ft} / \mathrm{s} / \mathrm{s}$ ), which would usually be written as $\mathrm{ft} / \mathrm{s}^{2}$.
- If $y$ is in newton-meters $(\mathrm{N} \cdot \mathrm{m})$ and $x$ is in meters $(\mathrm{m})$, then a rate of change of $y$ with respect to $x$ has units of newtons ( N ), since $\mathrm{N} \cdot \mathrm{m} / \mathrm{m}=\mathrm{N}$.
- If $y$ is in foot-pounds ( $\mathrm{ft} \cdot \mathrm{lb}$ ) and $x$ is in hours (h), then a rate of change of $y$ with respect to $x$ has units of foot-pounds per hour ( $\mathrm{ft} \cdot \mathrm{lb} / \mathrm{h}$ ).

concepts.title: Difference Quotient
concepts.one_liner: The expression $\frac{f(x+h)-f(x)}{h}$ is commonly called the difference quotient.
concepts.summary_md: The expression $\frac{f(x+h)-f(x)}{h}$ is commonly called the difference quotient.
concepts.motivation_md: The difference quotient is fundamental because it represents the average rate of change of a function over a small interval $h$. As $h$ approaches zero, this expression forms the basis for defining the instantaneous rate of change, or derivative, which is a cornerstone of calculus.
concepts.recap_md:
- The difference quotient is the expression $\frac{f(x+h)-f(x)}{h}$.
- It represents the average rate of change of $f(x)$ over the interval $[x, x+h]$.
concepts.raw_body:
The expression

$$
\frac{f(x+h)-f(x)}{h}
$$

that appears in (2) is commonly called the difference quotient.

concepts.title: Introduction to the Derivative
concepts.one_liner: In this section we will discuss the concept of a "derivative," which is the primary mathematical tool that is used to calculate and study rates of change.
concepts.summary_md: The derivative is introduced as the primary mathematical tool used to calculate and study rates of change. It provides a way to understand how quantities change with respect to one another.
concepts.motivation_md: Calculus often deals with how things change. While average rates of change are useful, many real-world phenomena require understanding instantaneous rates. The derivative provides the precise mathematical framework to analyze these instantaneous changes, from velocity to growth rates.
concepts.recap_md:
- The derivative is a core concept in calculus.
- It is the primary mathematical tool for calculating and studying rates of change.
concepts.raw_body: In this section we will discuss the concept of a "derivative," which is the primary mathematical tool that is used to calculate and study rates of change.

concepts.title: Notation for the Derivative at a Point
concepts.one_liner: This limit is so important that it has a special notation: $f^{\prime}\left(x_{0}\right)=\lim _{h \rightarrow 0} \frac{f\[x_{0}+h\]-f\[x_{0}\]}{h}$.
concepts.summary_md: The limit $\lim _{h \rightarrow 0} \frac{f\left(x_{0}+h\right)-f\left(x_{0}\right)}{h}$ is crucial and has special notation: $f^{\prime}\left(x_{0}\right)$. This value can be interpreted either as the slope of the tangent line to the curve $y=f(x)$ at $x=x_{0}$ or as the instantaneous rate of change of $y$ with respect to $x$ at $x=x_{0}$.
concepts.motivation_md: A special notation for this limit is introduced to streamline mathematical communication and highlight its significance. It serves as a concise way to refer to both the slope of a tangent line and the instantaneous rate of change at a specific point, which are central ideas in calculus.
concepts.recap_md:
- The notation $f^{\prime}\left(x_{0}\right)$ represents the limit of the difference quotient at $x_0$.
- It signifies either the slope of the tangent line or the instantaneous rate of change at $x_0$.

concepts.title: The Derivative Function
concepts.one_liner: The function $f^{\prime}$ defined by the formula $f^{\prime}(x)=\lim _{h \rightarrow 0} \frac{f(x+h)-f(x)}{h}$ is called the derivative of $f$ with respect to $x$.
concepts.summary_md: The function $f^{\prime}$ is defined by the formula $f^{\prime}(x)=\lim _{h \rightarrow 0} \frac{f(x+h)-f(x)}{h}$ and is called the derivative of $f$ with respect to $x$. The domain of $f^{\prime}$ consists of all $x$ in the domain of $f$ for which the limit exists.
concepts.motivation_md: Defining the derivative as a function, $f'(x)$, allows us to determine the instantaneous rate of change or the slope of the tangent line at any point $x$ in the function's domain, rather than just a single point. This provides a powerful tool for analyzing the behavior of a function across its entire domain.
concepts.recap_md:
- The derivative function $f^{\prime}(x)$ is defined by the limit of the difference quotient.
- Its domain consists of all $x$ in the domain of $f$ for which the limit exists.
aliases: Definition of a derivative and its interpretations

concepts.title: Derivative as a Slope-Producing Function
concepts.one_liner: You can think of $f^{\prime}$ as a "slope-producing function" in the sense that the value of $f^{\prime}(x)$ at $x=x_{0}$ is the slope of the tangent line to the graph of $f$ at $x=x_{0}$.
concepts.summary_md: The derivative $f^{\prime}$ can be understood as a "slope-producing function." This means that for any $x_{0}$, the value $f^{\prime}(x_{0})$ gives the slope of the tangent line to the graph of $f$ at that point. For example, for $f(x)=x^{2}$, its derivative $f^{\prime}(x)=2x$ yields the tangent slopes at various $x$ values.
concepts.motivation_md: Viewing the derivative as a "slope-producing function" provides a powerful geometric interpretation, allowing us to visualize the steepness and direction of a curve at any point. This understanding is crucial for analyzing the shape of graphs, identifying local extrema, and solving optimization problems.
concepts.recap_md:
- $f^{\prime}$ is a "slope-producing function."
- The value $f^{\prime}(x_{0})$ gives the slope of the tangent line to the graph of $f$ at $x=x_{0}$.
concepts.raw_body: You can think of $f^{\prime}$ as a "slope-producing function" in the sense that the value of $f^{\prime}(x)$ at $x=x_{0}$ is the slope of the tangent line to the graph of $f$ at $x=x_{0}$. This aspect of the derivative is illustrated in Figure 2.2.2, which shows the graphs of $f(x)=x^{2}$ and its derivative $f^{\prime}(x)=2 x$ (obtained in Example 1). The figure illustrates that the values of $f^{\prime}(x)=2 x$ at $x=-2,0$, and 2 correspond to the slopes of the tangent lines to the graph of $f(x)=x^{2}$ at those values of $x$.

concepts.title: Finding an Equation for the Tangent Line
concepts.one_liner: To find an equation for the tangent line to $y=f(x)$ at $x=x_{0}$, evaluate $f(x_0)$, find $f'(x_0)$ for the slope, and use the point-slope form.
concepts.summary_md: To find an equation for the tangent line to $y=f(x)$ at $x=x_{0}$, first evaluate $f\left(x_{0}\right)$ to get the point of tangency $\left(x_{0}, f\left(x_{0}\right)\right)$. Next, find $f^{\prime}(x)$ and evaluate $f^{\prime}\left(x_{0}\right)$ to get the slope $m$. Finally, substitute these values into the point-slope form: $y-f\left(x_{0}\right)=f^{\prime}\left(x_{0}\right)\left(x-x_{0}\right)$.
concepts.motivation_md: Finding the equation of a tangent line is crucial because it provides the best linear approximation of a function near a specific point. This linear approximation simplifies complex functions locally, enabling estimations and predictions, and is fundamental to understanding local behavior and concepts like linearization.
concepts.recap_md:
- Step 1: Evaluate $f\left(x_{0}\right)$ to get the point of tangency $\left(x_{0}, f\left(x_{0}\right)\right)$.
- Step 2: Find $f^{\prime}(x)$ and evaluate $f^{\prime}\left(x_{0}\right)$ to get the slope $m$.
- Step 3: Use the point-slope form: $y-f\left(x_{0}\right)=f^{\prime}\left(x_{0}\right)\left(x-x_{0}\right)$.
concepts.raw_body:
Finding an Equation for the Tangent Line to $y=f(x)$ at $x=x_{0}$.
Step 1. Evaluate $f\left(x_{0}\right)$; the point of tangency is $\left(x_{0}, f\left(x_{0}\right)\right)$.
Step 2. Find $f^{\prime}(x)$ and evaluate $f^{\prime}\left(x_{0}\right)$, which is the slope $m$ of the line.
Step 3. Substitute the value of the slope $m$ and the point $\left(x_{0}, f\left(x_{0}\right)\right)$ into the point-slope form of the line

$$
y-f\left(x_{0}\right)=f^{\prime}\left(x_{0}\right)\left(x-x_{0}\right)
$$

or, equivalently,

$$
\begin{equation*}
y=f\left(x_{0}\right)+f^{\prime}\left(x_{0}\right)\left(x-x_{0}\right) \tag{3}
\end{equation*}
$$

concepts.title: Instantaneous Velocity Function
concepts.one_liner: If $s=f(t)$ is the position function of a particle, then the instantaneous velocity function is $v(t)=f^{\prime}(t)=\lim _{h \rightarrow 0} \frac{f(t+h)-f(t)}{h}$.
concepts.summary_md: If $s=f(t)$ represents the position function of a particle in rectilinear motion, its instantaneous velocity at any time $t$ is given by the derivative of $f$. The function $v(t)=f^{\prime}(t)=\lim _{h \rightarrow 0} \frac{f(t+h)-f(t)}{h}$ is called the instantaneous velocity function or, more simply, the velocity function of the particle.
concepts.motivation_md: Defining instantaneous velocity as the derivative of the position function allows for a precise description of a particle's motion at any exact moment in time. This is crucial for analyzing dynamic systems, predicting future positions, and understanding concepts like acceleration, which depend on how velocity itself changes.
concepts.recap_md:
- If $s=f(t)$ is the position function, then $v(t)$ is the instantaneous velocity.
- $v(t)$ is defined as the derivative of the position function: $v(t)=f^{\prime}(t)$.

concepts.title: Introduction to Differentiability
concepts.one_liner: It is possible that the limit that defines the derivative of a function $f$ may not exist at certain points in the domain of $f$.
concepts.summary_md: The limit that defines the derivative of a function $f$ may not exist at certain points in its domain. At these points, the derivative is undefined. This possibility necessitates a formal definition of differentiability.
concepts.motivation_md: This concept introduces the idea that a derivative isn't always defined, setting the stage for a formal definition of "differentiable" to precisely identify where a function's derivative exists.
concepts.recap_md: - The derivative of a function may not exist at all points in its domain. - At points where the derivative's defining limit does not exist, the derivative is undefined.
concepts.raw_body: It is possible that the limit that defines the derivative of a function $f$ may not exist at certain points in the domain of $f$. At such points the derivative is undefined. To account for this possibility we make the following definition.

concepts.title: Differentiable at a Point
concepts.one_liner: A function $f$ is said to be differentiable at $ oldsymbol{x}_{\mathbf{0}}$ if the limit $f^{\prime}\left(x_{0}\right)=\lim _{h \rightarrow 0} \frac{f\left(x_{0}+h\right)-f\left(x_{0}\right)}{h}$ exists.
concepts.summary_md: A function $f$ is differentiable at $x_0$ if the limit $f^{\prime}\left(x_{0}\right)=\lim _{h \rightarrow 0} \frac{f\left(x_{0}+h\right)-f\left(x_{0}\right)}{h}$ exists. If $f$ is differentiable at each point of an open interval $(a, b)$, then it is differentiable on $(\boldsymbol{a}, \boldsymbol{b})$. This extends to infinite open intervals, and if differentiable on $(-\infty,+\infty)$, it is differentiable everywhere.
concepts.motivation_md: This definition provides a precise mathematical criterion for when a function has a derivative at a specific point or over an interval, formalizing the concept introduced previously and enabling rigorous analysis.
concepts.recap_md: - A function $f$ is differentiable at $x_0$ if the limit defining $f'(x_0)$ exists. - Differentiability can also be defined over open intervals, including infinite ones.

concepts.title: Geometric Interpretation of Differentiability
concepts.one_liner: Geometrically, a function $f$ is differentiable at $x_{0}$ if the graph of $f$ has a tangent line at $x_{0}$.
concepts.summary_md: A function $f$ is differentiable at $x_0$ if its graph has a tangent line at that point. Conversely, $f$ is not differentiable if secant lines do not approach a unique nonvertical limiting position. Common failures of differentiability, even for continuous functions, include corner points (where left and right limits of secant slopes differ) and points of vertical tangency (where secant slopes approach $+\infty$ or $-\infty$).
concepts.motivation_md: This interpretation provides an intuitive visual understanding of differentiability, connecting the abstract limit definition to the concrete shape of a function's graph. It also highlights common scenarios where differentiability fails.
concepts.recap_md: - Differentiability at $x_0$ means the graph has a tangent line at $x_0$. - Functions are not differentiable at corner points or points of vertical tangency. - At corner points, left and right limits of secant slopes differ.
concepts.raw_body:
Geometrically, a function $f$ is differentiable at $x_{0}$ if the graph of $f$ has a tangent line at $x_{0}$. Thus, $f$ is not differentiable at any point $x_{0}$ where the secant lines from $P\left(x_{0}, f\left(x_{0}\right)\right)$ to points $Q(x, f(x))$ distinct from $P$ do not approach a unique nonvertical limiting position as $x \rightarrow x_{0}$. Figure 2.2.6 illustrates two common ways in which a function that is continuous at $x_{0}$ can fail to be differentiable at $x_{0}$. These can be described informally as

- corner points
- points of vertical tangency

At a corner point, the slopes of the secant lines have different limits from the left and from the right, and hence the two-sided limit that defines the derivative does not exist (Figure 2.2.7). At a point of vertical tangency the slopes of the secant lines approach $+\infty$ or $-\infty$ from the left and from the right (Figure 2.2.8), so again the limit that defines the derivative does not exist.

concepts.title: Differentiability and Magnification
concepts.one_liner: Differentiability at $x_{0}$ can also be described informally in terms of the behavior of the graph of $f$ under increasingly stronger magnification at the point $P\left(x_{0}, f\left(x_{0}\right)\right)$.
concepts.summary_md: Differentiability at $x_0$ can be understood by observing the graph of $f$ under strong magnification at $P(x_0, f(x_0))$. If $f$ is differentiable, the magnified graph appears as a nonvertical line (the tangent line). At a corner point, the corner persists under magnification, never looking like a nonvertical line. At a point of vertical tangency, the magnified graph appears as a vertical line.
concepts.motivation_md: This informal description offers an intuitive way to visualize differentiability, making the concept more accessible by relating it to how a graph "smooths out" or reveals its true nature when zoomed in.
concepts.recap_md: - If $f$ is differentiable at $x_0$, its graph looks like a nonvertical line under strong magnification. - At a corner point, the corner persists under magnification. - At a point of vertical tangency, the graph looks like a vertical line under magnification.

concepts.title: Contrapositive Form of a Theorem
concepts.one_liner: A theorem that says "If statement $A$ is true, then statement $B$ is true" is equivalent to the theorem that says "If statement $B$ is not true, then statement $A$ is not true."
concepts.summary_md: A theorem stating "If A, then B" is logically equivalent to its contrapositive form: "If not B, then not A." These two statements convey the same truth. For example, the theorem "If $f$ is differentiable at $x_0$, then $f$ is continuous at $x_0$" has the contrapositive form "If a function $f$ is not continuous at $x_{0}$, then $f$ is not differentiable at $x_{0} .^{\prime\prime}$
concepts.motivation_md: Understanding contrapositive forms is crucial for logical reasoning in mathematics, allowing for alternative ways to prove or understand theorems, especially when direct proofs are difficult or less intuitive.
concepts.recap_md: - The contrapositive of "If A, then B" is "If not B, then not A." - A theorem and its contrapositive are logically equivalent. - This logical equivalence provides an alternative way to express or prove a theorem.
concepts.raw_body: A theorem that says "If statement $A$ is true, then statement $B$ is true" is equivalent to the theorem that says "If statement $B$ is not true, then statement $A$ is not true." The two theorems are called contrapositive forms of one another. Thus, Theorem 2.2.3 can be rewritten in contrapositive form as "If a function $f$ is not continuous at $x_{0}$, then $f$ is not differentiable at $x_{0} .^{\prime \prime}$

concepts.title: Relationship Between Differentiability and Continuity
concepts.one_liner: The next theorem shows that functions are not differentiable at points of discontinuity by proving that if $f$ is differentiable at a point, then it must be continuous at that point.
concepts.summary_md: Functions are known to be non-differentiable at corner points and points of vertical tangency. The upcoming theorem extends this understanding by demonstrating that functions are also not differentiable at points of discontinuity. This will be proven by showing that differentiability at a point implies continuity at that same point.
concepts.motivation_md: This introduction sets the stage for a fundamental theorem in calculus, establishing a crucial relationship between two core properties of functions: differentiability and continuity. It highlights that differentiability is a stronger condition than continuity.
concepts.recap_md: - Functions are not differentiable at corner points or points of vertical tangency. - The upcoming theorem will show that functions are also not differentiable at points of discontinuity. - This will be proven by showing that differentiability implies continuity.
concepts.raw_body: We already know that functions are not differentiable at corner points and points of vertical tangency. The next theorem shows that functions are not differentiable at points of discontinuity. We will do this by proving that if $f$ is differentiable at a point, then it must be continuous at that point.

concepts.title: Differentiability Implies Continuity
concepts.one_liner: If a function $f$ is differentiable at $x_{0}$, then $f$ is continuous at $x_{0}$.
concepts.summary_md: THEOREM 2.2.3 states a fundamental relationship: If a function $f$ is differentiable at a specific point $x_0$, then it necessarily follows that $f$ must also be continuous at that same point $x_0$.
concepts.motivation_md: This theorem establishes a foundational link between differentiability and continuity, proving that a "smooth" function (differentiable) must also be "unbroken" (continuous). This simplifies analysis by showing that differentiability implies a certain level of well-behavedness.
concepts.recap_md: - Differentiability at a point $x_0$ implies continuity at $x_0$. - This means if a function has a derivative at a point, it must be continuous there.
concepts.raw_body: ### 2.2.3 THEOREM If a function $f$ is differentiable at $x_{0}$, then $f$ is continuous at $x_{0}$.

concepts.title: Converse of Differentiability Implies Continuity is False
concepts.one_liner: The converse of Theorem 2.2.3 is false; that is, a function may be continuous at a point but not differentiable at that point.
concepts.summary_md: It is important to note that the converse of Theorem 2.2.3 is false: continuity at a point does not guarantee differentiability at that point. A function can be continuous but not differentiable, such as at corner points of continuous functions. For instance, $f(x)=|x|$ is continuous at $x=0$ but is not differentiable there.
concepts.motivation_md: This warning prevents a common misconception, clarifying that while differentiability implies continuity, the reverse is not true. It emphasizes that continuity is a necessary but not sufficient condition for differentiability.
concepts.recap_md: - The converse of "Differentiability implies Continuity" is false. - A function can be continuous at a point but not differentiable there. - Corner points, like in $f(x)=|x|$ at $x=0$, are examples of this.
concepts.raw_body:
## WARNING

The converse of Theorem 2.2.3 is false; that is, a function may be continuous at a point but not differentiable at that point. This occurs, for example, at corner points of continuous functions. For instance, $f(x)=|x|$ is continuous at $x=0$ but not differentiable there (Example 6).

concepts.title: Historical Significance of Differentiability and Continuity
concepts.one_liner: The relationship between continuity and differentiability was of great historical significance in the development of calculus.
concepts.summary_md: In the early nineteenth century, mathematicians believed that if a continuous function had many points of nondifferentiability, these points would be separated by smooth curve segments. This misconception was corrected by discoveries from Bernhard Bolzano (1834) and Karl Weierstrass (1860), who constructed continuous functions not differentiable at any point. This made mathematicians distrustful of geometric intuition, relying more on precise proof.
concepts.motivation_md: This concept highlights how early mathematicians' intuition about continuous functions was challenged by the discovery of nowhere-differentiable continuous functions. It emphasizes the need for rigorous mathematical proof over geometric intuition, a foundational shift in calculus.
concepts.recap_md: - Early mathematicians mistakenly thought continuous functions with many non-differentiable points would have smooth segments between them.- Bolzano (1834) and Weierstrass (1860) showed that continuous functions can be nowhere differentiable.- This led to greater reliance on rigorous proof over geometric intuition in mathematics.- Such functions are now fundamental in the study of fractals.
concepts.raw_body:
The relationship between continuity and differentiability was of great historical significance in the development of calculus. In the early nineteenth century mathematicians believed that if a continuous function had many points of nondifferentiability, these points, like the tips of a sawblade, would have to be separated from one another and joined by smooth curve segments (Figure 2.2.12). This misconception was corrected by a series of discoveries beginning in 1834. In that year a Bohemian priest, philosopher, and mathematician named Bernhard Bolzano discovered a procedure for constructing a continuous function that is not differentiable at any point. Later, in 1860, the great German mathematician Karl Weierstrass (biography on p. 102) produced the first formula for such a function. The graphs of such functions are impossible to draw; it is as if the corners are so numerous that any segment of the curve, when suitably enlarged, reveals more corners. The discovery of these functions was important in that it made mathematicians distrustful of their geometric intuition and more reliant on precise mathematical proof. Recently, such functions have started to play a fundamental role in the study of geometric objects called fractals. Fractals have revealed an order to natural phenomena that were previously dismissed as random and chaotic.
