Bernhard Bolzano (1781-1848) Bolzano, the son of an art dealer, was born in Prague, Bohemia (Czech Republic). He was educated at the University of Prague, and eventually won enough mathematical fame to be recommended for a mathematics chair there. However, Bolzano became an ordained Roman Catholic priest, and in 1805 he was appointed to a chair of Philosophy at the University of Prague. Bolzano was a man of great human compassion; he spoke out for educational reform, he voiced the right of individual conscience over government demands, and he lectured on the absurdity
of war and militarism. His views so disenchanted Emperor Franz I of Austria that the emperor pressed the Archbishop of Prague to have Bolzano recant his statements. Bolzano refused and was then forced to retire in 1824 on a small pension. Bolzano's main contribution to mathematics was philosophical. His work helped convince mathematicians that sound mathematics must ultimately rest on rigorous proof rather than intuition. In addition to his work in mathematics, Bolzano investigated problems concerning space, force, and wave propagation.

concepts.title: Left-hand derivative
concepts.one_liner: The left-hand derivative is defined as $f_{-}^{\prime}(x)=\lim _{h \rightarrow 0^{-}} \frac{f(x+h)-f(x)}{h}$.
concepts.summary_md: If a function $f$ is defined on a closed interval $[a, b]$ but not outside that interval, its derivative $f^{\prime}$ is not defined at the endpoints because derivatives are two-sided limits. To address this, we define the left-hand derivative as $f_{-}^{\prime}(x)=\lim _{h \rightarrow 0^{-}} \frac{f(x+h)-f(x)}{h}$.
concepts.motivation_md: Standard derivatives require two-sided limits, which are not possible at the endpoints of a closed interval where a function is defined. Left-hand derivatives allow us to discuss differentiability at the left endpoint or when approaching a point from the left.
concepts.recap_md: - The left-hand derivative $f_{-}^{\prime}(x)$ uses a limit as $h \rightarrow 0^{-}$.- It addresses cases where a function is defined only on an interval, like at a right endpoint.- It represents the slope of the tangent line approached from the left.
concepts.raw_body:
If a function $f$ is defined on a closed interval $[a, b]$ but not outside that interval, then $f^{\prime}$ is not defined at the endpoints of the interval because derivatives are two-sided limits. To deal with this we define left-hand derivatives and right-hand derivatives by

$$
f_{-}^{\prime}(x)=\lim _{h \rightarrow 0^{-}} \frac{f(x+h)-f(x)}{h} \quad \text { and } \quad f_{+}^{\prime}(x)=\lim _{h \rightarrow 0^{+}} \frac{f(x+h)-f(x)}{h}
$$

concepts.title: Right-hand derivative
concepts.one_liner: The right-hand derivative is defined as $f_{+}^{\prime}(x)=\lim _{h \rightarrow 0^{+}} \frac{f(x+h)-f(x)}{h}$.
concepts.summary_md: If a function $f$ is defined on a closed interval $[a, b]$ but not outside that interval, its derivative $f^{\prime}$ is not defined at the endpoints because derivatives are two-sided limits. To address this, we define the right-hand derivative as $f_{+}^{\prime}(x)=\lim _{h \rightarrow 0^{+}} \frac{f(x+h)-f(x)}{h}$.
concepts.motivation_md: Standard derivatives require two-sided limits, which are not possible at the endpoints of a closed interval where a function is defined. Right-hand derivatives allow us to discuss differentiability at the right endpoint or when approaching a point from the right.
concepts.recap_md: - The right-hand derivative $f_{+}^{\prime}(x)$ uses a limit as $h \rightarrow 0^{+}$.- It addresses cases where a function is defined only on an interval, like at a left endpoint.- It represents the slope of the tangent line approached from the right.

f_{-}^{\prime}(x)=\lim _{h \rightarrow 0^{-}} \frac{f(x+h)-f(x)}{h} \quad \text { and } \quad f_{+}^{\prime}(x)=\lim _{h \rightarrow 0^{+}} \frac{f(x+h)-f(x)}{h}

concepts.title: One-sided derivatives
concepts.one_liner: Left-hand and right-hand derivatives are collectively called one-sided derivatives.
concepts.summary_md: Left-hand and right-hand derivatives are called one-sided derivatives. Geometrically, $f_{-}^{\prime}(x)$ is the limit of the slopes of the secant lines as $x$ is approached from the left, and $f_{+}^{\prime}(x)$ is the limit of the slopes of the secant lines as $x$ is approached from the right.
concepts.motivation_md: One-sided derivatives are necessary to define differentiability at the endpoints of a closed interval or to analyze points where a function might have a sharp corner or cusp, where the two-sided derivative does not exist.

concepts.title: Differentiable on an interval
concepts.one_liner: A function $f$ is differentiable on an interval if it is differentiable at all interior points and the appropriate one-sided derivative exists at each included endpoint.
concepts.summary_md: A function $f$ is differentiable on an interval, such as $[a, b]$ or $[a,+\infty)$, if it is differentiable at all points *inside* the interval. Additionally, for any included endpoint, the *appropriate one-sided derivative* must exist at that endpoint.
concepts.motivation_md: The standard definition of differentiability applies to open intervals. This definition extends the concept to closed or half-open intervals, allowing us to discuss differentiability for functions defined over a specific domain, including their boundaries.
concepts.recap_md: - Differentiability on an interval requires differentiability at all interior points.- At included endpoints, the appropriate one-sided derivative must exist.- This definition applies to various interval types, including closed and half-open intervals.
concepts.raw_body: In general, we will say that $f$ is differentiable on an interval of the form $[a, b],[a,+\infty)$, $(-\infty, b],[a, b)$, or $(a, b]$ if it is differentiable at all points inside the interval and the appropriate one-sided derivative exists at each included endpoint.

concepts.title: Continuity and one-sided derivatives
concepts.one_liner: A function $f$ is continuous from the left where the left-hand derivative exists, and continuous from the right where the right-hand derivative exists.
concepts.summary_md: It can be proved that a function $f$ is continuous from the left at those points where the left-hand derivative exists. Similarly, the function is continuous from the right at those points where the right-hand derivative exists.
concepts.motivation_md: This relationship establishes a direct link between the existence of one-sided derivatives and one-sided continuity. It's a useful property for analyzing function behavior at endpoints or points where a function might not be fully differentiable but still exhibits continuity from one side.
concepts.recap_md: - Existence of a left-hand derivative implies continuity from the left.- Existence of a right-hand derivative implies continuity from the right.- This extends the general differentiability implies continuity rule to one-sided cases.
concepts.raw_body: It can be proved that a function $f$ is continuous from the left at those points where the left-hand derivative exists and is continuous from the right at those points where the right-hand derivative exists.

concepts.title: Common derivative notations
concepts.one_liner: Differentiation, the process of finding a derivative, is commonly denoted by $f^{\prime}(x)$, $\frac{d}{d x}[f(x)]$, $D_{x}[f(x)]$, $y^{\prime}(x)$, or $\frac{d y}{d x}$.
concepts.summary_md: The process of finding a derivative is called differentiation, an operation that associates a function $f^{\prime}$ with $f$. Common notations for the derivative when the independent variable is $x$ include $f^{\prime}(x)$, $\frac{d}{d x}[f(x)]$, and $D_{x}[f(x)]$. For a dependent variable $y=f(x)$, notations like $y^{\prime}(x)$ and $\frac{d y}{d x}$ are also used.
concepts.motivation_md: Understanding various derivative notations is crucial for reading and communicating mathematical ideas effectively. Different contexts or historical traditions might favor one notation over another, so familiarity ensures clarity and avoids confusion.
concepts.recap_md: - Differentiation is the process of finding a derivative.- Common notations include $f^{\prime}(x)$, $\frac{d}{d x}[f(x)]$, and $D_{x}[f(x)]$.- For $y=f(x)$, notations like $y^{\prime}(x)$ and $\frac{d y}{d x}$ are used.- The value at a point $x_0$ is denoted by adding `|` with $x=x_0$ or simply $f^{\prime}(x_0)$.
concepts.raw_body:
The process of finding a derivative is called differentiation. You can think of differentiation as an operation on functions that associates a function $f^{\prime}$ with a function $f$. When the independent variable is $x$, the differentiation operation is also commonly denoted by

$$
f^{\prime}(x)=\frac{d}{d x}[f(x)] \quad \text { or } \quad f^{\prime}(x)=D_{x}[f(x)]
$$

In the case where there is a dependent variable $y=f(x)$, the derivative is also commonly denoted by

$$
f^{\prime}(x)=y^{\prime}(x) \quad \text { or } \quad f^{\prime}(x)=\frac{d y}{d x}
$$

With the above notations, the value of the derivative at a point $x_{0}$ can be expressed as

$$
f^{\prime}\left(x_{0}\right)=\left.\frac{d}{d x}[f(x)]\right|_{x=x_{0}}, \quad f^{\prime}\left(x_{0}\right)=\left.D_{x}[f(x)]\right|_{x=x_{0}}, \quad f^{\prime}\left(x_{0}\right)=y^{\prime}\left(x_{0}\right), \quad f^{\prime}\left(x_{0}\right)=\left.\frac{d y}{d x}\right|_{x=x_{0}}
$$

concepts.title: Differentiation
concepts.one_liner: The process of finding a derivative is called differentiation.
concepts.summary_md: Differentiation is defined as the process of finding a derivative. It can be thought of as an operation on functions that associates a new function, $f^{\prime}$, with an original function, $f$.
concepts.motivation_md: Differentiation is a fundamental operation in calculus that allows us to determine rates of change, slopes of tangent lines, and optimize functions. It provides a powerful tool for analyzing how quantities change in relation to one another.
concepts.recap_md: - Differentiation is the process of calculating a derivative.- It transforms a function $f$ into its derivative function $f^{\prime}$.- It is a core operation in calculus.
concepts.raw_body: The process of finding a derivative is called differentiation. You can think of differentiation as an operation on functions that associates a function $f^{\prime}$ with a function $f$. When the independent variable is $x$, the differentiation operation is also commonly denoted by

concepts.title: Increment
concepts.one_liner: If a variable $w$ changes from some initial value $w_{0}$ to some final value $w_{1}$, then the final value minus the initial value is called an increment in $w$ and is denoted by $\Delta w=w_{1}-w_{0}$.
concepts.summary_md: An increment in a variable $w$ is defined as the change from an initial value $w_0$ to a final value $w_1$. It is calculated as the final value minus the initial value, denoted by $\Delta w = w_1 - w_0$.
concepts.motivation_md: Increments are fundamental for understanding rates of change. They quantify how much a variable has changed, which is essential for defining derivatives and understanding slopes of secant lines.
concepts.recap_md: - An increment $\Delta w$ represents the change in a variable $w$. - It is calculated as the final value $w_1$ minus the initial value $w_0$, so $\Delta w = w_1 - w_0$.

concepts.title: Alternative derivative formulas
concepts.one_liner: The derivative can be expressed using increments as $f^{\prime}(x)=\lim _{\Delta x \rightarrow 0} \frac{f(x+\Delta x)-f(x)}{\Delta x}$ or without increments as $f^{\prime}(x)=\lim _{w \rightarrow x} \frac{f(w)-f(x)}{w-x}$.
concepts.summary_md: The derivative $f'(x)$ can be written using an increment $\Delta x$ as $\lim _{\Delta x \rightarrow 0} \frac{f(x+\Delta x)-f(x)}{\Delta x}$. If $y=f(x)$, the numerator is $\Delta y=f(x+\Delta x)-f(x)$, leading to $\frac{d y}{d x}=\lim _{\Delta x \rightarrow 0} \frac{\Delta y}{\Delta x}$. Alternatively, by letting $w=x+h$, the derivative can be expressed as $\lim _{w \rightarrow x} \frac{f(w)-f(x)}{w-x}$.
concepts.motivation_md: Different forms of the derivative definition can be more convenient or insightful depending on the context. These alternative formulas provide flexibility in calculating derivatives and understanding their geometric and analytical interpretations.
concepts.recap_md: - The derivative $f'(x)$ can be defined using increments as $\lim _{\Delta x \rightarrow 0} \frac{f(x+\Delta x)-f(x)}{\Delta x}$. - If $y=f(x)$, this is equivalent to $\frac{d y}{d x}=\lim _{\Delta x \rightarrow 0} \frac{\Delta y}{\Delta x}$. - Another form, not using increments, is $f^{\prime}(x)=\lim _{w \rightarrow x} \frac{f(w)-f(x)}{w-x}$.

concepts.title: Derivative notation in physical applications
concepts.one_liner: When letters other than $x$ and $y$ are used for the independent and dependent variables, the derivative notations must be adjusted accordingly, such as $v(t)=\frac{d s}{d t}$ for position $s=f(t)$.
concepts.summary_md: When variables other than $x$ and $y$ are used for independent and dependent variables, derivative notations are adjusted. For instance, if $s=f(t)$ is a position function, the velocity function $v(t)$ is expressed as $v(t)=\frac{d s}{d t}=\lim _{\Delta t \rightarrow 0} \frac{\Delta s}{\Delta t}=\lim _{\Delta t \rightarrow 0} \frac{f(t+\Delta t)-f(t)}{\Delta t}$.
concepts.motivation_md: In physical applications, variables often have specific meanings (e.g., time $t$, position $s$, velocity $v$). Adapting derivative notation to these variables makes the mathematical expressions more intuitive and directly reflective of the physical quantities they represent.
concepts.recap_md: - Derivative notation adapts to the specific variables used for independent and dependent quantities. - For a position function $s=f(t)$, velocity $v(t)$ is denoted as $\frac{d s}{d t}$. - This notation still represents the limit definition: $v(t)=\lim _{\Delta t \rightarrow 0} \frac{\Delta s}{\Delta t}$.

concepts.title: Introduction to Techniques of Differentiation
concepts.one_liner: This section develops theorems to calculate derivatives more efficiently, moving beyond the limit definition.
concepts.summary_md: Previously, the derivative of a function $f$ was defined as a limit, which was used to calculate simple derivatives. This section aims to develop important theorems that will enable the calculation of derivatives more efficiently.
concepts.motivation_md: Calculating derivatives directly from the limit definition can be tedious and time-consuming, especially for complex functions. Developing differentiation rules (theorems) provides a systematic and much faster way to find derivatives.
concepts.recap_md: - The derivative was previously defined using limits. - This section introduces theorems to simplify derivative calculations. - The goal is to calculate derivatives more efficiently.
concepts.raw_body: In the last section we defined the derivative of a function $f$ as a limit, and we used that limit to calculate a few simple derivatives. In this section we will develop some important theorems that will enable us to calculate derivatives more efficiently.

concepts.title: The Derivative of a Constant Function
concepts.one_liner: The derivative of a constant function is 0; that is, if $c$ is any real number, then $\frac{d}{d x}[c]=0$.
concepts.summary_md: Theorem 2.3.1 states that the derivative of a constant function is 0. This means for any real number $c$, the derivative with respect to $x$ of $c$ is $\frac{d}{d x}[c]=0$.
concepts.motivation_md: This theorem provides the most basic differentiation rule. It reflects the intuitive idea that a constant function has no change, and thus its rate of change (derivative) is zero.
concepts.recap_md: - A constant function has a value that does not change. - The derivative of a constant function is always 0. - Mathematically, $\frac{d}{d x}[c]=0$ for any real number $c$.

concepts.title: Extended Power Rule
concepts.one_liner: The Extended Power Rule states that if $r$ is any real number, then $\frac{d}{d x}\left[x^{r}\right]=r x^{r-1}$.
concepts.summary_md: Theorem 2.3.3, known as the Extended Power Rule, provides a formula for differentiating functions of the form $x^r$. It states that if $r$ is any real number, then the derivative of $x^r$ with respect to $x$ is given by $\frac{d}{d x}\left[x^{r}\right]=r x^{r-1}$.
concepts.motivation_md: The Power Rule is a fundamental and widely used differentiation technique. It significantly simplifies finding derivatives of polynomial and rational functions, which would be very complex using the limit definition.
concepts.recap_md: - The Power Rule applies to functions of the form $x^r$, where $r$ is any real number. - To find the derivative, bring the exponent $r$ down as a coefficient. - Then, subtract 1 from the original exponent: $\frac{d}{d x}\left[x^{r}\right]=r x^{r-1}$.
aliases: Derivative of x^r for real r
Extension of the Power Rule to Real Exponents
The Power Rule (for positive integer exponents)

concepts.title: Constant Multiple Rule
concepts.one_liner: The Constant Multiple Rule states that if $f$ is differentiable at $x$ and $c$ is any real number, then $\frac{d}{d x}[c f(x)]=c \frac{d}{d x}[f(x)]$.
concepts.summary_md: Theorem 2.3.4, the Constant Multiple Rule, states that if a function $f$ is differentiable at $x$ and $c$ is any real number, then the function $c f$ is also differentiable at $x$. The derivative of a constant times a function is the constant times the derivative of the function: $\frac{d}{d x}[c f(x)]=c \frac{d}{d x}[f(x)]$.
concepts.motivation_md: This rule allows us to easily differentiate functions that are scaled by a constant. Instead of applying the limit definition to the entire scaled function, we can simply pull the constant out and differentiate the function itself, making calculations much simpler.
concepts.recap_md: - If a function $f(x)$ is multiplied by a constant $c$, its derivative is also multiplied by $c$. - The constant $c$ can be "pulled out" of the differentiation operation. - The rule is expressed as $\frac{d}{d x}[c f(x)]=c \frac{d}{d x}[f(x)]$.

concepts.title: Sum and Difference Rules
concepts.one_liner: The Sum and Difference Rules state that if $f$ and $g$ are differentiable at $x$, then $\frac{d}{d x}[f(x) \pm g(x)]=\frac{d}{d x}[f(x)] \pm \frac{d}{d x}[g(x)]$.
concepts.summary_md: Theorem 2.3.5, the Sum and Difference Rules, states that if two functions $f$ and $g$ are differentiable at $x$, then their sum $f+g$ and difference $f-g$ are also differentiable at $x$. The derivative of a sum is the sum of the derivatives: $\frac{d}{d x}[f(x)+g(x)]=\frac{d}{d x}[f(x)]+\frac{d}{d x}[g(x)]$. Similarly, the derivative of a difference is the difference of the derivatives: $\frac{d}{d x}[f(x)-g(x)]=\frac{d}{d x}[f(x)]-\frac{d}{d x}[g(x)]$.
concepts.motivation_md: These rules are crucial for differentiating functions composed of sums or differences of simpler functions. They allow us to break down complex expressions into manageable parts, applying differentiation rules to each term independently, which greatly simplifies the process.
concepts.recap_md: - The derivative of a sum of functions is the sum of their individual derivatives. - The derivative of a difference of functions is the difference of their individual derivatives. - This means $\frac{d}{d x}[f(x) \pm g(x)]=\frac{d}{d x}[f(x)] \pm \frac{d}{d x}[g(x)]$.

concepts.title: Differentiating Polynomials using Sum, Difference, and Constant Multiple Rules
concepts.one_liner: The constant multiple rule together with the extended versions of the sum and difference rules can be used to differentiate any polynomial.
concepts.summary_md: Formulas for sums and differences of two functions can be extended to any finite number of functions. For example, $(f+g+h)^{\prime}=f^{\prime}+g^{\prime}+h^{\prime}$. The constant multiple rule, along with these extended sum and difference rules, allows for the differentiation of any polynomial.
concepts.motivation_md: This concept explains how to apply basic differentiation rules (sum, difference, constant multiple) to more complex expressions like polynomials, which are common in calculus. It shows how to combine these fundamental rules to handle functions with multiple terms.
concepts.recap_md: - The sum and difference rules can be extended to any finite number of functions.- For example, $(f+g+h)^{\prime}=f^{\prime}+g^{\prime}+h^{\prime}$.- These rules, combined with the constant multiple rule, enable differentiating any polynomial.
concepts.raw_body:
Although Formulas (9) and (10) are stated for sums and differences of two functions, they can be extended to any finite number of functions. For example, by grouping and applying Formula (9) twice we obtain

$$
(f+g+h)^{\prime}=[(f+g)+h]^{\prime}=(f+g)^{\prime}+h^{\prime}=f^{\prime}+g^{\prime}+h^{\prime}
$$

As illustrated in the following example, the constant multiple rule together with the extended versions of the sum and difference rules can be used to differentiate any polynomial.

concepts.title: Higher Derivatives
concepts.one_liner: If $f^{\prime}$ is differentiable, then its derivative is denoted by $f^{\prime \prime}$ and is called the second derivative of $f$.
concepts.summary_md: The derivative $f^{\prime}$ of a function $f$ is itself a function and may have a derivative. If $f^{\prime}$ is differentiable, its derivative is $f^{\prime \prime}$, the second derivative. This process can continue to obtain third, fourth, and higher derivatives, denoted $f^{\prime}, f^{\prime \prime}, f^{\prime \prime \prime}, f^{(4)}, \ldots$ or $\frac{d y}{d x}, \frac{d^{2} y}{d x^{2}}, \frac{d^{3} y}{d x^{3}}, \ldots$. The number of times $f$ is differentiated is the order of the derivative, with $f^{(n)}(x)$ or $\frac{d^{n} y}{d x^{n}}$ denoting the $n$th order derivative.
concepts.motivation_md: Higher derivatives are crucial for understanding more complex properties of functions, such as concavity, inflection points, and acceleration in physics. They also form the basis for Taylor series and solving differential equations.
concepts.recap_md: - The derivative of a function can itself be differentiated, leading to higher-order derivatives.- The second derivative is denoted $f^{\prime \prime}$ or $\frac{d^{2} y}{d x^{2}}$.- The $n$th order derivative is denoted $f^{(n)}(x)$ or $\frac{d^{n} y}{d x^{n}}$.
concepts.raw_body:
The derivative $f^{\prime}$ of a function $f$ is itself a function and hence may have a derivative of its own. If $f^{\prime}$ is differentiable, then its derivative is denoted by $f^{\prime \prime}$ and is called the second derivative of $f$. As long as we have differentiability, we can continue the process
of differentiating to obtain third, fourth, fifth, and even higher derivatives of $f$. These successive derivatives are denoted by

$$
f^{\prime}, \quad f^{\prime \prime}=\left(f^{\prime}\right)^{\prime}, \quad f^{\prime \prime \prime}=\left(f^{\prime \prime}\right)^{\prime}, \quad f^{(4)}=\left(f^{\prime \prime \prime}\right)^{\prime}, \quad f^{(5)}=\left(f^{(4)}\right)^{\prime}, \ldots
$$

If $y=f(x)$, then successive derivatives can also be denoted by

$$
y^{\prime}, \quad y^{\prime \prime}, \quad y^{\prime \prime \prime}, \quad y^{(4)}, \quad y^{(5)}, \ldots
$$

Other common notations are

$$
\begin{aligned}
y^{\prime} & =\frac{d y}{d x}=\frac{d}{d x}[f(x)] \\
y^{\prime \prime} & =\frac{d^{2} y}{d x^{2}}=\frac{d}{d x}\left[\frac{d}{d x}[f(x)]\right]=\frac{d^{2}}{d x^{2}}[f(x)] \\
y^{\prime \prime \prime} & =\frac{d^{3} y}{d x^{3}}=\frac{d}{d x}\left[\frac{d^{2}}{d x^{2}}[f(x)]\right]=\frac{d^{3}}{d x^{3}}[f(x)] \\
\vdots & \vdots
\end{aligned}
$$

These are called, in succession, the first derivative, the second derivative, the third derivative, and so forth. The number of times that $f$ is differentiated is called the order of the derivative. A general $n$th order derivative can be denoted by

$$
\begin{equation*}
\frac{d^{n} y}{d x^{n}}=f^{(n)}(x)=\frac{d^{n}}{d x^{n}}[f(x)] \tag{11}
\end{equation*}
$$

and the value of a general $n$th order derivative at a specific point $x=x_{0}$ can be denoted by

$$
\begin{equation*}
\left.\frac{d^{n} y}{d x^{n}}\right|_{x=x_{0}}=f^{(n)}\left(x_{0}\right)=\left.\frac{d^{n}}{d x^{n}}[f(x)]\right|_{x=x_{0}} \tag{12}
\end{equation*}

concepts.title: Derivative of a product (initial exploration)
concepts.one_liner: The derivative of a product of two functions is not the product of their derivatives, as a simple example demonstrates.
concepts.summary_md: It might seem intuitive that the derivative of a product of two functions is the product of their derivatives, but this is false. For example, if $f(x)=x$ and $g(x)=x^2$, then $f'(x)g'(x) = (1)(2x) = 2x$. However, the product $h(x)=f(x)g(x)=x^3$ has a derivative $h'(x)=3x^2$. Therefore, the derivative of the product is not equal to the product of the derivatives.
concepts.motivation_md: This concept highlights a common misconception about derivatives and products, demonstrating through a counterexample why a specific rule (the Product Rule) is necessary. It sets the stage for introducing the correct method for differentiating products of functions.
concepts.recap_md: - The derivative of a product is NOT the product of the derivatives.- For $f(x)=x$ and $g(x)=x^2$, $(f \cdot g)' = 3x^2$, while $f' \cdot g' = 2x$.- A specific rule is needed for differentiating products of functions.
concepts.raw_body:
You might be tempted to conjecture that the derivative of a product of two functions is the product of their derivatives. However, a simple example will show this to be false. Consider the functions

$$
f(x)=x \quad \text { and } \quad g(x)=x^{2}
$$

The product of their derivatives is

$$
f^{\prime}(x) g^{\prime}(x)=(1)(2 x)=2 x
$$

Formula (1) can also be expressed as $(f \cdot g)^{\prime}=f \cdot g^{\prime}+g \cdot f^{\prime}$
but their product is $h(x)=f(x) g(x)=x^{3}$, so the derivative of the product is

$$
h^{\prime}(x)=3 x^{2}
$$

Thus, the derivative of the product is not equal to the product of the derivatives. The correct relationship, which is credited to Leibniz, is given by the following theorem.

concepts.title: The Product Rule
concepts.one_liner: If $f$ and $g$ are differentiable at $x$, then the derivative of their product $f \cdot g$ is given by $\frac{d}{d x}[f(x) g(x)]=f(x) \frac{d}{d x}[g(x)]+g(x) \frac{d}{d x}[f(x)]$.
concepts.summary_md: The Product Rule states that if functions $f$ and $g$ are differentiable at $x$, then their product $f \cdot g$ is also differentiable at $x$. The derivative of the product is given by the formula: $\frac{d}{d x}[f(x) g(x)]=f(x) \frac{d}{d x}[g(x)]+g(x) \frac{d}{d x}[f(x)]$. This rule is essential for finding derivatives of functions that are products of other functions.
concepts.motivation_md: The Product Rule provides the correct method for finding the derivative of a function that is formed by multiplying two other functions. It resolves the incorrect assumption that the derivative of a product is simply the product of the derivatives, which was disproven in the previous concept.
concepts.recap_md: - The Product Rule applies when differentiating a product of two differentiable functions, $f(x)g(x)$.- The formula is $\frac{d}{d x}[f(x) g(x)]=f(x) \frac{d}{d x}[g(x)]+g(x) \frac{d}{d x}[f(x)]$.- This rule is fundamental for calculus and is credited to Leibniz.

concepts.title: The Quotient Rule
concepts.one_liner: If $f$ and $g$ are differentiable at $x$ and $g(x) \neq 0$, then the derivative of their quotient $f / g$ is $\frac{d}{d x}\left[\frac{f(x)}{g(x)}\right]=\frac{g(x) \frac{d}{d x}[f(x)]-f(x) \frac{d}{d x}[g(x)]}{[g(x)]^{2}}$.
concepts.summary_md: The Quotient Rule states that if functions $f$ and $g$ are both differentiable at $x$, and $g(x) \neq 0$, then their quotient $f / g$ is differentiable at $x$. The derivative of the quotient is given by the formula: $\frac{d}{d x}\left[\frac{f(x)}{g(x)}\right]=\frac{g(x) \frac{d}{d x}[f(x)]-f(x) \frac{d}{d x}[g(x)]}{[g(x)]^{2}}$. This rule is crucial for differentiating rational functions.
concepts.motivation_md: The Quotient Rule provides a systematic way to find the derivative of functions expressed as a ratio of two other functions. It is essential for handling rational expressions and extends the toolkit for differentiation beyond sums, differences, products, and simple powers.
concepts.recap_md: - The Quotient Rule applies to functions of the form $\frac{f(x)}{g(x)}$ where $f$ and $g$ are differentiable and $g(x) \neq 0$.- The formula is $\frac{d}{d x}\left[\frac{f(x)}{g(x)}\right]=\frac{g(x) f^{\prime}(x)-f(x) g^{\prime}(x)}{[g(x)]^{2}}$.- Remember "low d high minus high d low over low squared."

concepts.title: Simplifying functions before applying the quotient rule
concepts.one_liner: Sometimes it is better to simplify a function first than to apply the quotient rule immediately.
concepts.summary_md: Before applying the quotient rule, it can often be advantageous to simplify the function algebraically. For example, differentiating $f(x)=\frac{x^{3 / 2}+x}{\sqrt{x}}$ is simpler if rewritten as $f(x)=x+\sqrt{x}$, rather than directly using the quotient rule.
concepts.motivation_md: Simplifying a function before differentiation can significantly reduce the complexity of the problem, making calculations faster and less prone to errors. This technique emphasizes strategic problem-solving over rote application of rules.
concepts.recap_md: - Always look for opportunities to simplify a function algebraically before differentiating.- Simplifying can transform a quotient into a sum or difference of simpler terms.- This approach can make differentiation much easier than directly applying the quotient rule.
concepts.raw_body:
Sometimes it is better to simplify a function first than to apply the quotient rule immediately. For example, it is easier to differentiate

$$
f(x)=\frac{x^{3 / 2}+x}{\sqrt{x}}
$$

by rewriting it as

$$
f(x)=x+\sqrt{x}
$$

as opposed to using the quotient rule.

concepts.title: Derivative of a reciprocal function
concepts.one_liner: The derivative of a reciprocal function $\left(\frac{1}{g}\right)^{\prime}$ can be found using the rule $-\frac{g^{\prime}}{g^{2}}$.
concepts.summary_md: A specific rule exists for differentiating a reciprocal function: $\left(\frac{1}{g}\right)^{\prime}=-\frac{g^{\prime}}{g^{2}}$. This rule can be derived from the quotient rule and is useful for finding derivatives of functions like $f(x)=\frac{1}{x^{2}+1}$.
concepts.motivation_md: This technique provides a specialized shortcut for a common type of quotient (a reciprocal function), making differentiation quicker and more efficient in these specific cases. It's a direct application of the quotient rule but presented as a standalone, frequently used result.
concepts.recap_md: - The derivative of a reciprocal function $\frac{1}{g(x)}$ is given by $-\frac{g^{\prime}(x)}{[g(x)]^{2}}$.- This rule is a special case derived from the Quotient Rule.- It simplifies finding derivatives for functions where the numerator is a constant.
concepts.raw_body:
Derive the following rule for differentiating a reciprocal:

$$
\left(\frac{1}{g}\right)^{\prime}=-\frac{g^{\prime}}{g^{2}}
$$

Use it to find the derivative of

$$
f(x)=\frac{1}{x^{2}+1}
$$

concepts.title: Derivatives of Trigonometric Functions
concepts.one_liner: The main objective of this section is to obtain formulas for the derivatives of the six basic trigonometric functions.
concepts.summary_md: This section aims to derive formulas for the derivatives of the six basic trigonometric functions: $\sin x, \cos x, \tan x, \cot x, \sec x$, and $\csc x$. It is crucial to note that these formulas are valid only when the variable $x$ is measured in radians. A review of trigonometric functions is available in Appendix B if needed, and certain limits from Theorem 1.6.5 will be utilized.
concepts.motivation_md: Understanding the derivatives of trigonometric functions is fundamental for analyzing periodic phenomena in physics, engineering, and other sciences. These derivatives are essential for calculating rates of change and optimization in contexts involving oscillations and waves.
concepts.recap_md: - This section focuses on deriving derivative formulas for $\sin x, \cos x, \tan x, \cot x, \sec x$, and $\csc x$.- All formulas assume the variable $x$ is measured in radians.- Prior knowledge of trigonometric functions and certain limits will be necessary.
concepts.raw_body:
### 2.5 DERIVATIVES OF TRIGONOMETRIC FUNCTIONS

Formulas (1) and (2) and the derivation of Formulas (3) and (4) are only valid if $h$ and $x$ are in radians. See Exercise 49 for how Formulas (3) and (4) change when $x$ is measured in degrees.

The main objective of this section is to obtain formulas for the derivatives of the six basic trigonometric functions. If needed, you will find a review of trigonometric functions in Appendix $B$.

We will assume in this section that the variable $x$ in the trigonometric functions $\sin x, \cos x$, $\tan x, \cot x, \sec x$, and $\csc x$ is measured in radians. Also, we will need the limits in Theorem 1.6.5, but restated as follows using $h$ rather than $x$ as the variable:

concepts.title: Derivation of the derivative of sin x
concepts.one_liner: The derivative of $f(x)=\sin x$ is derived by applying the limit definition of the derivative and simplifying the resulting expression.
concepts.summary_md: The derivative of $f(x)=\sin x$ is found by applying the definition of the derivative, $f^{\prime}(x) =\lim _{h \rightarrow 0} \frac{f(x+h)-f(x)}{h}$. This involves expanding $\sin(x+h)$, reorganizing terms, and using known limits such as $\lim _{h \rightarrow 0} \frac{\sin h}{h}=1$ and $\lim _{h \rightarrow 0} \frac{1-\cos h}{h}=0$ to arrive at $\cos x$.
concepts.motivation_md: Deriving the derivative of $\sin x$ from first principles is crucial for understanding how fundamental derivative rules are established. It demonstrates the application of the limit definition and foundational trigonometric limits, providing a basis for further calculus concepts.
concepts.recap_md:
- Start with the limit definition of the derivative for $f(x)=\sin x$.
- Expand $\sin(x+h)$ using the angle sum identity.
- Reorganize terms and apply the special limits $\lim _{h \rightarrow 0} \frac{\sin h}{h}=1$ and $\lim _{h \rightarrow 0} \frac{1-\cos h}{h}=0$.
- The final result is $\frac{d}{d x}[\sin x]=\cos x$.

concepts.title: Derivative of sin x
concepts.one_liner: The derivative of $\sin x$ with respect to $x$ is $\cos x$.
concepts.summary_md: The fundamental derivative rule for the sine function states that the derivative of $\sin x$ with respect to $x$ is $\cos x$, expressed as $\frac{d}{d x}[\sin x]=\cos x$.
concepts.motivation_md: This definition provides a fundamental rule for differentiating trigonometric functions, essential for calculating rates of change and slopes of tangent lines for functions involving $\sin x$ without needing to use the limit definition every time.
concepts.recap_md:
- The derivative of $\sin x$ is $\cos x$.
- This is a fundamental rule in calculus.

concepts.title: Derivative of cos x
concepts.one_liner: The derivative of $\cos x$ with respect to $x$ is $-\sin x$.
concepts.summary_md: The derivative rule for the cosine function states that the derivative of $\cos x$ with respect to $x$ is $-\sin x$, expressed as $\frac{d}{d x}[\cos x]=-\sin x$.
concepts.motivation_md: This definition establishes another core derivative rule for trigonometric functions, enabling efficient calculation of rates of change for expressions involving $\cos x$ and serving as a building block for more complex derivatives.
concepts.recap_md:
- The derivative of $\cos x$ is $-\sin x$.
- This is a key derivative rule for trigonometric functions.

concepts.title: Derivatives of tan x, sec x, cot x, csc x
concepts.one_liner: The derivatives of $\tan x$, $\sec x$, $\cot x$, and $\csc x$ are defined by specific formulas involving other trigonometric functions.
concepts.summary_md: This set of definitions provides the derivative rules for the remaining four basic trigonometric functions: $\frac{d}{d x}[\tan x]=\sec ^{2} x$, $\frac{d}{d x}[\sec x]=\sec x \tan x$, $\frac{d}{d x}[\cot x]=-\csc ^{2} x$, and $\frac{d}{d x}[\csc x]=-\csc x \cot x$.
concepts.motivation_md: These derivative formulas extend our ability to differentiate a wider range of trigonometric expressions. They are essential tools for analyzing the rates of change of functions involving tangent, secant, cotangent, and cosecant.
concepts.recap_md:
- $\frac{d}{d x}[\tan x]=\sec ^{2} x$
- $\frac{d}{d x}[\sec x]=\sec x \tan x$
- $\frac{d}{d x}[\cot x]=-\csc ^{2} x$
- $\frac{d}{d x}[\csc x]=-\csc x \cot x$

concepts.title: Derivation of the derivative of tan x
concepts.one_liner: Derivatives of $\tan x$, $\cot x$, $\sec x$, and $\csc x$ can be obtained by applying the quotient rule to their relationships with $\sin x$ and $\cos x$.
concepts.summary_md: The derivatives of $\tan x$, $\cot x$, $\sec x$, and $\csc x$ can be found using the quotient rule and the known derivatives of $\sin x$ and $\cos x$. For example, to find $\frac{d}{d x}[\tan x]$, one expresses $\tan x=\frac{\sin x}{\cos x}$ and applies the quotient rule, simplifying to $\frac{1}{\cos ^{2} x}=\sec ^{2} x$.
concepts.motivation_md: This technique demonstrates how to derive complex derivative rules from simpler ones, reducing the need to memorize every formula. It reinforces the application of the quotient rule and the interconnections between trigonometric functions.
concepts.recap_md:
- Express the trigonometric function (e.g., $\tan x$) in terms of $\sin x$ and $\cos x$.
- Apply the quotient rule using the derivatives of $\sin x$ and $\cos x$.
- Simplify the resulting expression using trigonometric identities to obtain the final derivative.
concepts.raw_body:
These can all be obtained using the definition of the derivative, but it is easier to use Formulas (3) and (4) and apply the quotient rule to the relationships

$$
\tan x=\frac{\sin x}{\cos x}, \quad \cot x=\frac{\cos x}{\sin x}, \quad \sec x=\frac{1}{\cos x}, \quad \csc x=\frac{1}{\sin x}
$$

For example,

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{d}{d x}[\tan x] & =\frac{d}{d x}\left[\frac{\sin x}{\cos x}\right]=\frac{\cos x \cdot \frac{d}{d x}[\sin x]-\sin x \cdot \frac{d}{d x}[\cos x]}{\cos ^{2} x} \\
& =\frac{\cos x \cdot \cos x-\sin x \cdot(-\sin x)}{\cos ^{2} x}=\frac{\cos ^{2} x+\sin ^{2} x}{\cos ^{2} x}=\frac{1}{\cos ^{2} x}=\sec ^{2} x
\end{aligned}
$$

concepts.title: Introduction to the Chain Rule
concepts.one_liner: The Chain Rule expresses the derivative of a composition $f \circ g$ in terms of the derivatives of $f$ and $g$, enabling differentiation of complicated functions.
concepts.summary_md: The Chain Rule provides a formula to find the derivative of a composite function $f(g(x))$. It allows us to differentiate complex functions using known derivatives of simpler functions. The name "chain rule" is appropriate because the desired derivative is obtained by a two-link "chain" of simpler derivatives, as illustrated by the car mileage and gasoline cost analogy.
concepts.motivation_md: Many real-world phenomena and mathematical functions are compositions of simpler functions. The Chain Rule is essential for calculating their rates of change, providing a powerful tool to differentiate functions like $\sin(x^2)$ or $(x^2+1)^3$ that cannot be handled by basic rules.
concepts.recap_md:
- The Chain Rule finds the derivative of a composite function $f(g(x))$.
- It links the derivatives of the 'outside' function $f$ and the 'inside' function $g$.
- This rule simplifies differentiating complex functions built from simpler ones.
concepts.raw_body:
In this section we will derive a formula that expresses the derivative of a composition $f \circ g$ in terms of the derivatives of $f$ and $g$. This formula will enable us to differentiate complicated functions using known derivatives of simpler functions.

![A bright orange convertible car drives down a tree-lined residential street. The car is angled away from the viewer, showing its rear and right side, with motion blur in the background suggesting...](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/84333fdc-d75a-4de5-aded-d41110c1154d-108.jpg?height=527&width=479&top_left_y=877&top_left_x=156)
Mike Brinson/Getty Images
The cost of a car trip is a combination of fuel efficiency and the cost of gasoline.

![A diagram illustrating the chain rule for derivatives. Three variables, $y$, $u$, and $x$, are arranged with arrows indicating a dependency chain from $x$ to $u$ to $y$. Above $y$ and $u$ is a box...](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/84333fdc-d75a-4de5-aded-d41110c1154d-108.jpg?height=358&width=339&top_left_y=1561&top_left_x=224)
- Figure 2.6.1

The name "chain rule" is appropriate because the desired derivative is obtained by a two-link "chain" of simpler derivatives.

## DERIVATIVES OF COMPOSITIONS

Suppose you are traveling to school in your car, which gets 20 miles per gallon of gasoline. The number of miles you can travel in your car without refueling is a function of the number of gallons of gas you have in the gas tank. In symbols, if $y$ is the number of miles you can travel and $u$ is the number of gallons of gas you have initially, then $y$ is a function of $u$, or $y=f(u)$. As you continue your travels, you note that your local service station is selling gasoline for $\$ 4$ per gallon. The number of gallons of gas you have initially is a function of the amount of money you spend for that gas. If $x$ is the number of dollars you spend on gas, then $u=g(x)$. Now 20 miles per gallon is the rate at which your mileage changes with respect to the amount of gasoline you use, so

$$
f^{\prime}(u)=\frac{d y}{d u}=20 \text { miles per gallon }
$$

Similarly, since gasoline costs $\$ 4$ per gallon, each dollar you spend will give you $1 / 4$ of a gallon of gas, and

$$
g^{\prime}(x)=\frac{d u}{d x}=\frac{1}{4} \text { gallons per dollar }
$$

Notice that the number of miles you can travel is also a function of the number of dollars you spend on gasoline. This fact is expressible as the composition of functions

$$
y=f(u)=f(g(x))
$$

You might be interested in how many miles you can travel per dollar, which is $d y / d x$. Intuition suggests that rates of change multiply in this case (see Figure 2.6.1), so

$$
\frac{d y}{d x}=\frac{d y}{d u} \cdot \frac{d u}{d x}=\frac{20 \text { miles }}{1 \text { gallon }} \cdot \frac{1 \text { gallons }}{4 \text { dollars }}=\frac{20 \text { miles }}{4 \text { dollars }}=5 \text { miles per dollar }
$$

concepts.title: The Chain Rule
concepts.one_liner: The Chain Rule states that if $g$ is differentiable at $x$ and $f$ is differentiable at $g(x)$, then $f \circ g$ is differentiable at $x$.
concepts.summary_md: Theorem 2.6.1, known as The Chain Rule, states that if $g$ is differentiable at $x$ and $f$ is differentiable at $g(x)$, then the composition $f \circ g$ is differentiable at $x$. If $y=f(g(x))$ and $u=g(x)$, then $y=f(u)$ and its derivative is given by $\frac{d y}{d x}=\frac{d y}{d u} \cdot \frac{d u}{d x}$.
concepts.motivation_md: This theorem provides the formal mathematical statement of the Chain Rule, establishing the conditions under which it applies and presenting the fundamental formula for calculating the derivative of a composite function. It is the cornerstone for differentiating a vast array of functions.
concepts.recap_md:
- If $y=f(g(x))$ and $u=g(x)$, then $y=f(u)$.
- The derivative is given by $\frac{d y}{d x}=\frac{d y}{d u} \cdot \frac{d u}{d x}$.
- This rule applies when both $f$ and $g$ are differentiable at their respective points.

concepts.title: Alternative Version of the Chain Rule
concepts.one_liner: An alternative version of the Chain Rule expresses the derivative of $f(g(x))$ as $f^{\prime}(g(x)) g^{\prime}(x)$, often remembered as 'derivative of the outside function evaluated at the inside function times the derivative of the inside function'.
concepts.summary_md: Formula (1) for the chain rule can be unwieldy in some problems. An alternative version expresses the chain rule as $\frac{d}{d x}[f(g(x))]=(f \circ g)^{\prime}(x)=f^{\prime}(g(x)) g^{\prime}(x)$. This is conveniently remembered as: 'The derivative of the outside function evaluated at the inside function times the derivative of the inside function.'
concepts.motivation_md: This alternative notation and verbal mnemonic simplify the application of the Chain Rule in practice, especially for complex functions. It provides a more direct way to compute derivatives without explicitly defining intermediate variables like $u$, making the process more intuitive and efficient.
concepts.recap_md:
- The Chain Rule can be written as $\frac{d}{d x}[f(g(x))]=f^{\prime}(g(x)) g^{\prime}(x)$.
- Identify $f$ as the 'outside function' and $g$ as the 'inside function'.
- Differentiate the outside function, evaluate it at the inside function, then multiply by the derivative of the inside function.

concepts.title: Generalized Derivative Formulas
concepts.one_liner: If we let $u=g(x)$ in (2), then we can rewrite that formula as $\frac{d}{d x}[f(u)]=f^{\prime}(u) \frac{d u}{d x}$.
concepts.summary_md: A useful third variation of the chain rule is presented, striking a middle ground between Formulas (1) and (2). By letting $u=g(x)$, the formula can be rewritten as $\frac{d}{d x}[f(u)]=f^{\prime}(u) \frac{d u}{d x}$.
concepts.motivation_md: This formula provides a more general and often more convenient way to apply the chain rule, especially when dealing with composite functions where the inner function is explicitly named as $u$. It simplifies the notation and application of the chain rule in various contexts.
concepts.recap_md: - The generalized derivative formula is $\frac{d}{d x}[f(u)]=f^{\prime}(u) \frac{d u}{d x}$.- It is a variation of the chain rule where $u$ represents an inner function $g(x)$.

concepts.title: Instantaneous growth rate
concepts.one_liner: The instantaneous growth rate is defined as $\frac{d N / d t}{N}$.
concepts.summary_md: The instantaneous growth rate is defined by the formula $\frac{d N / d t}{N}$. This rate is used to approximate growth at a specific moment, such as at the start of the year 2000, and should be expressed as a percentage with proper units.
concepts.motivation_md: Understanding instantaneous growth rate allows us to analyze how quickly a quantity is changing relative to its current size at any given moment. This is crucial in fields like biology, economics, and finance to model populations, investments, or other dynamic systems.
concepts.recap_md: - Instantaneous growth rate is defined as $\frac{d N / d t}{N}$.- It measures the relative rate of change of a quantity $N$ with respect to time $t$.
concepts.raw_body:
(b) The instantaneous growth rate is defined as

$$
\frac{d N / d t}{N}
$$

Use your answer to part (a) to approximate the instantaneous growth rate at the start of the year 2000. Express the result as a percentage and include the proper units.

concepts.title: Functions Defined Explicitly and Implicitly
concepts.one_liner: An equation of the form $y=f(x)$ defines $y$ explicitly as a function of $x$, while equations where $y$ is not alone on one side define $y$ implicitly.
concepts.summary_md: An equation like $y=f(x)$ defines $y$ explicitly as a function of $x$ because $y$ is isolated on one side. Conversely, functions are defined implicitly when $y$ is not alone, as in $y x+y+1=x$. Even if not explicitly solved, such an equation can still define $y$ as a function of $x$, for example, $y=\frac{x-1}{x+1}$.
concepts.motivation_md: Many important relationships in mathematics and science cannot be easily expressed with $y$ explicitly solved in terms of $x$. Understanding explicit and implicit definitions allows us to work with a broader range of functions and their properties, even when direct algebraic isolation of $y$ is difficult or impossible.
concepts.recap_md: - An explicit function has $y$ isolated on one side, e.g., $y=f(x)$.- An implicit function has $y$ mixed with $x$ on one or both sides, e.g., $yx+y+1=x$.- Implicit equations can often be rearranged to an explicit form, but not always easily.

concepts.title: Implicitly Defined Function
concepts.one_liner: An equation in $x$ and $y$ defines a function $f$ implicitly if the graph of $y=f(x)$ coincides with a portion of the graph of the equation.
concepts.summary_md: A given equation in $x$ and $y$ defines the function $f$ implicitly if the graph of $y=f(x)$ coincides with a portion of the graph of the equation. This means that the equation's graph contains the graph of the function.
concepts.motivation_md: This definition clarifies what it means for an equation to "define" a function implicitly. It establishes a graphical criterion, indicating that the function's graph must be a subset of the equation's graph, which is crucial for understanding the domain and range of such functions.
concepts.recap_md: - An equation implicitly defines a function $f$ if $y=f(x)$'s graph is part of the equation's graph.- This means the implicit equation contains the function's relationship.
concepts.raw_body: ### 3.1.1 DEFINITION We will say that a given equation in $x$ and $y$ defines the function $f$ implicitly if the graph of $y=f(x)$ coincides with a portion of the graph of the equation.

concepts.title: Implicit Differentiation
concepts.one_liner: Implicit differentiation is a method for obtaining derivatives by differentiating both sides of an equation before solving for $y$ in terms of $x$, treating $y$ as a differentiable function of $x$.
concepts.summary_md: Implicit differentiation is a method to find $d y / d x$ without explicitly solving an equation for $y$. It involves differentiating both sides of the equation with respect to $x$, treating $y$ as a differentiable function of $x$. For example, differentiating $xy=1$ yields $x \frac{d y}{d x}+y=0$, leading to $\frac{d y}{d x}=-\frac{y}{x}$.
concepts.motivation_md: Implicit differentiation is essential when it's difficult or impossible to solve an equation for $y$ explicitly in terms of $x$. It allows us to find the derivative $\frac{dy}{dx}$ for a wider range of functions, including those that define curves like circles or ellipses, which are not single functions.
concepts.recap_md: - Implicit differentiation allows finding $\frac{dy}{dx}$ without solving for $y$ explicitly.- Differentiate both sides of the equation with respect to $x$, treating $y$ as a function of $x$.- Use the chain rule when differentiating terms involving $y$.

concepts.title: Differentiability of Functions Defined Implicitly
concepts.one_liner: When differentiating implicitly, it is assumed that $y$ represents a differentiable function of $x$; if not, the resulting calculations may be meaningless.
concepts.summary_md: When performing implicit differentiation, it is crucial to assume that $y$ is a differentiable function of $x$. If this assumption is false, the calculations can lead to meaningless results. For instance, differentiating $x^{2}+y^{2}+1=0$ yields $\frac{d y}{d x}=-\frac{x}{y}$, but this equation has no real solutions for $x$ and $y$, meaning it defines no real function implicitly.
concepts.motivation_md: It's important to recognize that not all equations involving $x$ and $y$ implicitly define a differentiable function. This concept highlights a critical prerequisite for implicit differentiation: the existence of a differentiable function. Without this, applying the technique leads to invalid results, emphasizing the need for careful mathematical reasoning.
concepts.recap_md: - Implicit differentiation assumes $y$ is a differentiable function of $x$.- If no such function exists, the derivative obtained through implicit differentiation is meaningless.- Determining if an equation defines a differentiable function implicitly can be complex.

concepts.title: Derivative of ln x
concepts.one_liner: The derivative of the natural logarithm of $x$ is $\frac{d}{d x}[\ln x]=\frac{1}{x}$, for $x>0$.
concepts.summary_md: The derivative of the natural logarithm function, $\ln x$, with respect to $x$ is given by the formula $\frac{d}{d x}[\ln x]=\frac{1}{x}$. This formula is valid for all $x>0$.
concepts.motivation_md: The natural logarithm function appears frequently in calculus and its applications, especially in growth and decay models. Knowing its derivative is fundamental for solving problems involving exponential functions, logarithmic differentiation, and understanding rates of change in contexts where quantities grow proportionally to their current size.
concepts.recap_md: - The derivative of $\ln x$ is $\frac{1}{x}$.- This formula is valid only for $x>0$.

concepts.title: Derivative of log_b x
concepts.one_liner: The derivative of $\log _{b} x$ is $\frac{d}{d x}\left[\log _{b} x\right]=\frac{1}{x \ln b}$, for $x>0$.
concepts.summary_md: The derivative of the logarithm function with base $b$, $\log _{b} x$, with respect to $x$ is given by the formula $\frac{d}{d x}\left[\log _{b} xight]=\frac{1}{x \ln b}$. This formula is valid for all $x>0$.
concepts.motivation_md: While the natural logarithm is common, logarithms with other bases ($b$) are also used in various scientific and engineering contexts. This formula provides a general rule for differentiating any logarithmic function, allowing us to handle a broader range of problems involving logarithmic scales or relationships.
concepts.recap_md: - The derivative of $\log _{b} x$ is $\frac{1}{x \ln b}$.- This formula applies for $x>0$.- It generalizes the derivative of $\ln x$ (where $b=e$).

concepts.title: Derivative of ln u (Chain Rule)
concepts.one_liner: The derivative of $\ln u$ with respect to $x$ is $\frac{1}{u} \cdot \frac{d u}{d x}$.
concepts.summary_md: The derivative of $\ln u$ with respect to $x$ is given by the formula $\frac{d}{d x}[\ln u]=\frac{1}{u} \cdot \frac{d u}{d x}$.
concepts.motivation_md: This formula provides a fundamental rule for differentiating natural logarithm functions, especially when the argument `u` is itself a function of `x`, effectively incorporating the chain rule.
concepts.recap_md: - The derivative of $\ln u$ is $\frac{1}{u} \frac{d u}{d x}$.- This formula applies the chain rule for composite functions.

concepts.title: Derivative of log_b u (Chain Rule)
concepts.one_liner: The derivative of $\log _{b} u$ with respect to $x$ is $\frac{1}{u \ln b} \cdot \frac{d u}{d x}$.
concepts.summary_md: The derivative of $\log _{b} u$ with respect to $x$ is given by the formula $\frac{d}{d x}[\log _{b} u]=\frac{1}{u \ln b} \cdot \frac{d u}{d x}$.
concepts.motivation_md: This formula extends the differentiation of natural logarithms to logarithms of any base $b$, providing a general rule for such functions when the argument $u$ is a function of $x$.
concepts.recap_md: - The derivative of $\log _{b} u$ is $\frac{1}{u \ln b} \frac{d u}{d x}$.- This formula applies the chain rule and accounts for the base $b$.

concepts.title: Using logarithm properties before differentiation
concepts.one_liner: The properties of logarithms should be used to convert products, quotients, and exponents into sums, differences, and constant multiples before differentiating.
concepts.summary_md: When possible, the properties of logarithms in Theorem 0.5.2 should be used to convert products, quotients, and exponents into sums, differences, and constant multiples before differentiating a function involving logarithms.
concepts.motivation_md: This technique simplifies complex logarithmic expressions, making them easier to differentiate by transforming products and quotients into sums and differences, which are simpler to handle with derivative rules.
concepts.recap_md: - Use logarithm properties to expand expressions before differentiating.- Convert products to sums, quotients to differences, and exponents to constant multiples.
concepts.raw_body: When possible, the properties of logarithms in Theorem 0.5.2 should be used to convert products, quotients, and exponents into sums, differences, and constant multiples before differentiating a function involving logarithms.

concepts.title: Derivative of ln|x|
concepts.one_liner: The derivative of $\ln |x|$ with respect to $x$ is $\frac{1}{x}$, if $x \neq 0$.
concepts.summary_md: The derivative of $\ln |x|$ with respect to $x$ is $\frac{1}{x}$, provided $x \neq 0$.
concepts.motivation_md: This definition is crucial because it extends the derivative of $\ln x$ to negative values of $x$, allowing us to differentiate $\ln |x|$ over its entire domain where it is defined and differentiable.
concepts.recap_md: - The derivative of $\ln |x|$ is $\frac{1}{x}$.- This rule applies for all $x \neq 0$.

concepts.title: Logarithmic differentiation
concepts.one_liner: Logarithmic differentiation is a technique useful for differentiating functions composed of products, quotients, and powers.
concepts.summary_md: Logarithmic differentiation is a technique that is useful for differentiating functions that are composed of products, quotients, and powers.
concepts.motivation_md: This technique simplifies the differentiation of complex functions involving products, quotients, and powers by first taking the natural logarithm of both sides, applying logarithm properties, and then differentiating implicitly.
concepts.recap_md: - Logarithmic differentiation simplifies derivatives of complex products, quotients, and powers.- It involves taking the natural logarithm of both sides, using log properties, and then implicit differentiation.
concepts.raw_body: We now consider a technique called logarithmic differentiation that is useful for differentiating functions that are composed of products, quotients, and powers.

concepts.title: Proof of power rule for real exponents using logarithmic differentiation
concepts.one_liner: The power rule for real exponents, $d y / d x = r x^{r-1}$ for $y=x^r$, can be proven using logarithmic differentiation.
concepts.summary_md: The derivative $d y / d x$ for $y=x^{r}$, where $r$ is a real number, can be obtained by logarithmic differentiation. This involves taking the natural logarithm of both sides, $\ln |y|=r \ln |x|$, differentiating implicitly to get $\frac{1}{y} \frac{d y}{d x}=\frac{r}{x}$, and then solving for $\frac{d y}{d x}$ to yield $r x^{r-1}$.
concepts.motivation_md: This proof demonstrates how logarithmic differentiation can extend the power rule, previously established for integer or rational exponents, to any real exponent, thus broadening its applicability in calculus.
concepts.recap_md: - Start with $y=x^r$ and take the natural logarithm of both sides: $\ln |y|=r \ln |x|$.- Differentiate implicitly with respect to $x$: $\frac{1}{y} \frac{d y}{d x}=\frac{r}{x}$.- Solve for $\frac{d y}{d x}$ and substitute $y=x^r$ to get $r x^{r-1}$.

concepts.title: Relating the derivative of an inverse function to the derivative of the original function
concepts.one_liner: The derivative of a one-to-one function can be used to obtain the derivative of its inverse function.
concepts.summary_md: This section shows how the derivative of a one-to-one function can be used to obtain the derivative of its inverse function. This provides the tools needed to derive formulas for exponential functions from logarithmic functions, and for inverse trigonometric functions from trigonometric functions. The primary goal is to obtain a formula relating the derivative of $f^{-1}$ to the derivative of $f$.
concepts.motivation_md: Understanding how to find the derivative of an inverse function is crucial because it allows us to derive differentiation rules for important function types like exponential and inverse trigonometric functions, without having to start from first principles for each.
concepts.recap_md: - The derivative of a one-to-one function helps find the derivative of its inverse.- This idea is key for deriving derivative formulas for exponential and inverse trigonometric functions.- The goal is a formula relating $(f^{-1})'(x)$ to $f'(f^{-1}(x))$.
concepts.raw_body:
In this section we will show how the derivative of a one-to-one function can be used to obtain the derivative of its inverse function. This will provide the tools we need to obtain derivative formulas for exponential functions from the derivative formulas for logarithmic functions and to obtain derivative formulas for inverse trigonometric functions from the derivative formulas for trigonometric functions.

Our first goal in this section is to obtain a formula relating the derivative of the inverse function $f^{-1}$ to the derivative of the function $f$.
concepts.section_title: DERIVATIVES OF EXPONENTIAL AND INVERSE TRIGONOMETRIC FUNCTIONS

concepts.title: Formula for the derivative of an inverse function
concepts.one_liner: If $f$ is a differentiable and one-to-one function, its inverse's derivative is $\left(f^{-1}\right)^{\prime}(x)=\frac{1}{f^{\prime}\left(f^{-1}(x)\right)}$, provided $f^{\prime}\left(f^{-1}(x)\right) \neq 0$.
concepts.summary_md: If $f$ is a differentiable and one-to-one function, then the derivative of its inverse function, $\left(f^{-1}\right)^{\prime}(x)$, can be found using the formula $\frac{1}{f^{\prime}\left(f^{-1}(x)\right)}$, provided that $f^{\prime}\left(f^{-1}(x)\right) \neq 0$.
concepts.motivation_md: This formula provides a direct method to calculate the derivative of an inverse function without explicitly finding the inverse function first, simplifying the process for many complex functions.
concepts.recap_md: - The derivative of an inverse function $(f^{-1})'(x)$ is $\frac{1}{f^{\prime}\left(f^{-1}(x)\right)}$.- This formula applies when $f$ is differentiable and one-to-one.- The denominator $f^{\prime}\left(f^{-1}(x)\right)$ must not be zero.
concepts.section_title: DERIVATIVES OF EXPONENTIAL AND INVERSE TRIGONOMETRIC FUNCTIONS

concepts.title: Alternative formula for the derivative of an inverse function
concepts.one_liner: Also from $x=f(y)$ we have $d x / d y=f^{\prime}(y)$, which gives the following alternative version of Formula (2): $\frac{d y}{d x}=\frac{1}{d x / d y}$.
concepts.summary_md: Given $x=f(y)$, we know that $d x / d y=f^{\prime}(y)$. This leads to an alternative formula for the derivative of an inverse function: $\frac{d y}{d x}=\frac{1}{d x / d y}$. This is Formula (3).
concepts.motivation_md: This formula provides an alternative way to compute the derivative of an inverse function, especially useful when the inverse function $y=f^{-1}(x)$ is difficult to express explicitly, but $x=f(y)$ is readily differentiable with respect to $y$.
concepts.recap_md: - The derivative of an inverse function can be found using the reciprocal of the derivative of the original function with respect to its dependent variable. - If $x=f(y)$, then $\frac{d y}{d x}=\frac{1}{d x / d y}$.
concepts.section_title: DERIVATIVES OF EXPONENTIAL AND INVERSE TRIGONOMETRIC FUNCTIONS

concepts.title: Increasing or Decreasing Functions are One-to-One
concepts.one_liner: If the graph of a function $f$ is always increasing or always decreasing over the domain of $f$, then $f$ must have an inverse function.
concepts.summary_md: If a function $f$ is always increasing or always decreasing over its domain, its graph will be cut by a horizontal line in at most one point, meaning $f$ must have an inverse function. This is because $f$ is increasing where $f^{\prime}(x)>0$ and decreasing where $f^{\prime}(x)<0$.
concepts.motivation_md: This idea establishes a crucial link between the monotonic behavior of a function (increasing or decreasing) and its invertibility. It provides a way to determine if an inverse function exists without explicitly finding it, using the derivative.
concepts.recap_md: - A function is one-to-one if it is always increasing or always decreasing over its domain. - One-to-one functions pass the horizontal line test and therefore have an inverse function. - $f$ is increasing when $f^{\prime}(x)>0$ and decreasing when $f^{\prime}(x)<0$.

If the graph of a function $f$ is always increasing or always decreasing over the domain of $f$, then a horizontal line will cut the graph of $f$ in at most one point (Figure 3.3.2), so $f$

We will prove in the next chapter that $f$ is increasing on any interval on which $f^{\prime}(x)>0$ (since the graph has positive slope) and that $f$ is decreasing on any interval on which $f^{\prime}(x)<0$ (since the graph has negative slope). concepts.title: Theorem 3.3.1: Differentiability of Inverse Functions
concepts.one_liner: Suppose that the domain of a function $f$ is an open interval on which $f^{\prime}(x)>0$ or on which $f^{\prime}(x)<0$. Then $f$ is one-to-one, $f^{-1}(x)$ is differentiable at all values of $x$ in the range of $f$, and the derivative of $f^{-1}(x)$ is given by Formula (2).
concepts.summary_md: Theorem 3.3.1 states that if a function $f$ has a domain as an open interval where its derivative $f^{\prime}(x)$ is consistently positive or consistently negative, then $f$ is one-to-one. Consequently, its inverse function $f^{-1}(x)$ is differentiable for all $x$ in the range of $f$, and its derivative can be calculated using Formula (2).
concepts.motivation_md: This theorem provides a formal condition for when an inverse function is not only guaranteed to exist but also to be differentiable. It links the derivative of the original function to the differentiability and derivative of its inverse, which is crucial for calculus applications.
concepts.recap_md: - If $f^{\prime}(x)>0$ or $f^{\prime}(x)<0$ on an open interval, $f$ is one-to-one. - Under these conditions, the inverse function $f^{-1}(x)$ is differentiable. - The derivative of $f^{-1}(x)$ is given by Formula (2).

Then $f$ is one-to-one, $f^{-1}(x)$ is differentiable at all values of $x$ in the range of $f$, and the derivative of $f^{-1}(x)$ is given by Formula (2).

concepts.title: Derivatives of Exponential Functions
concepts.one_liner: Our next objective is to show that the general exponential function $b^{x}(b>0, b \neq 1)$ is differentiable everywhere and to find its derivative.
concepts.summary_md: The objective is to demonstrate that the general exponential function, $b^{x}$ (where $b>0$ and $b \neq 1$), is differentiable across its entire domain. The process involves finding a formula for its derivative, building upon established facts.
concepts.motivation_md: Exponential functions are fundamental in mathematics and science, modeling growth and decay. Understanding their derivatives is essential for analyzing rates of change in these contexts, such as population growth, radioactive decay, or compound interest.
concepts.recap_md: - The goal is to find the derivative of the general exponential function $b^{x}$. - Exponential functions $b^{x}$ (for $b>0, b \neq 1$) are differentiable everywhere.

concepts.title: Distinguishing between exponential and power functions
concepts.one_liner: It is important to distinguish between differentiating an exponential function $b^{x}$ (variable exponent and constant base) and a power function $x^{b}$ (variable base and constant exponent).
concepts.summary_md: It is crucial to differentiate between the process of finding the derivative of an exponential function, such as $b^{x}$ (where the exponent is a variable and the base is constant), and a power function, like $x^{b}$ (where the base is a variable and the exponent is constant). For example, $\frac{d}{d x}\left[x^{2}\right]=2 x$ is different from the derivative of $2^{x}$.
concepts.motivation_md: Students often confuse exponential functions with power functions due to similar notation. Clarifying this distinction is vital to apply the correct differentiation rules and avoid common errors.
concepts.recap_md: - Exponential functions have a constant base and a variable exponent (e.g., $b^x$). - Power functions have a variable base and a constant exponent (e.g., $x^b$). - Different rules apply for differentiating exponential and power functions.

It is important to distinguish between differentiating an exponential function $b^{x}$ (variable exponent and constant base) and a power function $x^{b}$ (variable base and constant exponent). For example, compare the derivative

\frac{d}{d x}\left[x^{2}\right]=2 x
$$

concepts.title: Derivative of b^x
concepts.one_liner: The derivative of the exponential function $b^{x}$ with respect to $x$ is given by $\frac{d}{d x}\left[b^{x}\right]=b^{x} \ln b$.
concepts.summary_md: The derivative of an exponential function with a constant base $b$ (where $b>0, b \neq 1$) and a variable exponent $x$ is defined as the function itself multiplied by the natural logarithm of its base. This is expressed by the formula: $\frac{d}{d x}\left[b^{x}\right]=b^{x} \ln b$.
concepts.motivation_md: This formula provides a direct method for calculating the rate of change of any general exponential function. It is fundamental for solving problems involving exponential growth and decay in various fields.
concepts.recap_md: - The derivative of $b^x$ is $b^x \ln b$. - This formula applies to any positive base $b \neq 1$.
concepts.section_title: DERIVATIVES OF EXPONENTIAL AND INVERSE TRIGONOMETRIC FUNCTIONS

concepts.title: Derivative of e^x
concepts.one_liner: The derivative of the natural exponential function $e^{x}$ with respect to $x$ is given by $\frac{d}{d x}\left[e^{x}\right]=e^{x}$.
concepts.summary_md: The derivative of the natural exponential function $e^{x}$ is uniquely simple: it is the function itself. This property makes $e^{x}$ a cornerstone in calculus and differential equations, expressed by the formula: $\frac{d}{d x}\left[e^{x}\right]=e^{x}$.
concepts.motivation_md: The natural exponential function $e^x$ is ubiquitous in mathematics, science, and engineering. Its unique property of being its own derivative simplifies many calculations and makes it ideal for modeling continuous growth processes.
concepts.recap_md: - The derivative of $e^x$ is $e^x$. - This is a fundamental differentiation rule for the natural exponential function.
concepts.section_title: DERIVATIVES OF EXPONENTIAL AND INVERSE TRIGONOMETRIC FUNCTIONS

concepts.title: Generalized derivatives of b^u and e^u
concepts.one_liner: Moreover, if $u$ is a differentiable function of $x$, then the generalized derivatives of $b^{u}$ and $e^{u}$ are $\frac{d}{d x}\left[b^{u}\right]=b^{u} \ln b \cdot \frac{d u}{d x}$ and $\frac{d}{d x}\left[e^{u}\right]=e^{u} \cdot \frac{d u}{d x}$.
concepts.summary_md: When the exponent is a differentiable function $u$ of $x$, the chain rule extends the derivative formulas for exponential functions. Specifically, for a general base $b$, $\frac{d}{d x}\left[b^{u}\right]=b^{u} \ln b \cdot \frac{d u}{d x}$, and for the natural base $e$, $\frac{d}{d x}\left[e^{u}\right]=e^{u} \cdot \frac{d u}{d x}$.
concepts.motivation_md: These generalized formulas, derived from the chain rule, are essential for differentiating composite exponential functions. They allow us to find derivatives when the exponent is not simply $x$ but a more complex function, greatly expanding the applicability of exponential differentiation.
concepts.recap_md: - If $u$ is a differentiable function of $x$, then $\frac{d}{d x}\left[b^{u}\right]=b^{u} \ln b \cdot \frac{d u}{d x}$. - If $u$ is a differentiable function of $x$, then $\frac{d}{d x}\left[e^{u}\right]=e^{u} \cdot \frac{d u}{d x}$. - These are applications of the chain rule to exponential functions.
concepts.section_title: DERIVATIVES OF EXPONENTIAL AND INVERSE TRIGONOMETRIC FUNCTIONS

concepts.title: Logarithmic differentiation for functions of the form u^v
concepts.one_liner: Functions of the form $f(x)=u^{v}$ in which $u$ and $v$ are nonconstant functions of $x$ can be differentiated using logarithmic differentiation.
concepts.summary_md: Functions of the form $f(x)=u^{v}$, where $u$ and $v$ are nonconstant functions of $x$, are neither purely exponential nor power functions. Logarithmic differentiation is a technique used to find the derivative of such functions.
concepts.motivation_md: This technique is necessary because standard power rule or exponential rule differentiation methods do not apply directly to functions where both the base and the exponent are nonconstant functions of x. Logarithmic differentiation simplifies the process by converting the exponentiation into multiplication.
concepts.recap_md: - Use for functions $f(x)=u^{v}$ where $u$ and $v$ are both nonconstant functions of $x$.- This form is neither a simple power function nor an exponential function.- The technique simplifies differentiation by taking the natural logarithm of both sides.
concepts.raw_body: Functions of the form $f(x)=u^{v}$ in which $u$ and $v$ are nonconstant functions of $x$ are neither exponential functions nor power functions. Functions of this form can be differentiated using logarithmic differentiation.

concepts.one_liner: To obtain formulas for the derivatives of the inverse trigonometric functions, we will need to use some of the identities given in Formulas (11) to (17) of Section 0.4.

concepts.motivation_md: Understanding how to derive these formulas is crucial for differentiating functions involving inverse trigonometric expressions. It allows for a deeper understanding of their properties and how they relate to standard trigonometric functions, rather than just memorizing the results.

concepts.title: Differentiability domain of arcsin x
concepts.one_liner: Observe that $\sin ^{-1} x$ is only differentiable on the interval $(-1,1)$, even though its domain is $[-1,1]$.
concepts.summary_md: The function $\sin ^{-1} x$ is differentiable only on the open interval $(-1,1)$, despite its domain being the closed interval $[-1,1]$. This occurs because the graph of $y=\sin x$ has horizontal tangent lines at $(\pi / 2,1)$ and $(-\pi / 2,-1)$, which translates to vertical tangent lines for $y=\sin ^{-1} x$ at $x= \pm 1$.
concepts.motivation_md: Understanding the differentiability domain is crucial for correctly applying derivative formulas and avoiding errors. It highlights that a function's domain and its differentiability domain are not always identical, especially for inverse functions where horizontal tangents become vertical.
concepts.recap_md: - The domain of $\sin ^{-1} x$ is $[-1,1]$.- The differentiability domain of $\sin ^{-1} x$ is $(-1,1)$.- Vertical tangent lines at $x=\pm 1$ prevent differentiability at these points.

This is because the graph of $y=\sin x$ has horizontal tangent lines at the points $(\pi / 2,1)$ and $(-\pi / 2,-1)$, so the graph of $y=\sin ^{-1} x$ has vertical tangent lines at $x= \pm 1$.

concepts.one_liner: The derivative of $\sin ^{-1} x$ with respect to $x$ is $\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-x^{2}}}$ for $-1<x<1$.

concepts.motivation_md: This formula provides a direct method for calculating the rate of change of the arcsin function. It is a fundamental result in calculus, enabling the differentiation of more complex functions that include $\sin^{-1}x$ as a component.

concepts.one_liner: The generalized derivative of $\sin ^{-1} u$ with respect to $x$ is $\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-u^{2}}} \frac{d u}{d x}$ for $-1<u<1$.

concepts.title: Derivatives of Inverse Trigonometric Functions
concepts.one_liner: This concept provides the complete set of formulas for the derivatives of all six inverse trigonometric functions, generalized with the chain rule.
concepts.summary_md: This definition presents the generalized derivative formulas for all six inverse trigonometric functions, where $u$ is a differentiable function of $x$. These include: $\frac{d}{d x}\left[\sin ^{-1} u\right] = \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-u^{2}}} \frac{d u}{d x}$, $\frac{d}{d x}\left[\cos ^{-1} u\right] = -\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-u^{2}}} \frac{d u}{d x}$, $\frac{d}{d x}\left[\tan ^{-1} u\right] = \frac{1}{1+u^{2}} \frac{d u}{d x}$, and others for $\cot^{-1}u$, $\sec^{-1}u$, and $\csc^{-1}u$.
concepts.motivation_md: These formulas are essential tools for differentiating a wide range of functions encountered in calculus and its applications. They allow for the precise calculation of rates of change for expressions involving inverse trigonometric functions, which appear frequently in geometry, physics, and engineering.
