Suppose that water is added to the flask so that the volume increases at a constant rate with respect to the time $t$, and let us examine the rate at which the water level $y$ rises with respect to $t$. Initially, the level $y$ will rise at a slow rate because of the wide base. However, as the diameter of the flask narrows, the rate at which the level $y$ rises will increase until the level is at the narrow point in the neck. From that point on the rate at which the level rises will decrease as the diameter gets wider and wider. Thus, the narrow point in the neck is the point at which the rate of change of $y$ with respect to $t$ changes from increasing to decreasing.
concepts.section_title: ANALYSIS OF FUNCTIONS I: INCREASE, DECREASE, AND CONCAVITY

concepts.title: Logistic Curves
concepts.one_liner: Population growth curves that are S-shaped, showing initial slow growth, then rapid growth, and finally a decline in growth rate approaching a limiting value, are called logistic growth curves.
concepts.summary_md: Logistic growth curves describe population growth in limited environments, typically appearing as S-shaped graphs. Initially, the population grows slowly, then more rapidly. At an inflection point, environmental factors cause the growth rate to decline, and the population approaches a limiting value, representing the maximum sustainable number of individuals.
concepts.motivation_md: Logistic curves model realistic growth scenarios where resources are finite, providing a more accurate representation than exponential growth. They are crucial for understanding population dynamics, resource management, and other phenomena where growth is constrained by environmental limits.
concepts.recap_md: - Logistic curves model population growth in limited environments.- They are S-shaped, showing slow, then rapid, then declining growth.- An inflection point marks where the growth rate begins to decline.- The population approaches a limiting value, representing carrying capacity.
concepts.raw_body:
## LOGISTIC CURVES

When a population grows in an environment in which space or food is limited, the graph of population versus time is typically an S-shaped curve of the form shown in Figure 4.1.16. The scenario described by this curve is a population that grows slowly at first and then more and more rapidly as the number of individuals producing offspring increases. However, at a certain point in time (where the inflection point occurs) the environmental factors begin to show their effect, and the growth rate begins a steady decline. Over an extended period of time the population approaches a limiting value that represents the upper limit on the number of individuals that the available space or food can sustain. Population growth curves of this type are called logistic growth curves.
concepts.section_title: ANALYSIS OF FUNCTIONS I: INCREASE, DECREASE, AND CONCAVITY

concepts.title: Introduction to Relative Maxima and Minima
concepts.one_liner: The tops of hills on a function's graph are called "relative maxima," and the bottoms of valleys are called "relative minima".
concepts.summary_md: Relative maxima are the high points in their immediate vicinity on a function's graph, analogous to hilltops in a mountain range. Relative minima are the low points in their immediate vicinity, like valley bottoms. These points are local extremes and are not necessarily the absolute highest or lowest points of the entire function.
concepts.motivation_md: Identifying relative maxima and minima is crucial for understanding the local behavior of a function, such as where it reaches peak or trough values within a specific interval. This helps in optimizing functions in various applications and sketching accurate graphs.
concepts.recap_md: - Relative maxima are local high points on a graph.- Relative minima are local low points on a graph.- These are local extremes, not necessarily global extremes.
concepts.raw_body: If we imagine the graph of a function $f$ to be a two-dimensional mountain range with hills and valleys, then the tops of the hills are called "relative maxima," and the bottoms of the valleys are called "relative minima" (Figure 4.2.1). The relative maxima are the high points in their immediate vicinity, and the relative minima are the low points. A relative maximum need not be the highest point in the entire mountain range, and a relative minimum need not be the lowest point-they are just high and low points relative to the nearby terrain. These ideas are captured in the following definition.
concepts.section_title: ANALYSIS OF FUNCTIONS II: RELATIVE EXTREMA; GRAPHING POLYNOMIALS

concepts.title: Relative Maximum, Relative Minimum, Relative Extremum
concepts.one_liner: If $f$ has either a relative maximum or a relative minimum at $x_{0}$, then $f$ is said to have a relative extremum at $x_{0}$.
concepts.summary_md: A function $f$ has a relative maximum at $x_{0}$ if $f(x_{0})$ is the largest value on an open interval containing $x_{0}$. Similarly, $f$ has a relative minimum at $x_{0}$ if $f(x_{0})$ is the smallest value on such an interval. If $f$ has either, it's a relative extremum.
concepts.motivation_md: This concept defines specific points where a function reaches local peaks or valleys. Understanding these points is crucial for analyzing function behavior, such as optimization problems, where we seek maximum or minimum values within a given domain.
concepts.recap_md: - A relative maximum occurs at $x_0$ if $f(x_0)$ is the largest value in an open interval around $x_0$.- A relative minimum occurs at $x_0$ if $f(x_0)$ is the smallest value in an open interval around $x_0$.- A relative extremum is either a relative maximum or a relative minimum.
concepts.raw_body: 4.2.1 DEFINITION A function $f$ is said to have a relative maximum at $x_{0}$ if there is an open interval containing $x_{0}$ on which $f\left(x_{0}\right)$ is the largest value, that is, $f\left(x_{0}\right) \geq f(x)$ for all $x$ in the interval. Similarly, $f$ is said to have a relative minimum at $x_{0}$ if there is an open interval containing $x_{0}$ on which $f\left(x_{0}\right)$ is the smallest value, that is, $f\left(x_{0}\right) \leq f(x)$ for all $x$ in the interval. If $f$ has either a relative maximum or a relative minimum at $x_{0}$, then $f$ is said to have a relative extremum at $x_{0}$.
concepts.section_title: ANALYSIS OF FUNCTIONS II: RELATIVE EXTREMA; GRAPHING POLYNOMIALS

concepts.title: Critical Point and Stationary Point
concepts.one_liner: A critical point for a function $f$ is a point in its domain where the graph has a horizontal tangent line or $f$ is not differentiable.
concepts.summary_md: A critical point for a function $f$ is defined as a point in the domain of $f$ at which either the graph of $f$ has a horizontal tangent line or $f$ is not differentiable. To distinguish, $x$ is called a stationary point of $f$ if $f^{\prime}(x)=0$. Critical points are candidates for relative extrema.
concepts.motivation_md: Critical points provide a systematic way to find potential locations of relative extrema. By identifying where the derivative is zero or undefined, we narrow down the search for local maximums and minimums, which is essential for optimization.
concepts.recap_md: - A critical point is where $f'(x)=0$ or $f'(x)$ is undefined.- A stationary point is a specific type of critical point where $f'(x)=0$.- Critical points are the only possible locations for relative extrema in the interior of a function's domain.
concepts.raw_body: The relative extrema for the five functions in Example 1 occur at points where the graphs of the functions have horizontal tangent lines. Figure 4.2.3 illustrates that a relative extremum can also occur at a point where a function is not differentiable. In general, we define a critical point for a function $f$ to be a point in the domain of $f$ at which either the graph of $f$ has a horizontal tangent line or $f$ is not differentiable. To distinguish between the two types of critical points we call $x$ a stationary point of $f$ if $f^{\prime}(x)=0$. The following theorem, which is proved in Appendix D, states that the critical points for a function form a complete set of candidates for relative extrema on the interior of the domain of the function.
concepts.section_title: ANALYSIS OF FUNCTIONS II: RELATIVE EXTREMA; GRAPHING POLYNOMIALS

concepts.title: Relative Extremum Implies Critical Point
concepts.one_liner: If $f$ has a relative extremum at $x=x_{0}$, then $x=x_{0}$ is a critical point of $f$.
concepts.summary_md: Theorem 4.2.2 states that if a function $f$ has a relative extremum at a point $x_0$ within an open interval, then $x_0$ must be a critical point of $f$. This means either $f^{\prime}(x_{0})=0$ or $f$ is not differentiable at $x_{0}$.
concepts.motivation_md: This theorem is fundamental because it establishes that we only need to check critical points when searching for relative extrema. It significantly narrows down the possibilities, making the process of finding local maximums and minimums much more efficient and systematic.
concepts.recap_md: - If a function has a relative extremum at $x_0$, then $x_0$ must be a critical point.- This implies that at $x_0$, either $f'(x_0)=0$ or $f$ is not differentiable.- This theorem provides a necessary condition for relative extrema.
concepts.raw_body: 4.2.2 THEOREM Suppose that $f$ is a function defined on an open interval containing the point $x_{0}$. If $f$ has a relative extremum at $x=x_{0}$, then $x=x_{0}$ is a critical point of $f$; that is, either $f^{\prime}\left(x_{0}\right)=0$ or $f$ is not differentiable at $x_{0}$.
concepts.section_title: ANALYSIS OF FUNCTIONS II: RELATIVE EXTREMA; GRAPHING POLYNOMIALS

concepts.title: Introduction to the First Derivative Test
concepts.one_liner: A function $f$ has a relative extremum at those critical points where $f^{\prime}$ changes sign.
concepts.summary_md: Theorem 4.2.2 states that relative extrema occur at critical points, but not every critical point is an extremum. Observations show that relative extrema occur where the derivative $f^{\prime}$ changes sign around $x_0$, while critical points without extrema have the same sign of $f^{\prime}$ on both sides.
concepts.motivation_md: While critical points identify *potential* extrema, this introduction highlights that not all critical points are actual extrema. The "First Derivative Test" is needed to distinguish between critical points that are extrema and those that are not, by examining the sign changes of the derivative.
concepts.recap_md: - Not all critical points correspond to relative extrema.- Relative extrema occur at critical points where the first derivative $f'$ changes sign.- If $f'$ does not change sign at a critical point, there is no relative extremum.
concepts.raw_body:
Theorem 4.2.2 asserts that the relative extrema must occur at critical points, but it does not say that a relative extremum occurs at every critical point. For example, for the eight critical points in Figure 4.2.6, relative extrema occur at each $x_{0}$ in the top row but not at any $x_{0}$ in the bottom row. Moreover, at the critical points in the first row the derivatives have opposite signs on the two sides of $x_{0}$, whereas at the critical points in the second row the signs of the derivatives are the same on both sides. This suggests:

A function $f$ has a relative extremum at those critical points where $f^{\prime}$ changes sign.
concepts.section_title: ANALYSIS OF FUNCTIONS II: RELATIVE EXTREMA; GRAPHING POLYNOMIALS

concepts.title: First Derivative Test
concepts.one_liner: The First Derivative Test uses the sign changes of $f^{\prime}(x)$ around a critical point $x_0$ to determine if it's a relative maximum, minimum, or neither.
concepts.summary_md: The First Derivative Test states that if $f$ is continuous at a critical point $x_{0}$: (a) A relative maximum occurs if $f^{\prime}(x)>0$ to the left of $x_{0}$ and $f^{\prime}(x)<0$ to the right. (b) A relative minimum occurs if $f^{\prime}(x)<0$ to the left and $f^{\prime}(x)>0$ to the right. (c) No relative extremum exists if $f^{\prime}(x)$ has the same sign on both sides of $x_{0}$.
concepts.motivation_md: This test provides a definitive method to classify critical points as relative maxima, minima, or neither. It leverages the relationship between the sign of the first derivative and the increasing/decreasing behavior of the function, allowing for precise identification of local extrema.
concepts.recap_md: - If $f'$ changes from positive to negative at $x_0$, $f$ has a relative maximum.- If $f'$ changes from negative to positive at $x_0$, $f$ has a relative minimum.- If $f'$ does not change sign at $x_0$, there is no relative extremum.
concepts.raw_body:
4.2.3 THEOREM (First Derivative Test) Suppose that $f$ is continuous at a critical point $x_{0}$.
(a) If $f^{\prime}(x)>0$ on an open interval extending left from $x_{0}$ and $f^{\prime}(x)<0$ on an open interval extending right from $x_{0}$, then $f$ has a relative maximum at $x_{0}$.
(b) If $f^{\prime}(x)<0$ on an open interval extending left from $x_{0}$ and $f^{\prime}(x)>0$ on an open interval extending right from $x_{0}$, then $f$ has a relative minimum at $x_{0}$.
(c) If $f^{\prime}(x)$ has the same sign on an open interval extending left from $x_{0}$ as it does on an open interval extending right from $x_{0}$, then $f$ does not have a relative extremum at $x_{0}$.
concepts.section_title: ANALYSIS OF FUNCTIONS II: RELATIVE EXTREMA; GRAPHING POLYNOMIALS

concepts.title: Geometric Basis for Second Derivative Test
concepts.one_liner: A function $f$ has a relative maximum at a stationary point if the graph of $f$ is concave down, and a relative minimum if it is concave up.
concepts.summary_md: Another test for relative extrema is based on geometric observation: A function $f$ has a relative maximum at a stationary point if its graph is concave down on an open interval containing that point. Conversely, it has a relative minimum if the graph is concave up on such an interval.
concepts.motivation_md: This introduction sets the stage for the Second Derivative Test by linking the concavity of a function's graph to the nature of its stationary points. It offers an alternative, often quicker, way to classify extrema compared to analyzing sign changes of the first derivative.
concepts.recap_md: - Concavity can indicate the nature of relative extrema at stationary points.- Concave down at a stationary point suggests a relative maximum.- Concave up at a stationary point suggests a relative minimum.
concepts.raw_body: There is another test for relative extrema that is based on the following geometric observation: A function $f$ has a relative maximum at a stationary point if the graph of $f$ is concave down on an open interval containing that point, and it has a relative minimum if it is concave up (Figure 4.2.7).
concepts.section_title: ANALYSIS OF FUNCTIONS II: RELATIVE EXTREMA; GRAPHING POLYNOMIALS

concepts.title: Second Derivative Test
concepts.one_liner: The Second Derivative Test uses the sign of $f^{\prime \prime}(x_0)$ at a stationary point $x_0$ to classify it as a relative maximum or minimum.
concepts.summary_md: The Second Derivative Test states that if $f$ is twice differentiable at $x_{0}$: (a) If $f^{\prime}(x_{0})=0$ and $f^{\prime \prime}(x_{0})>0$, $f$ has a relative minimum at $x_{0}$. (b) If $f^{\prime}(x_{0})=0$ and $f^{\prime \prime}(x_{0})<0$, $f$ has a relative maximum at $x_{0}$. (c) If $f^{\prime}(x_{0})=0$ and $f^{\prime \prime}(x_{0})=0$, the test is inconclusive.
concepts.motivation_md: This test provides an efficient way to classify stationary points without analyzing derivative signs on intervals. By simply evaluating the second derivative at the point, we can quickly determine if it's a local maximum or minimum, provided the test is conclusive.
concepts.recap_md: - If $f'(x_0)=0$ and $f''(x_0)>0$, then $f$ has a relative minimum at $x_0$.- If $f'(x_0)=0$ and $f''(x_0)<0$, then $f$ has a relative maximum at $x_0$.- If $f'(x_0)=0$ and $f''(x_0)=0$, the test is inconclusive.
concepts.raw_body:
4.2.4 THEOREM (Second Derivative Test) Suppose that $f$ is twice differentiable at the point $x_{0}$.
(a) If $f^{\prime}\left(x_{0}\right)=0$ and $f^{\prime \prime}\left(x_{0}\right)>0$, then $f$ has a relative minimum at $x_{0}$.
(b) If $f^{\prime}\left(x_{0}\right)=0$ and $f^{\prime \prime}\left(x_{0}\right)<0$, then $f$ has a relative maximum at $x_{0}$.
(c) If $f^{\prime}\left(x_{0}\right)=0$ and $f^{\prime \prime}\left(x_{0}\right)=0$, then the test is inconclusive; that is, $f$ may have a relative maximum, a relative minimum, or neither at $x_{0}$.
concepts.section_title: ANALYSIS OF FUNCTIONS II: RELATIVE EXTREMA; GRAPHING POLYNOMIALS

concepts.title: Introduction to Geometric Implications of Root Multiplicity
concepts.one_liner: The behavior of a polynomial's graph near a real root is determined by the multiplicity of that root.
concepts.summary_md: To analyze and graph polynomials, it's helpful to understand how the graph behaves near its roots. A root $x=r$ of a polynomial $p(x)$ has multiplicity $m$ if $(x-r)^m$ divides $p(x)$ but $(x-r)^{m+1}$ does not. The behavior of a polynomial near a real root is determined by its multiplicity.
concepts.motivation_md: Understanding root multiplicity helps predict the local shape of a polynomial's graph at its x-intercepts. This knowledge is crucial for sketching accurate graphs and analyzing polynomial behavior without needing to plot many points or perform extensive derivative analysis.
concepts.recap_md: - Root multiplicity influences a polynomial's graph behavior near its roots.- A root $x=r$ has multiplicity $m$ if $(x-r)^m$ divides $p(x)$ but $(x-r)^{m+1}$ does not.- A root of multiplicity 1 is called a simple root.
concepts.raw_body:
Our final goal in this section is to outline a general procedure that can be used to analyze and graph polynomials. To do so, it will be helpful to understand how the graph of a polynomial behaves in the vicinity of its roots. For example, it would be nice to know what property of the polynomial in Example 5 produced the inflection point and horizontal tangent at the root $x=0$.

Recall that a root $x=r$ of a polynomial $p(x)$ has multiplicity $\boldsymbol{m}$ if $(x-r)^{m}$ divides $p(x)$ but $(x-r)^{m+1}$ does not. A root of multiplicity 1 is called a simple root. Figure 4.2.9 and the following theorem show that the behavior of a polynomial in the vicinity of a real root is determined by the multiplicity of that root (we omit the proof).

concepts.title: Root Multiplicity and Simple Root

The behavior of a polynomial in the vicinity of a real root is determined by the multiplicity of that root.
concepts.motivation_md: Understanding root multiplicity helps predict how a polynomial's graph behaves near its x-intercepts. This concept is crucial for analyzing the shape of the graph, specifically whether it crosses the x-axis or is tangent to it, and if it has an inflection point.

A root of multiplicity 1 is called a simple root. concepts.title: Geometric Implications of Multiplicity
concepts.one_liner: The geometric implications of multiplicity describe how the graph of a polynomial behaves at a root $x=r$ based on its multiplicity $m$.
concepts.summary_md: Suppose $p(x)$ is a polynomial with a root of multiplicity $m$ at $x=r$. If $m$ is even, the graph of $y=p(x)$ is tangent to the $x$-axis at $x=r$ but does not cross it. If $m$ is odd and greater than 1, the graph is tangent to the $x$-axis, crosses it, and has an inflection point there. If $m=1$ (a simple root), the graph is not tangent to the $x$-axis but crosses it.
concepts.motivation_md: This theorem provides a direct link between the algebraic property of root multiplicity and the visual behavior of a polynomial's graph. It allows us to quickly infer key features like tangency, crossing, and inflection points at x-intercepts without extensive calculus calculations.
concepts.recap_md: - If multiplicity $m$ is even, the graph is tangent to the $x$-axis at $x=r$ but does not cross it.- If $m$ is odd and greater than 1, the graph is tangent to the $x$-axis at $x=r$, crosses it, and has an inflection point.- If $m=1$ (simple root), the graph is not tangent to the $x$-axis at $x=r$ but crosses it.
concepts.raw_body:
4.2.5 THE GEOMETRIC IMPLICATIONS OF MULTIPLICITY Suppose that $p(x)$ is a polynomial with a root of multiplicity $m$ at $x=r$.
(a) If $m$ is even, then the graph of $y=p(x)$ is tangent to the $x$-axis at $x=r$, does not cross the $x$-axis there, and does not have an inflection point there.
(b) If $m$ is odd and greater than 1 , then the graph is tangent to the $x$-axis at $x=r$, crosses the $x$-axis there, and also has an inflection point there.
(c) If $m=1$ (so that the root is simple), then the graph is not tangent to the $x$-axis at $x=r$, crosses the $x$-axis there, and may or may not have an inflection point there.

concepts.title: Overview of Polynomial Analysis and Graphing
concepts.one_liner: The purpose of curve sketching has changed from drawing graphs by hand to using calculus to identify important features of computer-generated graphs.
concepts.summary_md: The goal of curve sketching is now to use calculus to identify important features of computer-generated graphs, rather than drawing them by hand. Polynomials are simple to analyze, with key features including symmetry, intercepts, relative extrema, inflection points, and end behavior. All polynomials have a domain of $(-\infty,+\infty)$, are continuous and differentiable everywhere. A polynomial of degree $n(>2)$ has at most $n$ x-intercepts, $n-1$ relative extrema, and $n-2$ inflection points.
concepts.motivation_md: Understanding the general properties of polynomials simplifies their analysis and graphing. By knowing their inherent characteristics, we can efficiently identify critical features like extrema and inflection points, which might be missed by simple computational tools.
concepts.recap_md: - Curve sketching now focuses on identifying important features of graphs, not just drawing them.- Polynomials are continuous, differentiable everywhere, and their domain is $(-\infty,+\infty)$.- A polynomial of degree $n$ has at most $n$ x-intercepts, $n-1$ relative extrema, and $n-2$ inflection points.
concepts.raw_body:
Historically, the term "curve sketching" meant using calculus to help draw the graph of a function by hand-the graph was the goal. Since graphs can now be produced with great precision using calculators and computers, the purpose of curve sketching has changed. Today, we typically start with a graph produced by a calculator or computer, then use curve sketching to identify important features of the graph that the calculator or computer might have missed. Thus, the goal of curve sketching is no longer the graph itself, but rather the information it reveals about the function.

Polynomials are among the simplest functions to graph and analyze. Their significant features are symmetry, intercepts, relative extrema, inflection points, and the behavior as $x \rightarrow+\infty$ and as $x \rightarrow-\infty$. Figure 4.2.11 shows the graphs of four polynomials in $x$. The graphs in Figure 4.2.11 have properties that are common to all polynomials:

- The natural domain of a polynomial is $(-\infty,+\infty)$.
- Polynomials are continuous everywhere.
- Polynomials are differentiable everywhere, so their graphs have no corners or vertical tangent lines.
- The graph of a nonconstant polynomial eventually increases or decreases without bound as $x \rightarrow+\infty$ and as $x \rightarrow-\infty$. This is because the limit of a nonconstant polynomial as $x \rightarrow+\infty$ or as $x \rightarrow-\infty$ is $\pm \infty$, depending on the sign of the term of highest degree and whether the polynomial has even or odd degree [see Formulas (17) and (18) of Section 1.3 and the related discussion].
- The graph of a polynomial of degree $n(>2)$ has at most $n x$-intercepts, at most $n-1$ relative extrema, and at most $n-2$ inflection points. This is because the $x$ intercepts, relative extrema, and inflection points of a polynomial $p(x)$ are among the real solutions of the equations $p(x)=0, p^{\prime}(x)=0$, and $p^{\prime \prime}(x)=0$, and the polynomials in these equations have degree $n, n-1$, and $n-2$, respectively. Thus, for example, the graph of a quadratic polynomial has at most two $x$-intercepts, one relative extremum, and no inflection points; and the graph of a cubic polynomial has at most three $x$-intercepts, two relative extrema, and one inflection point.
concepts.section_title: ANALYSIS OF FUNCTIONS II: RELATIVE EXTREMA; GRAPHING POLYNOMIALS

concepts.title: Properties of Graphs
concepts.one_liner: Key properties of interest in a function's graph include symmetries, intercepts, extrema, intervals of increase/decrease, asymptotes, periodicity, concavity, inflection points, and end behavior.
concepts.summary_md: When analyzing a function's graph, properties of interest include symmetries, $x$- and $y$-intercepts, relative extrema, intervals of increase/decrease, asymptotes, periodicity, concavity, inflection points, and behavior as $x \rightarrow \pm \infty$. Not all properties are relevant for every function family; for instance, asymptotes are for rational functions, and periodicity for trigonometric functions. The specific objectives of your analysis will determine which characteristics to focus on.
concepts.motivation_md: Identifying specific properties of a graph allows for a comprehensive understanding of a function's behavior. Knowing which properties are relevant to a particular function family helps streamline the analysis, focusing efforts on features that provide the most insight.
concepts.recap_md: - Important graph properties include intercepts, extrema, concavity, and end behavior.- Some properties, like asymptotes or periodicity, are specific to certain function families.- The objectives of your analysis dictate which graph characteristics to focus on.
concepts.raw_body:
## PROPERTIES OF GRAPHS

In many problems, the properties of interest in the graph of a function are:

- symmetries
- $x$-intercepts
- relative extrema
- intervals of increase and decrease
- asymptotes
- periodicity
- $y$-intercepts
- concavity
- inflection points
- behavior as $x \rightarrow+\infty$ or as $x \rightarrow-\infty$

Some of these properties may not be relevant in certain cases; for example, asymptotes are characteristic of rational functions but not of polynomials, and periodicity is characteristic of
trigonometric functions but not of polynomial or rational functions. Thus, when analyzing the graph of a function $f$, it helps to know something about the general properties of the family to which it belongs.

In a given problem you will usually have a definite objective for your analysis of a graph. For example, you may be interested in showing all of the important characteristics of the function, you may only be interested in the behavior of the graph as $x \rightarrow+\infty$ or as $x \rightarrow-\infty$, or you may be interested in some specific feature such as a particular inflection point. Thus, your objectives in the problem will dictate those characteristics on which you want to focus.
concepts.section_title: ANALYSIS OF FUNCTIONS III: RATIONAL FUNCTIONS, CUSPS, AND VERTICAL TANGENTS

concepts.title: Graphing Rational Functions
concepts.one_liner: Rational functions, defined as $f(x)=P(x) / Q(x)$ where $P(x)$ and $Q(x)$ are polynomials, have graphs more complex than polynomials due to asymptotes and discontinuities.
concepts.summary_md: A rational function is defined as $f(x)=P(x) / Q(x)$, where $P(x)$ and $Q(x)$ are polynomials. Their graphs are more complex than polynomial graphs due to potential asymptotes and discontinuities. If $P(x)$ and $Q(x)$ share no common factors, a specific set of steps can provide enough information to accurately sketch the graph.
concepts.motivation_md: Rational functions introduce new complexities like asymptotes and discontinuities not present in polynomials. A structured approach is needed to accurately graph these functions, especially when the numerator and denominator share no common factors, to reveal their true behavior.
concepts.recap_md: - A rational function is a ratio of two polynomials, $f(x)=P(x) / Q(x)$.- Rational function graphs are more complex than polynomials due to asymptotes and discontinuities.- A specific procedure helps sketch rational functions when $P(x)$ and $Q(x)$ have no common factors.
concepts.raw_body:
## GRAPHING RATIONAL FUNCTIONS

Recall that a rational function is a function of the form $f(x)=P(x) / Q(x)$ in which $P(x)$ and $Q(x)$ are polynomials. Graphs of rational functions are more complicated than those of polynomials because of the possibility of asymptotes and discontinuities (see Figure 0.3.11, for example). If $P(x)$ and $Q(x)$ have no common factors, then the information obtained in the following steps will usually be sufficient to obtain an accurate sketch of the graph of a rational function.
concepts.section_title: ANALYSIS OF FUNCTIONS III: RATIONAL FUNCTIONS, CUSPS, AND VERTICAL TANGENTS

concepts.title: Graphing a Rational Function if Numerator and Denominator have no Common Factors
concepts.one_liner: To graph a rational function $f(x)=P(x)/Q(x)$ with no common factors, follow steps including finding symmetries, intercepts, asymptotes, sign changes, end behavior, and analyzing derivatives.
concepts.summary_md: Graphing a rational function $f(x)=P(x)/Q(x)$ where $P(x)$ and $Q(x)$ have no common factors involves several steps. First, determine symmetries, $x$- and $y$-intercepts, and vertical asymptotes by finding where $Q(x)=0$. Next, analyze the sign of $f(x)$ in intervals defined by intercepts and asymptotes. Determine end behavior and horizontal asymptotes by computing limits as $x \rightarrow \pm \infty$. Finally, use $f'(x)$ and $f''(x)$ to find intervals of increase/decrease, concavity, extrema, and inflection points to sketch the graph.
concepts.motivation_md: This systematic approach ensures all critical features of a rational function's graph are identified. By breaking down the complex task into manageable steps, it helps to accurately visualize the function's behavior, including its discontinuities and asymptotic trends.
concepts.recap_md: - Start by finding symmetries, intercepts, and vertical asymptotes ($Q(x)=0$).- Analyze the sign of $f(x)$ in intervals and determine end behavior for horizontal asymptotes.- Use $f'(x)$ and $f''(x)$ to find increasing/decreasing intervals, concavity, extrema, and inflection points to sketch the graph.
concepts.raw_body:
## Graphing a Rational Function $f(x)=P(x) / Q(x)$ if $P(x)$ and $Q(x)$ have no Common Factors

Step 1. (symmetries). Determine whether there is symmetry about the $y$-axis or the origin.

Step 2. ( $\boldsymbol{x}$ - and $\boldsymbol{y}$-intercepts). Find the $x$ - and $y$-intercepts.
Step 3. (vertical asymptotes). Find the values of $x$ for which $Q(x)=0$. The graph has a vertical asymptote at each such value.

Step 4. (sign of $\boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{x}))$. The only places where $f(x)$ can change sign are at the $x$ intercepts or vertical asymptotes. Mark the points on the $x$-axis at which these occur and calculate a sample value of $f(x)$ in each of the open intervals determined by these points. This will tell you whether $f(x)$ is positive or negative over that interval.

Step 5. (end behavior). Determine the end behavior of the graph by computing the limits of $f(x)$ as $x \rightarrow+\infty$ and as $x \rightarrow-\infty$. If either limit has a finite value $L$, then the line $y=L$ is a horizontal asymptote.

Step 6. (derivatives). Find $f^{\prime}(x)$ and $f^{\prime \prime}(x)$.
Step 7. (conclusions and graph). Analyze the sign changes of $f^{\prime}(x)$ and $f^{\prime \prime}(x)$ to determine the intervals where $f(x)$ is increasing, decreasing, concave up, and concave down. Determine the locations of all stationary points, relative extrema, and inflection points. Use the sign analysis of $f(x)$ to determine the behavior of the graph in the vicinity of the vertical asymptotes. Sketch a graph of $f$ that exhibits these conclusions.
concepts.section_title: ANALYSIS OF FUNCTIONS III: RATIONAL FUNCTIONS, CUSPS, AND VERTICAL TANGENTS

concepts.title: Rational Functions with Oblique or Curvilinear Asymptotes
concepts.one_liner: When the numerator's degree exceeds the denominator's, rational functions can have oblique (slant) or curvilinear asymptotes, which are non-horizontal lines or curves the function approaches.
concepts.summary_md: If a rational function $f(x)=P(x)/Q(x)$ has a numerator degree greater than its denominator, it can have oblique or curvilinear asymptotes. By polynomial division, $f(x)$ can be rewritten as $q(x) + r(x)/Q(x)$, where $r(x)/Q(x) \rightarrow 0$ as $x \rightarrow \pm \infty$. Thus, $y=q(x)$ is the asymptote. It's an oblique line if $\text{deg}(P) = \text{deg}(Q)+1$, and curvilinear if $\text{deg}(P) \ge \text{deg}(Q)+2$.
concepts.motivation_md: Understanding oblique and curvilinear asymptotes is essential for accurately graphing rational functions where the numerator's degree is higher than the denominator's. These asymptotes describe the function's long-term behavior, providing a more complete picture than just horizontal or vertical asymptotes.
concepts.recap_md: - Oblique or curvilinear asymptotes occur when the degree of the numerator is greater than the degree of the denominator.- Polynomial division yields $f(x)=q(x)+r(x)/Q(x)$, where $y=q(x)$ is the asymptote.- The asymptote is oblique if $\text{deg}(P) = \text{deg}(Q)+1$, and curvilinear if $\text{deg}(P) \ge \text{deg}(Q)+2$.
concepts.raw_body:
## RATIONAL FUNCTIONS WITH OBLIQUE OR CURVILINEAR ASYMPTOTES

In the rational functions of Examples 1 and 2, the degree of the numerator did not exceed the degree of the denominator, and the asymptotes were either vertical or horizontal. If the numerator of a rational function has greater degree than the denominator, then other kinds of "asymptotes" are possible. For example, consider the rational functions

$$
\begin{equation*}
f(x)=\frac{x^{2}+1}{x} \quad \text { and } \quad g(x)=\frac{x^{3}-x^{2}-8}{x-1} \tag{1}
\end{equation*}
$$

By division we can rewrite these as

$$
f(x)=x+\frac{1}{x} \quad \text { and } \quad g(x)=x^{2}-\frac{8}{x-1}
$$

Since the second terms both approach 0 as $x \rightarrow+\infty$ or as $x \rightarrow-\infty$, it follows that

$$
\begin{array}{ll}
(f(x)-x) \rightarrow 0 & \text { as } x \rightarrow+\infty \text { or as } x \rightarrow-\infty \\
\left(g(x)-x^{2}\right) \rightarrow 0 & \text { as } x \rightarrow+\infty \text { or as } x \rightarrow-\infty
\end{array}
$$

Geometrically, this means that the graph of $y=f(x)$ eventually gets closer and closer to the line $y=x$ as $x \rightarrow+\infty$ or as $x \rightarrow-\infty$. The line $y=x$ is called an oblique or slant asymptote of $f$. Similarly, the graph of $y=g(x)$ eventually gets closer and closer to the parabola $y=x^{2}$ as $x \rightarrow+\infty$ or as $x \rightarrow-\infty$. The parabola is called a curvilinear asymptote of $g$. The graphs of the functions in (1) are shown in Figures 4.3.3 and 4.3.4.

In general, if $f(x)=P(x) / Q(x)$ is a rational function, then we can find quotient and remainder polynomials $q(x)$ and $r(x)$ such that

$$
f(x)=q(x)+\frac{r(x)}{Q(x)}
$$

and the degree of $r(x)$ is less than the degree of $Q(x)$. Then $r(x) / Q(x) \rightarrow 0$ as $x \rightarrow+\infty$ and as $x \rightarrow-\infty$, so $y=q(x)$ is an asymptote of $f$. This asymptote will be an oblique line if the degree of $P(x)$ is one greater than the degree of $Q(x)$, and it will be curvilinear if the degree of $P(x)$ exceeds that of $Q(x)$ by two or more. Problems involving these kinds of asymptotes are given in the exercises (Exercises 17 and 18).

concepts.title: Oblique or Slant Asymptote
concepts.one_liner: An oblique or slant asymptote is a line that a function's graph approaches as $x$ tends to positive or negative infinity.
concepts.summary_md: An oblique or slant asymptote is a line that the graph of a function $y=f(x)$ eventually gets closer and closer to as $x \rightarrow+\infty$ or as $x \rightarrow-\infty$. Similarly, a curvilinear asymptote is a curve (like a parabola) that the graph approaches under the same conditions.
concepts.motivation_md: Oblique and curvilinear asymptotes describe the long-term behavior of functions that don't have horizontal asymptotes. They provide a more precise understanding of how the graph behaves at the extremes of its domain, which is crucial for accurate sketching and analysis.
concepts.recap_md: - An oblique (slant) asymptote is a line that a function's graph approaches as $x \rightarrow \pm \infty$.- A curvilinear asymptote is a curve (e.g., a parabola) that a function's graph approaches as $x \rightarrow \pm \infty$.- These asymptotes describe the end behavior of functions, particularly rational functions where the numerator's degree exceeds the denominator's.
concepts.raw_body: Geometrically, this means that the graph of $y=f(x)$ eventually gets closer and closer to the line $y=x$ as $x \rightarrow+\infty$ or as $x \rightarrow-\infty$. The line $y=x$ is called an oblique or slant asymptote of $f$. Similarly, the graph of $y=g(x)$ eventually gets closer and closer to the parabola $y=x^{2}$ as $x \rightarrow+\infty$ or as $x \rightarrow-\infty$. The parabola is called a curvilinear asymptote of $g$. The graphs of the functions in (1) are shown in Figures 4.3.3 and 4.3.4.

concepts.title: Curvilinear Asymptote
concepts.one_liner: The parabola is called a curvilinear asymptote of $g$ when the graph of $y=g(x)$ eventually gets closer and closer to it as $x \rightarrow+\infty$ or as $x \rightarrow-\infty$.
concepts.summary_md: The graph of $y=g(x)$ eventually gets closer and closer to the parabola $y=x^{2}$ as $x \rightarrow+\infty$ or as $x \rightarrow-\infty$. This parabola is called a curvilinear asymptote of $g$.
concepts.motivation_md: This concept extends the idea of asymptotes beyond straight lines to more complex curves, allowing for a more precise description of a function's end behavior when it approaches a non-linear function.
concepts.recap_md: - A curvilinear asymptote is a curve (like a parabola) that a function's graph approaches as $x \rightarrow \pm \infty$. - It generalizes the concept of oblique or slant asymptotes, which are straight lines.
concepts.raw_body: Geometrically, this means that the graph of $y=f(x)$ eventually gets closer and closer to the line $y=x$ as $x \rightarrow+\infty$ or as $x \rightarrow-\infty$. The line $y=x$ is called an oblique or slant asymptote of $f$. Similarly, the graph of $y=g(x)$ eventually gets closer and closer to the parabola $y=x^{2}$ as $x \rightarrow+\infty$ or as $x \rightarrow-\infty$. The parabola is called a curvilinear asymptote of $g$. The graphs of the functions in (1) are shown in Figures 4.3.3 and 4.3.4.
concepts.section_title: ANALYSIS OF FUNCTIONS III: RATIONAL FUNCTIONS, CUSPS, AND VERTICAL TANGENTS

concepts.title: Graphs with Vertical Tangents and Cusps
concepts.one_liner: Graphs of functions involving radicals or fractional exponents can have vertical tangent lines or cusps at points where the function is not differentiable.
concepts.summary_md: Functions involving radicals or fractional exponents often have curve elements like vertical tangents and cusps. In these cases, the function is not differentiable at $x_{0}$ because the secant line approaches a vertical position. A vertical tangent line occurs at $(x_{0}, f(x_{0}))$. A cusp occurs at $x_{0}$ when $f^{\prime}(x)$ approaches $+\infty$ from one side and $-\infty$ from the other.
concepts.motivation_md: Understanding vertical tangents and cusps is crucial for accurately sketching graphs, especially for functions that are not differentiable at certain points. These features reveal important local behavior that standard derivative tests might miss.
concepts.recap_md: - Vertical tangents and cusps occur where a function is not differentiable. - A vertical tangent means the secant line approaches a vertical position. - A cusp occurs when $f'(x)$ approaches $\pm\infty$ from different sides of $x_0$.
concepts.raw_body:
## GRAPHS WITH VERTICAL TANGENTS AND CUSPS

Figure 4.3.5 shows four curve elements that are commonly found in graphs of functions that involve radicals or fractional exponents. In all four cases, the function is not differentiable at $x_{0}$ because the secant line through $\left(x_{0}, f\left(x_{0}\right)\right)$ and $(x, f(x))$ approaches a vertical position as $x$ approaches $x_{0}$ from either side. Thus, in each case, the curve has a vertical tangent line at ( $x_{0}, f\left(x_{0}\right)$ ). In parts ( $a$ ) and ( $b$ ) of the figure, there is an inflection point at $x_{0}$ because there is a change in concavity at that point. In parts ( $c$ ) and ( $d$ ), where $f^{\prime}(x)$ approaches $+\infty$ from one side of $x_{0}$ and $-\infty$ from the other side, we say that the graph has a cusp at $x_{0}$.
concepts.section_title: ANALYSIS OF FUNCTIONS III: RATIONAL FUNCTIONS, CUSPS, AND VERTICAL TANGENTS

concepts.title: Vertical Tangent Line
concepts.one_liner: A curve has a vertical tangent line at $(x_{0}, f(x_{0}))$ if the function is not differentiable at $x_{0}$ and the secant line approaches a vertical position as $x$ approaches $x_{0}$.
concepts.summary_md: A vertical tangent line occurs at $(x_{0}, f(x_{0}))$ when the function is not differentiable at $x_{0}$. This happens because the secant line through $(x_{0}, f(x_{0}))$ and $(x, f(x))$ approaches a vertical position as $x$ approaches $x_{0}$ from either side.
concepts.motivation_md: Vertical tangent lines represent points where the rate of change becomes infinitely steep. Identifying them is crucial for understanding the full behavior of a function's graph, especially where differentiability breaks down.
concepts.recap_md: - A vertical tangent line exists at $x_0$ if the function is not differentiable there. - This means the slope of the secant line approaches infinity (vertical position) as $x$ approaches $x_0$.
concepts.raw_body: Figure 4.3.5 shows four curve elements that are commonly found in graphs of functions that involve radicals or fractional exponents. In all four cases, the function is not differentiable at $x_{0}$ because the secant line through $\left(x_{0}, f\left(x_{0}\right)\right)$ and $(x, f(x))$ approaches a vertical position as $x$ approaches $x_{0}$ from either side. Thus, in each case, the curve has a vertical tangent line at ( $x_{0}, f\left(x_{0}\right)$ ). In parts ( $a$ ) and ( $b$ ) of the figure, there is an inflection point at $x_{0}$ because there is a change in concavity at that point. In parts ( $c$ ) and ( $d$ ), where $f^{\prime}(x)$ approaches $+\infty$ from one side of $x_{0}$ and $-\infty$ from the other side, we say that the graph has a cusp at $x_{0}$.
concepts.section_title: ANALYSIS OF FUNCTIONS III: RATIONAL FUNCTIONS, CUSPS, AND VERTICAL TANGENTS

concepts.title: Cusp
concepts.one_liner: A graph has a cusp at $x_{0}$ when $f^{\prime}(x)$ approaches $+\infty$ from one side of $x_{0}$ and $-\infty$ from the other side.
concepts.summary_md: A cusp occurs at $x_{0}$ in a graph when the function is not differentiable at that point. Specifically, $f^{\prime}(x)$ approaches $+\infty$ from one side of $x_{0}$ and $-\infty$ from the other side. These features are common in graphs of functions involving radicals or fractional exponents.
concepts.motivation_md: Cusps represent sharp, pointed turns in a graph where the function is not smooth. Recognizing cusps helps in accurately depicting the shape of a function and understanding its differentiability properties.
concepts.recap_md: - A cusp is a point where the function is not differentiable. - At a cusp, $f'(x)$ approaches $\infty$ from one side and $-\infty$ from the other side of $x_0$.
concepts.raw_body: Figure 4.3.5 shows four curve elements that are commonly found in graphs of functions that involve radicals or fractional exponents. In all four cases, the function is not differentiable at $x_{0}$ because the secant line through $\left(x_{0}, f\left(x_{0}\right)\right)$ and $(x, f(x))$ approaches a vertical position as $x$ approaches $x_{0}$ from either side. Thus, in each case, the curve has a vertical tangent line at ( $x_{0}, f\left(x_{0}\right)$ ). In parts ( $a$ ) and ( $b$ ) of the figure, there is an inflection point at $x_{0}$ because there is a change in concavity at that point. In parts ( $c$ ) and ( $d$ ), where $f^{\prime}(x)$ approaches $+\infty$ from one side of $x_{0}$ and $-\infty$ from the other side, we say that the graph has a cusp at $x_{0}$.

concepts.title: Graphing Other Kinds of Functions
concepts.one_liner: The calculus tools used for graphing polynomials and rational functions can also be applied to analyze and graph trigonometric, logarithmic, exponential, and other functions.
concepts.summary_md: Calculus provides a universal set of tools for analyzing and graphing various types of functions. These methods, previously applied to polynomials, rational functions, and functions with cusps or vertical tangent lines, are equally effective for trigonometric, logarithmic, and exponential functions, among others.
concepts.motivation_md: This concept highlights the broad applicability of calculus techniques. It assures learners that the analytical skills developed for specific function types are transferable, making calculus a powerful tool for understanding diverse mathematical models.
concepts.recap_md: - Calculus tools are versatile for graphing many function types. - Methods for polynomials and rational functions extend to trigonometric, logarithmic, and exponential functions.
concepts.raw_body:
## GRAPHING OTHER KINDS OF FUNCTIONS

We have discussed methods for graphing polynomials, rational functions, and functions with cusps and vertical tangent lines. The same calculus tools that we used to analyze these functions can also be used to analyze and graph trigonometric functions, logarithmic and exponential functions, and an endless variety of other kinds of functions.

concepts.title: Graphing Using Calculus and Technology Together
concepts.one_liner: Combining calculus with graphing technology allows us to precisely locate features like extrema and inflection points, and to identify any missing details in a technology-generated graph.
concepts.summary_md: Traditionally, calculus has been used to produce graphs. Now, the approach is reversed: start with a graph from a graphing utility and use calculus tools to determine the exact locations of relative extrema, inflection points, and other suggested features. This also helps identify any important features that might be missing from the technology-generated graph.
concepts.motivation_md: While graphing utilities provide quick visualizations, they can sometimes be misleading or imprecise. Combining technology with calculus ensures accuracy, allowing for the precise identification of critical points and a deeper understanding of a function's behavior.
concepts.recap_md: - Calculus can be used to verify and refine graphs generated by technology. - The goal is to find exact locations of extrema and inflection points. - Calculus helps identify features a graphing utility might miss.
concepts.raw_body:
## GRAPHING USING CALCULUS AND TECHNOLOGY TOGETHER

Thus far in this chapter we have used calculus to produce graphs of functions; the graph was the end result. Now we will work in the reverse direction by starting with a graph produced by a graphing utility. Our goal will be to use the tools of calculus to determine the exact locations of relative extrema, inflection points, and other features suggested by that graph and to determine whether the graph may be missing some important features that we would like to see.

concepts.title: Introduction to Absolute Maxima and Minima
concepts.one_liner: This section focuses on finding the largest and smallest values of a function over an interval, representing the absolute highest and lowest points on its graph.
concepts.summary_md: Relative maxima and minima are the high and low points in a function's immediate vicinity, like hilltops and valley bottoms. This section addresses the broader problem of finding the absolute highest and lowest points over the entire domain or a specified interval, which means finding the largest and smallest values of a function.
concepts.motivation_md: While relative extrema identify local peaks and valleys, many real-world problems require finding the absolute best or worst outcome, such as maximum profit or minimum cost. This concept provides the tools to solve such optimization problems.
concepts.recap_md: - Relative extrema are local high/low points. - Absolute extrema are the highest/lowest points over an entire interval. - The goal is to find the largest and smallest values a function attains.
concepts.raw_body: At the beginning of Section 4.2 we observed that if the graph of a function $f$ is viewed as a two-dimensional mountain range (Figure 4.2.1), then the relative maxima and minima correspond to the tops of the hills and the bottoms of the valleys; that is, they are the high and low points in their immediate vicinity. In this section we will be concerned with the more encompassing problem of finding the highest and lowest points over the entire mountain range, that is, we will be looking for the top of the highest hill and the bottom of the deepest valley. In mathematical terms, we will be looking for the largest and smallest values of a function over an interval.

concepts.title: Absolute Maximum, Absolute Minimum, and Absolute Extremum
concepts.one_liner: A function $f$ has an absolute maximum at $x_{0}$ if $f(x) \leq f\left(x_{0}\right)$ for all $x$ in the interval, and an absolute minimum if $f\left(x_{0}\right) \leq f(x)$.
concepts.summary_md: Given an interval in a function's domain and a point $x_{0}$ within it, $f$ has an absolute maximum at $x_{0}$ if $f(x) \leq f\left(x_{0}\right)$ for all $x$ in the interval. Conversely, $f$ has an absolute minimum at $x_{0}$ if $f\left(x_{0}\right) \leq f(x)$ for all $x$ in the interval. An absolute extremum refers to either an absolute maximum or an absolute minimum.
concepts.motivation_md: This formal definition provides the precise mathematical criteria for identifying the highest and lowest values a function attains over a given interval. It is fundamental for solving optimization problems in various fields.
concepts.recap_md: - An absolute maximum at $x_0$ means $f(x_0)$ is the greatest value in the interval. - An absolute minimum at $x_0$ means $f(x_0)$ is the least value in the interval. - An absolute extremum is either an absolute maximum or an absolute minimum.
concepts.raw_body: 4.4.1 DEFINITION Consider an interval in the domain of a function $f$ and a point $x_{0}$ in that interval. We say that $f$ has an absolute maximum at $x_{0}$ if $f(x) \leq f\left(x_{0}\right)$ for all $x$ in the interval, and we say that $f$ has an absolute minimum at $x_{0}$ if $f\left(x_{0}\right) \leq f(x)$ for all $x$ in the interval. We say that $f$ has an absolute extremum at $x_{0}$ if it has either an absolute maximum or an absolute minimum at that point.

concepts.title: Extreme-Value Theorem validity on infinite open intervals
concepts.one_liner: Theorem 4.4.3 is also valid on infinite open intervals, that is, intervals of the form $(- rac{\infty}{},+\infty),(a,+\infty)$, and $(- rac{\infty}{}, b)$.
concepts.summary_md: Theorem 4.4.3 is also valid on infinite open intervals, that is, intervals of the form $(- rac{\infty}{},+\infty),(a,+\infty)$, and $(- rac{\infty}{}, b)$.
concepts.motivation_md: The Extreme-Value Theorem typically applies to finite closed intervals. This remark extends its applicability, allowing us to consider absolute extrema on unbounded domains, which is crucial for analyzing functions over their natural domains.
concepts.recap_md: - The Extreme-Value Theorem (Theorem 4.4.3) applies to infinite open intervals. - These intervals include $(- rac{\infty}{},+\infty)$, $(a,+\infty)$, and $(- rac{\infty}{}, b)$.
concepts.raw_body:
## REMARK

Theorem 4.4.3 is also valid on infinite open intervals, that is, intervals of the form $(-\infty,+\infty),(a,+\infty)$, and $(-\infty, b)$.

concepts.title: Extreme-Value Theorem
concepts.one_liner: If a function $f$ is continuous on a finite closed interval $[a, b]$, then $f$ has both an absolute maximum and an absolute minimum on $[a, b]$.
concepts.summary_md: If a function $f$ is continuous on a finite closed interval $[a, b]$, then $f$ has both an absolute maximum and an absolute minimum on $[a, b]$.
concepts.motivation_md: This theorem guarantees the existence of absolute extrema for continuous functions on closed intervals. This is fundamental because it assures us that we can always find the highest and lowest points of such functions within a given bounded range, which is essential for optimization problems.
concepts.recap_md: - If $f$ is continuous on a finite closed interval $[a, b]$, then $f$ has an absolute maximum. - If $f$ is continuous on a finite closed interval $[a, b]$, then $f$ also has an absolute minimum on $[a, b]$.
concepts.raw_body: 4.4.2 THEOREM (Extreme-Value Theorem) If a function $f$ is continuous on a finite closed interval $[a, b]$, then $f$ has both an absolute maximum and an absolute minimum on $[a, b]$.

concepts.title: Extreme-Value Theorem as an existence theorem
concepts.one_liner: The Extreme-Value Theorem is an example of what mathematicians call an existence theorem, stating conditions under which certain objects, like absolute extrema, exist.
concepts.summary_md: The Extreme-Value Theorem is an example of what mathematicians call an existence theorem. Such theorems state conditions under which certain objects exist, in this case absolute extrema. Knowing that an object exists and finding it are two separate things. We will now address methods for determining the locations of absolute extrema under the conditions of the Extreme-Value Theorem.
concepts.motivation_md: Understanding that the Extreme-Value Theorem is an existence theorem helps clarify its role: it guarantees that extrema do exist under specific conditions, but it doesn't provide a method for finding them. This distinction sets the stage for learning techniques to locate these extrema.
concepts.recap_md: - An existence theorem states conditions under which certain mathematical objects exist. - The Extreme-Value Theorem guarantees the existence of absolute extrema for continuous functions on finite closed intervals. - Existence theorems do not provide methods for finding the objects they guarantee.
concepts.raw_body: The Extreme-Value Theorem is an example of what mathematicians call an existence theorem. Such theorems state conditions under which certain objects exist, in this case absolute extrema. However, knowing that an object exists and finding it are two separate things. We will now address methods for determining the locations of absolute extrema under the conditions of the Extreme-Value Theorem.

concepts.title: Interior Absolute Extrema are Critical Points
concepts.one_liner: If $f$ is continuous on $[a, b]$, its absolute extrema occur either at endpoints or at critical points within the open interval $(a, b)$.
concepts.summary_md: If $f$ is continuous on the finite closed interval $[a, b]$, then the absolute extrema of $f$ occur either at the endpoints of the interval or inside on the open interval $(a, b)$. If the absolute extrema happen to fall inside, then the following theorem tells us that they must occur at critical points of $f$.
concepts.motivation_md: This theorem is crucial because it narrows down the search for absolute extrema. Instead of checking every point in an interval, we only need to examine the function's values at the endpoints and its critical points, significantly simplifying the process of finding extrema.
concepts.recap_md: - For a continuous function on $[a, b]$, absolute extrema occur at endpoints or within $(a, b)$. - If an absolute extremum is in the interior $(a, b)$, it must be a critical point.
concepts.raw_body: If $f$ is continuous on the finite closed interval $[a, b]$, then the absolute extrema of $f$ occur either at the endpoints of the interval or inside on the open interval $(a, b)$. If the absolute extrema happen to fall inside, then the following theorem tells us that they must occur at critical points of $f$.

concepts.title: Procedure for Finding Absolute Extrema on a Finite Closed Interval
concepts.one_liner: To find absolute extrema of a continuous function on $[a, b]$, evaluate $f$ at critical points in $(a, b)$ and at endpoints $a, b$, then identify the largest and smallest values.
concepts.summary_md: To find the absolute extrema of a continuous function $f$ on a finite closed interval $[a, b]$: First, find the critical points of $f$ in $(a, b)$. Next, evaluate $f$ at all critical points and at the endpoints $a$ and $b$. Finally, the largest of these values is the absolute maximum, and the smallest is the absolute minimum.
concepts.motivation_md: This procedure provides a systematic and reliable method for locating absolute extrema. By combining the insights from the Extreme-Value Theorem and the Critical Point Theorem, it reduces the problem to a finite number of calculations, making it practical for solving optimization problems.
concepts.recap_md: - Step 1: Find all critical points of $f$ within the open interval $(a, b)$. - Step 2: Evaluate $f$ at these critical points and at the interval's endpoints $a$ and $b$. - Step 3: The largest value from Step 2 is the absolute maximum, and the smallest is the absolute minimum.
concepts.raw_body:
## A Procedure for Finding the Absolute Extrema of a Continuous Function fon a Finite Closed Interval [ $a, b$ ]

Step 1. Find the critical points of $f$ in ( $a, b$ ).
Step 2. Evaluate $f$ at all the critical points and at the endpoints $a$ and $b$.
Step 3. The largest of the values in Step 2 is the absolute maximum value of $f$ on $[a, b]$ and the smallest value is the absolute minimum.

concepts.title: Conclusions about Absolute Extrema on Infinite Intervals
concepts.one_liner: For continuous functions on infinite intervals, the existence of absolute extrema depends on the behavior of the function's limits as $x$ approaches $\pm\infty$.
concepts.summary_md: For a function $f$ continuous everywhere on $(- rac{\infty}{},+\infty)$: if $\lim _{x \rightarrow-\infty} f(x)=+\infty$ and $\lim _{x \rightarrow+\infty} f(x)=+\infty$, $f$ has an absolute minimum but no absolute maximum. If both limits are $-\infty$, $f$ has an absolute maximum but no absolute minimum. If limits go to opposite infinities, $f$ has neither.
concepts.motivation_md: While the Extreme-Value Theorem applies to closed intervals, many real-world problems involve functions on infinite domains. This concept provides guidelines for determining the existence of absolute extrema in such cases, based on the function's end behavior, which is crucial for broader optimization applications.
concepts.recap_md: - If $\lim_{x \rightarrow \pm\infty} f(x) = +\infty$, $f$ has an absolute minimum but no absolute maximum. - If $\lim_{x \rightarrow \pm\infty} f(x) = -\infty$, $f$ has an absolute maximum but no absolute minimum. - If limits at $\pm\infty$ are opposite infinities, $f$ has neither absolute maximum nor minimum.

concepts.title: Conclusions about Absolute Extrema on Open Intervals
concepts.one_liner: For continuous functions on finite open intervals, the existence of absolute extrema depends on the behavior of the function's limits as $x$ approaches the interval's endpoints.
concepts.summary_md: For a function $f$ continuous on an open interval $(a, b)$: if $\lim _{x \rightarrow a^{+}} f(x)=+\infty$ and $\lim _{x \rightarrow b^{-}} f(x)=+\infty$, $f$ has an absolute minimum but no absolute maximum. If both limits are $-\infty$, $f$ has an absolute maximum but no absolute minimum. If limits at endpoints are opposite infinities, $f$ has neither.
concepts.motivation_md: Unlike closed intervals, open intervals do not guarantee the existence of absolute extrema. This concept provides a framework to analyze the behavior of functions near the boundaries of open intervals using limits, helping to determine if extrema exist or if the function's values become unbounded.
concepts.recap_md: - If $\lim_{x \rightarrow a^{+}} f(x) = +\infty$ and $\lim_{x \rightarrow b^{-}} f(x) = +\infty$, $f$ has an absolute minimum but no absolute maximum. - If $\lim_{x \rightarrow a^{+}} f(x) = -\infty$ and $\lim_{x \rightarrow b^{-}} f(x) = -\infty$, $f$ has an absolute maximum but no absolute minimum. - If limits at endpoints are opposite infinities, $f$ has neither absolute maximum nor minimum.

concepts.title: Functions with One Relative Extremum
concepts.one_liner: If a continuous function has exactly one relative extremum on an interval, that extremum is also the absolute extremum for the entire interval.
concepts.summary_md: If a continuous function $f$ has exactly one relative extremum on an interval, say at $x_{0}$: (a) If $f$ has a relative minimum at $x_{0}$, then $f\left(x_{0}\right)$ is the absolute minimum of $f$ on the interval. (b) If $f$ has a relative maximum at $x_{0}$, then $f\left(x_{0}\right)$ is the absolute maximum of $f$ the interval.
concepts.motivation_md: This theorem provides a powerful shortcut for finding absolute extrema in specific scenarios. When a function is continuous and has only one "peak" or "valley" on an interval, this theorem allows us to immediately conclude that this single relative extremum is also the global extremum, simplifying analysis.
concepts.recap_md: - If a continuous function $f$ has exactly one relative extremum at $x_0$ on an interval. - If this is a relative minimum, then $f(x_0)$ is the absolute minimum on the interval. - If this is a relative maximum, then $f(x_0)$ is the absolute maximum on the interval.
concepts.raw_body:
4.4.4 THEOREM Suppose that $f$ is continuous and has exactly one relative extremum on an interval, say at $x_{0}$.
(a) If $f$ has a relative minimum at $x_{0}$, then $f\left(x_{0}\right)$ is the absolute minimum of $f$ on the interval.
(b) If $f$ has a relative maximum at $x_{0}$, then $f\left(x_{0}\right)$ is the absolute maximum of $f$ the interval.

concepts.title: Classification of Optimization Problems
concepts.one_liner: Applied optimization problems are classified based on whether they reduce to maximizing or minimizing a continuous function over a finite closed interval or an infinite/non-closed interval.
concepts.summary_md: Applied optimization problems fall into two categories: those that reduce to maximizing or minimizing a continuous function over a finite closed interval, and those over an infinite or non-closed finite interval. For the first type, the Extreme-Value Theorem (4.4.2) guarantees a solution found by examining critical points and endpoints. For the second type, a solution may or may not exist, and Theorem 4.4.4 or ingenuity may be needed.
concepts.motivation_md: Classifying optimization problems helps determine if a solution is guaranteed and which mathematical techniques are appropriate for finding it. Different types of intervals (closed, open, infinite) require distinct approaches, leveraging theorems like the Extreme-Value Theorem or requiring more advanced methods.
concepts.recap_md: - Problems are classified by the domain of the function: finite closed interval or infinite/non-closed interval.- Finite closed interval problems are guaranteed a solution by the Extreme-Value Theorem.- Infinite/non-closed interval problems may or may not have a solution and often require more ingenuity.
concepts.raw_body:
The applied optimization problems that we will consider in this section fall into the following two categories:

- Problems that reduce to maximizing or minimizing a continuous function over a finite closed interval.
- Problems that reduce to maximizing or minimizing a continuous function over an infinite interval or a finite interval that is not closed.

For problems of the first type the Extreme-Value Theorem (4.4.2) guarantees that the problem has a solution, and we know that the solution can be obtained by examining the values of the function at the critical points and at the endpoints. However, for problems of the second type there may or may not be a solution. If the function is continuous and has exactly one relative extremum of the appropriate type on the interval, then Theorem 4.4.4 guarantees the existence of a solution and provides a method for finding it. In cases where this theorem is not applicable some ingenuity may be required to solve the problem.

concepts.title: A Procedure for Solving Applied Maximum and Minimum Problems
concepts.one_liner: This procedure outlines five steps for solving applied maximum and minimum problems, from drawing a figure to applying calculus techniques.
concepts.summary_md: A procedure for solving applied maximum and minimum problems involves five steps: 1. Draw an appropriate figure and label relevant quantities. 2. Find a formula for the quantity to be maximized or minimized. 3. Express the quantity as a function of one variable by eliminating others. 4. Determine the interval of possible values for this variable. 5. Use calculus techniques to find the maximum or minimum.
concepts.motivation_md: Applied optimization problems can be complex, involving multiple variables and constraints. This five-step procedure provides a systematic framework to break down these problems, ensuring all necessary components are addressed to successfully find maximum or minimum values.
concepts.recap_md: - Step 1: Draw and label a figure.- Step 2: Formulate the quantity to be optimized.- Step 3: Reduce to a function of one variable.- Step 4: Determine the domain (interval) for the variable.- Step 5: Apply calculus techniques to find the extremum.
concepts.raw_body:
## A Procedure for Solving Applied Maximum and Minimum Problems

Step 1. Draw an appropriate figure and label the quantities relevant to the problem.
Step 2. Find a formula for the quantity to be maximized or minimized.
Step 3. Using the conditions stated in the problem to eliminate variables, express the quantity to be maximized or minimized as a function of one variable.

Step 4. Find the interval of possible values for this variable from the physical restrictions in the problem.

Step 5. If applicable, use the techniques of the preceding section to obtain the maximum or minimum.

concepts.title: An Application to Economics
concepts.one_liner: Calculus can be applied to economics to optimize business functions like cost, revenue, and profit, helping firms determine production levels for maximum profit.
concepts.summary_md: In economics, key functions are total cost $C(x)$, total revenue $R(x)$, and total profit $P(x)$ for producing and selling $x$ units. These are related by $P(x)=R(x)-C(x)$. The total cost $C(x)$ is a sum of overhead $a$ (fixed costs) and manufacturing cost $M(x)$ (variable costs), often modeled as $C(x)=a+bx+cx^2$. Revenue is $R(x)=px$ for price $p$ per unit.
concepts.motivation_md: Businesses aim to maximize profit or minimize cost. Calculus provides the tools to analyze economic functions like cost, revenue, and profit, allowing firms to determine optimal production levels, pricing strategies, and resource allocation to achieve their financial goals.
concepts.recap_md: - Economists use cost $C(x)$, revenue $R(x)$, and profit $P(x)$ functions, where $P(x)=R(x)-C(x)$.- Total cost $C(x)$ includes fixed overhead and variable manufacturing costs.- Firms use calculus to find the number of units $x$ that maximize profit $P(x)$ within production limits.

concepts.title: Cost, Revenue, and Profit Functions
concepts.one_liner: The cost function $C(x)$, revenue function $R(x)$, and profit function $P(x)$ describe the total cost, revenue, and profit for producing and selling $x$ units.
concepts.summary_md: The cost function $C(x)$ is the total cost of producing $x$ units. The revenue function $R(x)$ is the total revenue from selling $x$ units. The profit function $P(x)$ is the total profit from selling $x$ units. If all units produced are sold, these functions are related by $P(x)=R(x)-C(x)$.
concepts.motivation_md: These functions are fundamental to economic analysis, providing a mathematical framework to quantify a business's financial performance. Defining them clearly is the first step in applying calculus to optimize business operations.
concepts.recap_md: - $C(x)$ is total cost for $x$ units.- $R(x)$ is total revenue for $x$ units.- $P(x)$ is total profit for $x$ units, and $P(x)=R(x)-C(x)$.
concepts.raw_body:

$R(x)=$ total revenue from selling $x$ units of the product during the time period
$P(x)=$ total profit obtained by selling $x$ units of the product during the time period

concepts.title: Overhead and Manufacturing Cost
concepts.one_liner: Overhead ($a$) represents fixed costs independent of production, while manufacturing cost ($M(x)$) represents variable costs dependent on the number of items produced.
concepts.summary_md: Overhead ($a$) is a constant cost, including fixed expenses like rent and insurance, that does not depend on the number of units produced ($x$). It must be paid even if nothing is produced. Manufacturing cost ($M(x)$) is a function representing variable costs, such as materials and labor, which depend on the number of items manufactured.
concepts.motivation_md: Understanding the components of total cost is crucial for businesses to analyze their cost structure and identify areas for cost reduction or efficiency improvements. Differentiating fixed from variable costs is a foundational concept in economic analysis.
concepts.recap_md: - Overhead ($a$) is a fixed cost, independent of production volume.- Manufacturing cost ($M(x)$) is a variable cost, dependent on production volume.- Total cost $C(x)$ is the sum of overhead and manufacturing cost: $C(x) = a + M(x)$.
concepts.raw_body: where $a$ is a constant, called overhead, and $M(x)$ is a function representing manufacturing cost. The overhead, which includes such fixed costs as rent and insurance, does not depend on $x$; it must be paid even if nothing is produced. On the other hand, the manufacturing cost $M(x)$, which includes such items as cost of materials and labor, depends on the number of items manufactured. concepts.title: Marginal Analysis
concepts.one_liner: Marginal analysis interprets the derivatives of profit, revenue, and cost functions as the additional profit, revenue, or cost from producing one more unit.
concepts.summary_md: Economists define marginal profit $P'(x)$, marginal revenue $R'(x)$, and marginal cost $C'(x)$ as the additional profit, revenue, and cost, respectively, from producing and selling one additional unit when current levels are at $x$ units. This interpretation stems from the local linear approximation of these functions, where $P(x+1) \approx P(x)+P'(x)$, implying $P(x+1)-P(x) \approx P'(x)$.
concepts.motivation_md: Marginal analysis provides a powerful tool for making incremental business decisions. By understanding the immediate impact of producing one more unit, firms can optimize production levels, pricing, and resource allocation to maximize efficiency and profitability.
concepts.recap_md: - Marginal profit ($P'(x)$), marginal revenue ($R'(x)$), and marginal cost ($C'(x)$) are derivatives of their respective functions.- These marginal quantities approximate the change in profit, revenue, or cost from producing one additional unit.- The approximation relies on the local linear approximation: $f(x+1) \approx f(x)+f'(x)$.
concepts.raw_body:
## MARGINAL ANALYSIS

Economists call $P^{\prime}(x), R^{\prime}(x)$, and $C^{\prime}(x)$ the marginal profit, marginal revenue, and marginal cost, respectively; and they interpret these quantities as the additional profit, revenue, and cost that result from producing and selling one additional unit of the product when the production and sales levels are at $x$ units. These interpretations follow from the local linear approximations of the profit, revenue, and cost functions. For example, it follows from Formula (2) of Section 3.5 that when the production and sales levels are at $x$ units the local linear approximation of the profit function is

$$
P(x+\Delta x) \approx P(x)+P^{\prime}(x) \Delta x
$$

Thus, if $\Delta x=1$ (one additional unit produced and sold), this formula implies

$$
P(x+1) \approx P(x)+P^{\prime}(x)
$$

and hence the additional profit that results from producing and selling one additional unit can be approximated as

$$
P(x+1)-P(x) \approx P^{\prime}(x)
$$

Similarly, $R(x+1)-R(x) \approx R^{\prime}(x)$ and $C(x+1)-C(x) \approx C^{\prime}(x)$.

These quantities are interpreted as the additional profit, revenue, and cost that result from producing and selling one additional unit of the product when production and sales levels are at $x$ units.
concepts.motivation_md: Precisely defining marginal quantities is essential for applying calculus to economic decision-making. These definitions form the basis for understanding how changes in production affect a firm's financial outcomes, leading to optimal strategies.

concepts.title: A Basic Principle of Economics
concepts.one_liner: Maximum profit occurs when marginal revenue equals marginal cost, meaning the cost of an additional unit approximately equals the revenue it generates.
concepts.summary_md: A basic principle of economics states that maximum profit occurs when marginal revenue equals marginal cost, i.e., $R'(x) = C'(x)$. This is because $P'(x) = R'(x) - C'(x)$, so $P'(x)=0$ (for a maximum) implies $R'(x)=C'(x)$. This means the cost of manufacturing and selling an additional unit is approximately equal to the revenue generated by that unit.
concepts.motivation_md: This principle provides a critical rule for businesses seeking to maximize their profits. By equating marginal revenue and marginal cost, firms can identify the optimal production level where adding another unit no longer increases overall profit, guiding efficient resource allocation.
concepts.recap_md: - Maximum profit occurs when $P'(x)=0$.- Since $P'(x)=R'(x)-C'(x)$, maximum profit implies $R'(x)=C'(x)$.- This means marginal revenue equals marginal cost at the point of maximum profit.- At maximum profit, the additional cost of one unit equals the additional revenue from it.
