concepts.title: Fermat's principle in optics
concepts.one_liner: Fermat's principle in optics states that light traveling from one point to another follows that path for which the total travel time is minimum.
concepts.summary_md: Fermat's principle in optics states that light traveling from one point to another follows the path for which the total travel time is minimum. In a uniform medium, paths of "minimum time" and "shortest distance" are the same, so light travels along a straight line. For a light ray bouncing off a flat mirror, the principle implies the path minimizes total distance, leading to the angle of incidence equaling the angle of reflection.
concepts.motivation_md: This principle provides a fundamental explanation for how light behaves, allowing us to derive laws of reflection and refraction from a single, elegant optimization principle. It explains why light travels in straight lines in uniform media and how it interacts with surfaces.
concepts.recap_md:
- Light follows the path of minimum travel time.
- In a uniform medium, this means the path of shortest distance (a straight line).
- For reflection, it implies the angle of incidence $\theta_{1}$ equals the angle of reflection $\theta_{2}$.
concepts.raw_body: 62. Fermat's principle (biography on p.275) in optics states that light traveling from one point to another follows that path for which the total travel time is minimum. In a uniform medium, the paths of "minimum time" and "shortest distance" turn out to be the same, so that light, if unobstructed, travels along a straight line. Assume that we have a light source, a flat mirror, and an observer in a uniform medium. If a light ray leaves the source, bounces off the mirror, and travels on to the observer, then its path will consist of two line segments, as shown in Figure Ex-62. According to Fermat's principle, the path will be such that the total travel time $t$ is minimum or, since the medium is uniform, the path will be such that the total distance traveled from $A$ to $P$ to $B$ is as small as possible. Assuming the minimum occurs when $d t / d x=0$, show that the light ray will strike the mirror at the point $P$ where the "angle of incidence" $\theta_{1}$ equals the "angle of reflection" $\theta_{2}$.

concepts.title: Snell's law of refraction
concepts.one_liner: Snell's law of refraction states that the path of the light ray will be such that $\frac{\sin \theta_{1}}{v_{1}}=\frac{\sin \theta_{2}}{v_{2}}$.
concepts.summary_md: Fermat's principle explains why light rays traveling between two uniform media, like air and water, undergo bending (refraction). Light travels at different speeds in different media. The path of shortest time is not a straight line, but a broken line path allowing light to take advantage of higher speeds. Snell's law states that this path satisfies $\frac{\sin \theta_{1}}{v_{1}}=\frac{\sin \theta_{2}}{v_{2}}$, where $v_1, v_2$ are speeds and $\theta_1, \theta_2$ are angles in each medium.
concepts.motivation_md: Snell's law describes how light bends when passing from one medium to another, a phenomenon called refraction. This principle is crucial for understanding lenses, prisms, and how our eyes perceive objects underwater, explaining why objects appear distorted.
concepts.recap_md:
- Light refracts (bends) when passing between media with different speeds.
- The path taken minimizes travel time, as per Fermat's principle.
- Snell's law mathematically describes this bending: $\frac{\sin \theta_{1}}{v_{1}}=\frac{\sin \theta_{2}}{v_{2}}$.
concepts.raw_body:
63. Fermat's principle (Exercise 62) also explains why light rays traveling between air and water undergo bending (refraction). Imagine that we have two uniform media (such as air and water) and a light ray traveling from a source $A$ in one medium to an observer $B$ in the other medium (Figure Ex-63). It is known that light travels at a constant speed in a uniform medium, but more slowly in a dense medium (such as water) than in a thin medium (such as air). Consequently, the path of shortest time from $A$ to $B$ is not necessarily a straight line, but rather some broken line path $A$ to $P$ to $B$ allowing the light to take greatest advantage of its higher speed through the thin medium. Snell's law of refraction (biography on p. 288) states that the path of the light ray will be such that

$$
\frac{\sin \theta_{1}}{v_{1}}=\frac{\sin \theta_{2}}{v_{2}}
$$

where $v_{1}$ is the speed of light in the first medium, $v_{2}$ is the speed of light in the second medium, and $\theta_{1}$ and $\theta_{2}$ are the angles shown in Figure Ex-63. Show that this follows from the assumption that the path of minimum time occurs when $d t / d x=0$.

concepts.title: Least squares principle
concepts.one_liner: The least squares principle states that an estimate $\bar{x}$ of an unknown quantity $x$ should be chosen to minimize $s=\left(x_{1}-\bar{x}\right)^{2}+\left(x_{2}-\bar{x}\right)^{2}+\cdots+\left(x_{n}-\bar{x}\right)^{2}$.
concepts.summary_md: When an unknown physical quantity $x$ is measured multiple times, the measurements $x_{1}, x_{2}, \ldots, x_{n}$ often vary. To obtain an estimate $\bar{x}$ of $x$ from these varying measurements, the least squares principle is used. This principle states that the estimate $\bar{x}$ should be chosen to minimize the sum of the squares of the differences between each measurement and the estimate: $s=\left(x_{1}-\bar{x}\right)^{2}+\left(x_{2}-\bar{x}\right)^{2}+\cdots+\left(x_{n}-\bar{x}\right)^{2}$.
concepts.motivation_md: Measurements of physical quantities are rarely perfect, often varying due to external factors. The least squares principle provides a robust method to find the "best" estimate from a set of imperfect measurements by minimizing the impact of random errors, leading to a more reliable result.
concepts.recap_md:
- Measurements of a quantity $x$ often vary ($x_1, \ldots, x_n$).
- The least squares principle estimates $\bar{x}$ by minimizing the sum of squared differences.
- The sum to minimize is $s=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left(x_{i}-\bar{x}\right)^{2}$.
concepts.raw_body:
65. If an unknown physical quantity $x$ is measured $n$ times, the measurements $x_{1}, x_{2}, \ldots, x_{n}$ often vary because of uncontrollable factors such as temperature, atmospheric pressure, and so forth. Thus, a scientist is often faced with the problem of using $n$ different observed measurements to obtain an estimate $\bar{x}$ of an unknown quantity $x$. One method for making such an estimate is based on the least squares principle, which states that the estimate $\bar{x}$
should be chosen to minimize

$$
s=\left(x_{1}-\bar{x}\right)^{2}+\left(x_{2}-\bar{x}\right)^{2}+\cdots+\left(x_{n}-\bar{x}\right)^{2}
$$

concepts.title: Introduction to Rectilinear Motion
concepts.one_liner: This section continues the study of rectilinear motion, defining acceleration mathematically and using calculus tools for deeper analysis.
concepts.summary_md: This section focuses on rectilinear motion, building upon earlier concepts. It will mathematically define "acceleration" and demonstrate how calculus tools can be applied to analyze rectilinear motion in greater detail, providing a deeper understanding of particle movement along a straight line.
concepts.motivation_md: Understanding rectilinear motion is fundamental in physics and engineering. Calculus provides the essential tools to precisely describe and predict the position, velocity, and acceleration of objects moving in a straight line, which is a building block for more complex motion.
concepts.recap_md:
- Rectilinear motion is motion along a straight line.
- This section will define acceleration using calculus.
- Calculus tools will be used for in-depth analysis of this motion.
concepts.raw_body:
### 4.6 RECTILINEAR MOTION

In this section we will continue the study of rectilinear motion that we began in Section 2.1. We will define the notion of "acceleration" mathematically, and we will show how the tools of calculus developed earlier in this chapter can be used to analyze rectilinear motion in more depth.

concepts.title: Velocity function
concepts.one_liner: The velocity function $v(t)$ for a particle in rectilinear motion is defined as the derivative of its position function $s(t)$, so $v(t)=s^{\prime}(t)=\frac{d s}{d t}$.
concepts.summary_md: The instantaneous velocity of a particle in rectilinear motion is defined as the derivative of its position function. If a particle's position is given by $s(t)$, then its velocity function $v(t)$ is $v(t)=s^{\prime}(t)=\frac{d s}{d t}$. This formula formalizes the relationship between an object's location and how fast and in what direction it is moving at any given instant.
concepts.motivation_md: The velocity function is essential for describing how an object's position changes over time. It allows us to quantify both the speed and direction of motion, providing a complete picture of an object's movement at any given instant.
concepts.recap_md:
- Velocity is the rate of change of position.
- For position $s(t)$, the velocity function is $v(t)=s^{\prime}(t)$.
- This is also expressed as $v(t)=\frac{d s}{d t}$.

concepts.title: Interpreting the sign of velocity
concepts.one_liner: The sign of the velocity indicates the direction of a particle's motion: positive for the positive direction, negative for the negative direction, and zero when momentarily stopped.
concepts.summary_md: The sign of the velocity function $v(t)$ reveals the direction of a particle's movement. A positive $v(t)$ signifies that the position $s$ is increasing, meaning the particle moves in the positive direction. Conversely, a negative $v(t)$ indicates that $s$ is decreasing, so the particle moves in the negative direction. If $v(t)=0$, the particle is momentarily at rest.
concepts.motivation_md: Understanding the sign of velocity is crucial for fully interpreting motion. It allows us to not only know how fast an object is moving but also in which direction, which is essential for analyzing trajectories, turning points, and overall movement patterns.
concepts.recap_md:
- $v(t) > 0$ means the particle moves in the positive direction.
- $v(t) < 0$ means the particle moves in the negative direction.
- $v(t) = 0$ means the particle is momentarily stopped.
concepts.raw_body: The sign of the velocity tells which way the particle is moving-a positive value for $v(t)$ means that $s$ is increasing with time, so the particle is moving in the positive direction, and a negative value for $v(t)$ means that $s$ is decreasing with time, so the particle is moving in the negative direction. If $v(t)=0$, then the particle has momentarily stopped.

concepts.title: Speed function
concepts.one_liner: The speed function is defined as the absolute value of the instantaneous velocity, $|v(t)|=\left|s^{\prime}(t)\right|=\left|\frac{d s}{d t}\right|$.
concepts.summary_md: The instantaneous speed of a particle is the absolute value of its instantaneous velocity. Therefore, the speed function is defined as $|v(t)|=\left|s^{\prime}(t)\right|=\left|\frac{d s}{d t}\right|$. This means speed quantifies how fast an object is moving, regardless of its direction, by taking the magnitude of its velocity.
concepts.motivation_md: While velocity tells us both speed and direction, sometimes we only care about how fast an object is moving, irrespective of its path. The speed function provides this scalar magnitude, which is useful in many practical applications like calculating fuel consumption or travel time.
concepts.recap_md:
- Speed is the absolute value of velocity.
- The speed function is $|v(t)|$.
- It can also be written as $\left|s^{\prime}(t)\right|$ or $\left|\frac{d s}{d t}\right|$.

concepts.title: Acceleration function
concepts.one_liner: The acceleration function $a(t)$ is defined as the rate at which instantaneous velocity changes with time, $a(t)=v^{\prime}(t)=\frac{d v}{d t}$.
concepts.summary_md: In rectilinear motion, instantaneous acceleration is the rate at which instantaneous velocity changes over time. If a particle has velocity function $v(t)$, its acceleration function is $a(t)=v^{\prime}(t)=\frac{d v}{d t}$. Alternatively, since $v(t)=s^{\prime}(t)$, acceleration can be expressed as the second derivative of the position function: $a(t)=s^{\prime \prime}(t)=\frac{d^{2} s}{d t^{2}}$.
concepts.motivation_md: Acceleration is crucial for understanding how forces affect motion, as it describes how an object's velocity changes. It allows us to predict future velocities and positions, and is fundamental in fields like engineering, physics, and vehicle design.
concepts.recap_md:
- Acceleration is the rate of change of velocity.
- For velocity $v(t)$, the acceleration function is $a(t)=v^{\prime}(t)=\frac{d v}{d t}$.
- It is also the second derivative of the position function: $a(t)=s^{\prime \prime}(t)=\frac{d^{2} s}{d t^{2}}$.

concepts.title: Speeding up and slowing down
concepts.one_liner: A particle in rectilinear motion is speeding up when its speed is increasing and slowing down when its speed is decreasing.
concepts.summary_md: A particle in rectilinear motion is speeding up when its speed is increasing and slowing down when its speed is decreasing. While an object speeding up is often called "accelerating" and slowing down "decelerating," this intuition holds for positive motion but not always for negative motion. A particle with negative velocity is speeding up when its acceleration is negative and slowing down when its acceleration is positive.
concepts.motivation_md: This concept clarifies the precise definitions of "speeding up" and "slowing down" in physics, especially when dealing with motion in both positive and negative directions. It addresses common misconceptions about the direct relationship between acceleration's sign and whether an object is speeding up or slowing down.
concepts.recap_md: - Speeding up means speed is increasing; slowing down means speed is decreasing. - For negative velocity, negative acceleration means speeding up, and positive acceleration means slowing down.
concepts.raw_body:
We will say that a particle in rectilinear motion is speeding up when its speed is increasing and is slowing down when its speed is decreasing. In everyday language an object that is speeding up is said to be "accelerating" and an object that is slowing down is said to be "decelerating"; thus, one might expect that a particle in rectilinear motion will be speeding up when its acceleration is positive and slowing down when it is negative. Although this is true for a particle moving in the positive direction, it is not true for a particle moving in the

If $a(t)=0$ over a certain time interval, what does this tell you about the motion of the particle during that time?
negative direction-a particle with negative velocity is speeding up when its acceleration is negative and slowing down when its acceleration is positive. This is because a positive acceleration implies an increasing velocity, and increasing a negative velocity decreases its absolute value; similarly, a negative acceleration implies a decreasing velocity, and decreasing a negative velocity increases its absolute value.

concepts.title: Interpreting the sign of acceleration
concepts.one_liner: A particle in rectilinear motion is speeding up when its velocity and acceleration have the same sign and slowing down when they have opposite signs.
concepts.summary_md: A particle in rectilinear motion is speeding up when its velocity and acceleration have the same sign. Conversely, the particle is slowing down when its velocity and acceleration have opposite signs.
concepts.motivation_md: This rule provides a concise and definitive way to determine if a particle is speeding up or slowing down, regardless of its direction of motion. It simplifies the analysis by focusing on the relationship between the signs of velocity and acceleration, resolving ambiguities from simply looking at acceleration's sign.
concepts.recap_md: - Speeding up occurs when velocity and acceleration have the same sign. - Slowing down occurs when velocity and acceleration have opposite signs.
concepts.raw_body: > INTERPRETING THE SIGN OF ACCELERATION A particle in rectilinear motion is speeding up when its velocity and acceleration have the same sign and slowing down when they have opposite signs.

concepts.title: Analyzing position-time curve for position and velocity
concepts.one_liner: The position versus time curve contains all of the significant information about the position and velocity of a particle in rectilinear motion.
concepts.summary_md: The position versus time curve provides crucial information about a particle's motion. If $s(t)>0$, the particle is on the positive side of the $s$-axis, and if $s(t)<0$, it's on the negative side. The slope of the curve at any time equals the instantaneous velocity. Positive slope means positive velocity and movement in the positive direction, while negative slope means negative velocity and movement in the negative direction. A zero slope indicates the particle is momentarily stopped.
concepts.motivation_md: This technique allows for a visual and intuitive understanding of a particle's motion by interpreting its position-time graph. It connects graphical features like position and slope directly to physical quantities like position and velocity, making complex motion easier to analyze without explicit equations.
concepts.recap_md: - The sign of $s(t)$ indicates the particle's position relative to the origin. - The slope of the $s(t)$ curve represents instantaneous velocity. - Positive slope means positive velocity; negative slope means negative velocity; zero slope means the particle is momentarily stopped.
concepts.raw_body:
The position versus time curve contains all of the significant information about the position and velocity of a particle in rectilinear motion:

- If $s(t)>0$, the particle is on the positive side of the $s$-axis.
- If $s(t)<0$, the particle is on the negative side of the $s$-axis.
- The slope of the curve at any time is equal to the instantaneous velocity at that time.
- Where the curve has positive slope, the velocity is positive and the particle is moving in the positive direction.
- Where the curve has negative slope, the velocity is negative and the particle is moving in the negative direction.
- Where the slope of the curve is zero, the velocity is zero, and the particle is momentarily stopped.

concepts.title: Analyzing position-time curve for acceleration
concepts.one_liner: Information about the acceleration of a particle in rectilinear motion can also be deduced from the position versus time curve by examining its concavity.
concepts.summary_md: Information about a particle's acceleration can be deduced from the position versus time curve by examining its concavity. The curve is concave up where $s^{\prime \prime}(t)>0$, meaning the particle has a positive acceleration. Conversely, where the curve is concave down, $s^{\prime \prime}(t)<0$, indicating the particle has a negative acceleration.
concepts.motivation_md: This concept extends the graphical analysis of motion to include acceleration, providing a visual link between the second derivative of position and the concavity of the position-time curve. It allows for a complete qualitative understanding of motion (position, velocity, and acceleration) directly from a single graph.
concepts.recap_md: - Concave up on the position-time curve means positive acceleration ($s^{\prime \prime}(t)>0$). - Concave down on the position-time curve means negative acceleration ($s^{\prime \prime}(t)<0$).
concepts.raw_body: Information about the acceleration of a particle in rectilinear motion can also be deduced from the position versus time curve by examining its concavity. For example, we know that the position versus time curve will be concave up on intervals where $s^{\prime \prime}(t)>0$ and will be concave down on intervals where $s^{\prime \prime}(t)<0$. But we know from (4) that $s^{\prime \prime}(t)$ is the acceleration, so that on intervals where the position versus time curve is concave up the particle has a positive acceleration, and on intervals where it is concave down the particle has a negative acceleration.

concepts.title: Introduction to Newton's Method
concepts.one_liner: Newton's Method is a technique that is usually more efficient for approximating the roots of an equation $f(x)=0$ than the Intermediate-Value Theorem.
concepts.summary_md: Newton's Method is a technique for approximating the roots of an equation $f(x)=0$. It is generally more efficient than methods like the Intermediate-Value Theorem and is widely used in commercial and scientific computer programs for finding roots.
concepts.motivation_md: Finding exact roots of complex equations can be impossible or very difficult. Newton's Method provides a powerful and efficient iterative technique to approximate these roots numerically, which is crucial for practical applications in science and engineering where precise analytical solutions are not feasible.
concepts.recap_md: - Newton's Method approximates roots of $f(x)=0$. - It is often more efficient than the Intermediate-Value Theorem. - It is used in many computer programs for root finding.
concepts.raw_body:
### 4.7 NEWTON'S METHOD

In Section 1.5 we showed how to approximate the roots of an equation $f(x)=0$ using the Intermediate-Value Theorem. In this section we will study a technique, called "Newton's Method," that is usually more efficient than that method. Newton's Method is the technique used by many commercial and scientific computer programs for finding roots.

concepts.title: Newton's Method Formula
concepts.one_liner: Newton's Method uses the iterative formula $x_{n+1}=x_{n}-\frac{f\left(x_{n}\right)}{f^{\prime}\left(x_{n}\right)}$ to approximate roots.
concepts.summary_md: Newton's Method is defined by the iterative formula: $x_{n+1}=x_{n}-\frac{f\left(x_{n}\right)}{f^{\prime}\left(x_{n}\right)}$, for $n=1,2,3, \ldots$. This formula generates successive approximations to a root of the equation $f(x)=0$.
concepts.motivation_md: This formula is the core of Newton's Method, providing the mathematical rule for generating increasingly accurate approximations of a function's root. It leverages the tangent line at a given point to find a better estimate for where the function crosses the x-axis.
concepts.recap_md: - The formula is $x_{n+1}=x_{n}-\frac{f\left(x_{n}\right)}{f^{\prime}\left(x_{n}\right)}$. - It generates a sequence of approximations $x_1, x_2, x_3, \ldots$. - Each $x_{n+1}$ is derived from the previous approximation $x_n$.

concepts.title: Some Difficulties with Newton's Method
concepts.one_liner: While Newton's Method often converges quickly, it can fail if $f^{\prime}\left(x_{n}\right)=0$, or by converging to a different root, or failing to converge altogether.
concepts.summary_md: Newton's Method, despite its speed, can encounter difficulties. It fails if $f^{\prime}\left(x_{n}\right)=0$ for some $n$, leading to division by zero, as the tangent line is parallel to the $x$-axis. The method may also overlook the intended root and converge to another, or it may fail to converge entirely, as demonstrated by the example $x^{1/3}=0$ with $x_0=1$ where approximations diverge.
concepts.motivation_md: Understanding the limitations of Newton's Method is crucial for its effective application. Knowing when and why it might fail helps users choose appropriate starting values, interpret results, and consider alternative numerical methods when necessary, preventing incorrect conclusions or endless computations.
concepts.recap_md: - Newton's Method fails if $f^{\prime}\left(x_{n}\right)=0$, causing division by zero. - It may converge to an unintended root or fail to converge at all. - Divergence can occur, as seen with $f(x)=x^{1/3}$ and $x_0=1$.
concepts.raw_body:
## SOME DIFFICULTIES WITH NEWTON'S METHOD

When Newton's Method works, the approximations usually converge toward the solution with dramatic speed. However, there are situations in which the method fails. For example, if $f^{\prime}\left(x_{n}\right)=0$ for some $n$, then (4) involves a division by zero, making it impossible to generate $x_{n+1}$. However, this is to be expected because the tangent line to $y=f(x)$ is parallel to the $x$-axis where $f^{\prime}\left(x_{n}\right)=0$, and hence this tangent line does not cross the $x$-axis to generate the next approximation (Figure 4.7.4).

Newton's Method can fail for other reasons as well; sometimes it may overlook the root you are trying to find and converge to a different root, and sometimes it may fail to converge altogether. For example, consider the equation

$$
x^{1 / 3}=0
$$

which has $x=0$ as its only solution, and try to approximate this solution by Newton's Method with a starting value of $x_{0}=1$. Letting $f(x)=x^{1 / 3}$, Formula (4) becomes

$$
x_{n+1}=x_{n}-\frac{\left(x_{n}\right)^{1 / 3}}{\frac{1}{3}\left(x_{n}\right)^{-2 / 3}}=x_{n}-3 x_{n}=-2 x_{n}
$$

Beginning with $x_{1}=1$, the successive values generated by this formula are

$$
x_{1}=1, \quad x_{2}=-2, \quad x_{3}=4, \quad x_{4}=-8, \ldots
$$

which obviously do not converge to $x=0$. Figure 4.7.5 illustrates what is happening geometrically in this situation.

Figure 4.7.5
![A graph of the function $y = x^{1/3}$ is shown, illustrating the divergence of Newton's Method when approximating the root $x=0$. The sequence of approximations starts at $x_1=1$. A vertical dashed...](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/84333fdc-d75a-4de5-aded-d41110c1154d-234.jpg?height=241&width=727&top_left_y=476&top_left_x=921)

To learn more about the conditions under which Newton's Method converges and for a discussion of error questions, you should consult a book on numerical analysis. For a more in-depth discussion of Newton's Method and its relationship to contemporary studies of chaos and fractals, you may want to read the article, "Newton's Method and Fractal Patterns," by Philip Straffin, which appears in Applications of Calculus, MAA Notes, Vol. 3, No. 29, 1993, published by the Mathematical Association of America.

concepts.title: Rolle's Theorem; Mean-Value Theorem
concepts.one_liner: This section introduces Rolle's Theorem and the Mean-Value Theorem.
concepts.summary_md: This section serves as an introduction to two fundamental theorems in calculus: Rolle's Theorem and the Mean-Value Theorem. These theorems are crucial for understanding the behavior of differentiable functions.
concepts.motivation_md: Rolle's Theorem and the Mean-Value Theorem are foundational for proving many other important results in calculus, such as the relationship between derivatives and increasing/decreasing functions. They provide guarantees about the existence of specific points where a function's derivative takes on certain values, which is essential for theoretical understanding.
concepts.recap_md: - This concept introduces Rolle's Theorem. - It also introduces the Mean-Value Theorem.
concepts.raw_body: ### 4.8 ROLLE'S THEOREM; MEAN-VALUE THEOREM

concepts.title: Rolle's Theorem (informal introduction)
concepts.one_liner: Rolle's Theorem states that if a differentiable function intersects the x-axis at two places, then between them there must be at least one place where the tangent line is horizontal.
concepts.summary_md: Rolle's Theorem is a special case of the Mean-Value Theorem. It states that if the graph of a differentiable function intersects the $x$-axis at two places, $a$ and $b$, then somewhere between $a$ and $b$ there must be at least one place where the tangent line is horizontal.
concepts.motivation_md: This informal introduction presents Rolle's Theorem as a geometrically intuitive fact and a foundational special case of the more general Mean-Value Theorem. It sets the stage for understanding the precise mathematical statement and its implications.
concepts.recap_md: - Rolle's Theorem is a special case of the Mean-Value Theorem. - If a differentiable function crosses the x-axis at $a$ and $b$, its tangent line must be horizontal somewhere between $a$ and $b$.
concepts.raw_body: We will begin with a special case of the Mean-Value Theorem, called Rolle's Theorem, in honor of the mathematician Michel Rolle. This theorem states the geometrically obvious fact that if the graph of a differentiable function intersects the $x$-axis at two places, $a$ and $b$, then somewhere between $a$ and $b$ there must be at least one place where the tangent line is horizontal (Figure 4.8.1). The precise statement of the theorem is as follows.

concepts.title: Rolle's Theorem
concepts.one_liner: If $f$ is continuous on $[a, b]$, differentiable on $(a, b)$, and $f(a)=f(b)=0$, then there is a $c$ in $(a, b)$ such that $f^{\prime}(c)=0$.
concepts.summary_md: Rolle's Theorem states that if a function $f$ is continuous on the closed interval $[a, b]$ and differentiable on the open interval $(a, b)$, and if $f(a)=0$ and $f(b)=0$, then there is at least one point $c$ in $(a, b)$ such that $f^{\prime}(c)=0$.
concepts.motivation_md: Rolle's Theorem provides a precise mathematical statement for a geometrically intuitive idea: if a smooth curve starts and ends at the same height, it must have a horizontal tangent somewhere in between. It serves as a foundational step towards the more general Mean-Value Theorem.
concepts.recap_md: - Requires $f$ to be continuous on $[a, b]$ and differentiable on $(a, b)$. - If $f(a)=0$ and $f(b)=0$, then there exists $c \in (a, b)$ where $f^{\prime}(c)=0$.
concepts.raw_body:
4.8.1 THEOREM (Rolle's Theorem) Let $f$ be continuous on the closed interval $[a, b]$ and differentiable on the open interval ( $a, b$ ). If

$$
f(a)=0 \quad \text { and } \quad f(b)=0
$$

then there is at least one point $c$ in the interval $(a, b)$ such that $f^{\prime}(c)=0$.

concepts.title: Mean-Value Theorem (informal introduction)
concepts.one_liner: The Mean-Value Theorem states that between any two points on a differentiable function's graph, there's a place where the tangent line is parallel to the secant line joining those points.
concepts.summary_md: Rolle's Theorem is a special case of a more general result, called the Mean-Value Theorem. Geometrically, this theorem states that between any two points $A(a, f(a))$ and $B(b, f(b))$ on the graph of a differentiable function $f$, there is at least one place where the tangent line to the graph is parallel to the secant line joining $A$ and $B$.
concepts.motivation_md: The Mean-Value Theorem generalizes Rolle's Theorem, extending the idea of a horizontal tangent to a tangent parallel to any secant line. This provides a powerful tool for relating the local behavior (instantaneous rate of change) of a function to its global behavior (average rate of change) over an interval.
concepts.recap_md: - The Mean-Value Theorem is a generalization of Rolle's Theorem. - It states that a tangent line exists parallel to the secant line connecting two points on a differentiable function's graph.
concepts.raw_body: Rolle's Theorem is a special case of a more general result, called the Mean-Value Theorem. Geometrically, this theorem states that between any two points $A(a, f(a))$ and $B(b, f(b))$ on the graph of a differentiable function $f$, there is at least one place where the tangent line to the graph is parallel to the secant line joining $A$ and $B$ (Figure 4.8.5).

concepts.title: Mean-Value Theorem
concepts.one_liner: If $f$ is continuous on $[a, b]$ and differentiable on $(a, b)$, then there is a $c$ in $(a, b)$ such that $f^{\prime}(c)=\frac{f(b)-f(a)}{b-a}$.
concepts.summary_md: The Mean-Value Theorem states that if a function $f$ is continuous on the closed interval $[a, b]$ and differentiable on the open interval $(a, b)$, then there is at least one point $c$ in $(a, b)$ such that $f^{\prime}(c)=\frac{f(b)-f(a)}{b-a}$.
concepts.motivation_md: The Mean-Value Theorem provides a fundamental link between the average rate of change of a function over an interval and its instantaneous rate of change at some point within that interval. It is a cornerstone for proving many other important theorems in calculus, relating local and global properties of functions.
concepts.recap_md: - Requires $f$ to be continuous on $[a, b]$ and differentiable on $(a, b)$. - Guarantees a point $c$ where the instantaneous rate of change $f'(c)$ equals the average rate of change $\frac{f(b)-f(a)}{b-a}$.

concepts.title: Velocity Interpretation of the Mean-Value Theorem
concepts.one_liner: The Mean-Value Theorem implies that at least once during a trip, the instantaneous velocity must equal the average velocity, which aligns with real-world experience.
concepts.summary_md: The Mean-Value Theorem has a nice interpretation when $x=f(t)$ is a position versus time curve. The right side of the MVT equation is the average velocity, and the left side is the instantaneous velocity. This means that at least once during a time interval, the instantaneous velocity must equal the average velocity, matching real-world experience.
concepts.motivation_md: This interpretation helps students connect the abstract mathematical concept of the Mean-Value Theorem to a tangible, real-world scenario. It makes the theorem more intuitive and demonstrates its practical relevance in physics and everyday experience.
concepts.recap_md: - For a position function $x=f(t)$, the MVT's right side is average velocity. - The MVT's left side is instantaneous velocity at time $c$. - This means instantaneous velocity must equal average velocity at least once during a trip.
concepts.raw_body:
## VELOCITY INTERPRETATION OF THE MEAN-VALUE THEOREM

There is a nice interpretation of the Mean-Value Theorem in the situation where $x=f(t)$ is the position versus time curve for a car moving along a straight road. In this case, the right side of (1) is the average velocity of the car over the time interval from $a \leq t \leq b$, and the left side is the instantaneous velocity at time $t=c$. Thus, the Mean-Value Theorem implies that at least once during the time interval the instantaneous velocity must equal the
average velocity. This agrees with our real-world experience-if the average velocity for a trip is $40 \mathrm{mi} / \mathrm{h}$, then sometime during the trip the speedometer has to read $40 \mathrm{mi} / \mathrm{h}$.

concepts.title: Consequences of the Mean-Value Theorem
concepts.one_liner: The Mean-Value Theorem is the starting point for many important results in calculus, including proving fundamental tools for analyzing graphs of functions.
concepts.summary_md: The Mean-Value Theorem is a foundational result in calculus, serving as the starting point for many important theorems. For example, it can be used to prove Theorem 4.1.2, which is a fundamental tool for analyzing graphs of functions.
concepts.motivation_md: This section highlights the significance of the Mean-Value Theorem not just as a standalone result, but as a powerful lemma. It motivates further study by showing how the MVT underpins other crucial theorems used for understanding function behavior and graph analysis.
concepts.recap_md: - The Mean-Value Theorem is a foundational result in calculus. - It is used to prove many other important theorems. - An example is using it to prove Theorem 4.1.2 for analyzing function graphs.
concepts.raw_body:
## CONSEQUENCES OF THE MEAN-VALUE THEOREM

We stated at the beginning of this section that the Mean-Value Theorem is the starting point for many important results in calculus. As an example of this, we will use it to prove Theorem 4.1.2, which was one of our fundamental tools for analyzing graphs of functions.

concepts.title: Theorem 4.1.2 (Revisited)
concepts.one_liner: For a continuous and differentiable function $f$ on $[a, b]$, $f'(x)>0$ means $f$ is increasing, $f'(x)<0$ means $f$ is decreasing, and $f'(x)=0$ means $f$ is constant.
concepts.summary_md: Theorem 4.1.2 states that for a function $f$ continuous on $[a, b]$ and differentiable on $(a, b)$: (a) If $f^{\prime}(x)>0$ for every $x$ in $(a, b)$, then $f$ is increasing on $[a, b]$. (b) If $f^{\prime}(x)<0$ for every $x$ in $(a, b)$, then $f$ is decreasing on $[a, b]$. (c) If $f^{\prime}(x)=0$ for every $x$ in $(a, b)$, then $f$ is constant on $[a, b]$.
concepts.motivation_md: This theorem provides a direct and powerful method for analyzing the behavior of functions based on their derivatives. It allows us to determine where a function is increasing, decreasing, or constant, which is crucial for sketching graphs, finding extrema, and understanding function properties.
concepts.recap_md: - If $f'(x)>0$ on $(a, b)$, then $f$ is increasing on $[a, b]$. - If $f'(x)<0$ on $(a, b)$, then $f$ is decreasing on $[a, b]$. - If $f'(x)=0$ on $(a, b)$, then $f$ is constant on $[a, b]$.
concepts.raw_body:
4.1.2 THEOREM (Revisited) Let $f$ be a function that is continuous on a closed interval $[a, b]$ and differentiable on the open interval ( $a, b$ ).
(a) If $f^{\prime}(x)>0$ for every value of $x$ in ( $a, b$ ), then $f$ is increasing on $[a, b]$.
(b) If $f^{\prime}(x)<0$ for every value of $x$ in $(a, b)$, then $f$ is decreasing on $[a, b]$.
(c) If $f^{\prime}(x)=0$ for every value of $x$ in $(a, b)$, then $f$ is constant on $[a, b]$.

concepts.title: The Constant Difference Theorem (introduction)
concepts.one_liner: A function whose derivative is zero on an interval must be constant on that interval, a result that can be applied to the difference of two functions.
concepts.summary_md: From our earliest study of derivatives, we know the derivative of a constant is zero. Part (c) of Theorem 4.1.2 is the converse: a function whose derivative is zero on an interval must be constant on that interval. Applying this to the difference of two functions yields the Constant Difference Theorem.
concepts.motivation_md: This concept builds upon the fundamental relationship between a function and its derivative. It establishes that if two functions have the same derivative over an interval, they can only differ by a constant. This is crucial for understanding antiderivatives and the uniqueness of solutions to differential equations.
concepts.recap_md: - The derivative of a constant is zero. - Conversely, a function with a zero derivative on an interval must be constant. - This principle extends to the difference of two functions, leading to the Constant Difference Theorem.
concepts.raw_body:
## THE CONSTANT DIFFERENCE THEOREM

We know from our earliest study of derivatives that the derivative of a constant is zero. Part (c) of Theorem 4.1.2 is the converse of that result; that is, a function whose derivative is zero on an interval must be constant on that interval. If we apply this to the difference of two functions, we obtain the following useful theorem.

concepts.title: Constant Difference Theorem
concepts.one_liner: If $f$ and $g$ are differentiable on an interval, and if $f^{\prime}(x)=g^{\prime}(x)$ for all $x$ in that interval, then $f-g$ is constant on the interval.
concepts.summary_md: The Constant Difference Theorem states that if two functions, $f$ and $g$, are differentiable on an interval and have the same derivative, $f^{\prime}(x)=g^{\prime}(x)$, for all $x$ in that interval, then their difference, $f-g$, is constant. This means there exists a constant $k$ such that $f(x)-g(x)=k$, or $f(x)=g(x)+k$.
concepts.motivation_md: This theorem is crucial for understanding the relationship between antiderivatives. It establishes that if two functions have the same rate of change, they must differ by only a constant, which is fundamental to integration.
concepts.recap_md: - If $f'(x) = g'(x)$ on an interval, then $f(x) - g(x) = k$ for some constant $k$. - This implies $f(x) = g(x) + k$.
concepts.raw_body:
4.8.3 THEOREM (Constant Difference Theorem) If $f$ and $g$ are differentiable on an interval, and if $f^{\prime}(x)=g^{\prime}(x)$ for all $x$ in that interval, then $f-g$ is constant on the interval; that is, there is a constant $k$ such that $f(x)-g(x)=k$ or, equivalently,

$$
f(x)=g(x)+k
$$

concepts.title: Geometric Interpretation of the Constant Difference Theorem
concepts.one_liner: Geometrically, the Constant Difference Theorem tells us that if $f$ and $g$ have the same derivative on an interval, then the graphs of $f$ and $g$ are vertical translations of each other over that interval.
concepts.summary_md: The Constant Difference Theorem has a clear geometric interpretation: if two functions, $f$ and $g$, share the same derivative on a given interval, their graphs are simply vertical translations of one another over that interval. This means one graph can be shifted up or down to perfectly align with the other.
concepts.motivation_md: Understanding the geometric interpretation helps visualize the implications of the Constant Difference Theorem. It provides a concrete image for why functions with the same derivative must differ by a constant, showing them as parallel curves.
concepts.recap_md: - If $f'(x) = g'(x)$ on an interval, their graphs are vertical translations. - This means one graph can be shifted vertically to match the other.
concepts.raw_body: Geometrically, the Constant Difference Theorem tells us that if $f$ and $g$ have the same derivative on an interval, then the graphs of $f$ and $g$ are vertical translations of each other over that interval (Figure 4.8.8).

concepts.title: Theorem 4.4.3: Absolute Extremum on an Open Interval
concepts.one_liner: If $f$ has an absolute extremum on an open interval ( $a, b$ ), then it must occur at a critical point of $f$.
concepts.summary_md: Theorem 4.4.3 states that for a function $f$ defined on an open interval $(a, b)$, if an absolute extremum (either a maximum or minimum) exists within that interval, it must necessarily be located at a critical point of the function $f$.
concepts.motivation_md: This theorem provides a powerful tool for finding absolute extrema on open intervals. Instead of searching the entire interval, we can narrow our focus to only the critical points, significantly simplifying the optimization process.
concepts.recap_md: - An absolute extremum on an open interval $(a, b)$ must be a critical point. - This theorem helps locate absolute maxima or minima efficiently.
concepts.raw_body: [^2]:    4.4.3 THEOREM If $f$ has an absolute extremum on an open interval ( $a, b$ ), then it must occur at a critical point of $f$.

This in turn suggests that the value of $m_{\mathrm{sec}}$ will get closer and closer to the value of $m_{\tan }$ as $P$ moves toward $Q$ along the curve. However, to say that $Q\fleft(x, x^{2}ight)$ gets closer and closer to $P(1,1)$ is algebraically equivalent to saying that $x$ gets closer and closer to 1 . Thus, the problem of finding $m_{\tan }$ reduces to finding the "limiting value" of $m_{\text {sec }}$ in Formula (2) as $x$ gets closer and closer to 1 (but with $x \neq 1$ to ensure that $P$ and $Q$ remain distinct).![A graph in a Cartesian coordinate system shows the parabola $y=x^2$ in blue and the line $y=2x-1$ in purple. items.raw_body:
Example 1 Find an equation for the tangent line to the parabola $y=x^{2}$ at the point $P(1,1)$.

Solution. If we can find the slope $m_{\tan }$ of the tangent line at $P$, then we can use the point $P$ and the point-slope formula for a line (Web Appendix G) to write the equation of the tangent line as

$$
\begin{equation*}
y-1=m_{\tan }(x-1) \tag{1}
\end{equation*}
$$

To find the slope $m_{\text {tan }}$, consider the secant line through $P$ and a point $Q\left(x, x^{2}\right)$ on the parabola that is distinct from $P$. The slope $m_{\text {sec }}$ of this secant line is

$$
\begin{equation*}
m_{\mathrm{sec}}=\frac{x^{2}-1}{x-1} \tag{2}
\end{equation*}
$$

Figure 1.1.4a suggests that if we now let $Q$ move along the parabola, getting closer and closer to $P$, then the limiting position of the secant line through $P$ and $Q$ will coincide with that of the tangent line at $P$. This in turn suggests that the value of $m_{\mathrm{sec}}$ will get closer and closer to the value of $m_{\tan }$ as $P$ moves toward $Q$ along the curve. However, to say that $Q\left(x, x^{2}\right)$ gets closer and closer to $P(1,1)$ is algebraically equivalent to saying that $x$ gets closer and closer to 1 . Thus, the problem of finding $m_{\tan }$ reduces to finding the "limiting value" of $m_{\text {sec }}$ in Formula (2) as $x$ gets closer and closer to 1 (but with $x \neq 1$ to ensure that $P$ and $Q$ remain distinct).

![A graph in a Cartesian coordinate system shows the parabola $y=x^2$ in blue and the line $y=2x-1$ in purple. The line is tangent to the parabola at the point $P(1,1)$, which is marked with a blue...](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/84333fdc-d75a-4de5-aded-d41110c1154d-003.jpg?height=541&width=469&top_left_y=198&top_left_x=214)
- Figure 1.1.5

![The image displays two diagrams illustrating area decomposition. The left diagram shows an L-shaped region composed of two rectangles, labeled $A_1$ and $A_2$. The right diagram shows a pentagon...](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/84333fdc-d75a-4de5-aded-d41110c1154d-003.jpg?height=168&width=467&top_left_y=848&top_left_x=214)
Δ Figure 1.1.6

We can rewrite (2) as

$$
m_{\mathrm{sec}}=\frac{x^{2}-1}{x-1}=\frac{(x-1)(x+1)}{(x-1)}=x+1
$$

where the cancellation of the factor $(x-1)$ is allowed because $x \neq 1$. It is now evident that $m_{\text {sec }}$ gets closer and closer to 2 as $x$ gets closer and closer to 1 . Thus, $m_{\tan }=2$ and (1) implies that the equation of the tangent line is

$$
y-1=2(x-1) \quad \text { or equivalently } \quad y=2 x-1
$$

Figure 1.1.5 shows the graph of $y=x^{2}$ and this tangent line. $\square$

items.title: Conjecture about the limit of (x-1)/(sqrt(x)-1) as x approaches 1
items.prompt_md: Use numerical evidence to make a conjecture about the value of $$\lim _{x \rightarrow 1} \frac{x-1}{\sqrt{x}-1}$$
items.solution_md: Although the function $$f(x)=\frac{x-1}{\sqrt{x}-1}$$ is undefined at $x=1$, this has no bearing on the limit. Table 1.1.1 shows sample $x$-values approaching 1 from the left side and from the right side. In both cases the corresponding values of $f(x)$, calculated to six decimal places, appear to get closer and closer to 2 , and hence we conjecture that $$\lim _{x \rightarrow 1} \frac{x-1}{\sqrt{x}-1}=2$$ This is consistent with the graph of $f$ shown in Figure 1.1.9. In the next section we will show how to obtain this result algebraically.

items.title: The Relationship Between One-Sided and Two-Sided Limits
items.prompt_md: The two-sided limit of a function $f(x)$ exists at $a$ if and only if both of the one-sided limits exist at $a$ and have the same value; that is, $$\lim _{x \rightarrow a} f(x)=L \quad \text { if and only if } \quad \lim _{x \rightarrow a^{-}} f(x)=L=\lim _{x \rightarrow a^{+}} f(x)$$
items.raw_body:
1.1.3 THE RELATIONSHIP BETWEEN ONE-SIDED AND TWO-SIDED LIMITS The twosided limit of a function $f(x)$ exists at $a$ if and only if both of the one-sided limits exist at $a$ and have the same value; that is,

$$
\lim _{x \rightarrow a} f(x)=L \quad \text { if and only if } \quad \lim _{x \rightarrow a^{-}} f(x)=L=\lim _{x \rightarrow a^{+}} f(x)
$$

items.title: Explain why lim x->0 |x|/x does not exist
items.prompt_md: Explain why $$\lim _{x \rightarrow 0} \frac{|x|}{x}$$ does not exist.
items.solution_md: As $x$ approaches 0 , the values of $f(x)=|x| / x$ approach -1 from the left and approach 1 from the right [see(13)]. Thus, the one-sided limits at 0 are not the same.
items.raw_body:
Example 4 Explain why

$$
\lim _{x \rightarrow 0} \frac{|x|}{x}
$$

does not exist.

Solution. As $x$ approaches 0 , the values of $f(x)=|x| / x$ approach -1 from the left and approach 1 from the right [see(13)]. Thus, the one-sided limits at 0 are not the same.

items.title: Find one-sided and two-sided limits from Figure 1.1.13
items.prompt_md: For the functions in Figure 1.1.13, find the one-sided and two-sided limits at $x=a$ if they exist.
items.solution_md: The functions in all three figures have the same one-sided limits as $x \rightarrow a$, since the functions are identical, except at $x=a$. These limits are $$\lim _{x \rightarrow a^{+}} f(x)=3 \quad \text { and } \quad \lim _{x \rightarrow a^{-}} f(x)=1$$ In all three cases the two-sided limit does not exist as $x \rightarrow a$ because the one-sided limits are not equal.
items.raw_body:
Example 5 For the functions in Figure 1.1.13, find the one-sided and two-sided limits at $x=a$ if they exist.

Solution. The functions in all three figures have the same one-sided limits as $x \rightarrow a$, since the functions are identical, except at $x=a$. These limits are

$$
\lim _{x \rightarrow a^{+}} f(x)=3 \quad \text { and } \quad \lim _{x \rightarrow a^{-}} f(x)=1
$$

In all three cases the two-sided limit does not exist as $x \rightarrow a$ because the one-sided limits are not equal.

items.solution_md: Solution. items.title: Example 7
items.prompt_md: For the functions in Figure 1.1.16, describe the limits at $x=a$ in appropriate limit notation.
items.solution_md: Solution (a). In Figure 1.1.16a, the function increases without bound as $x$ approaches $a$ from the right and decreases without bound as $x$ approaches $a$ from the left. Thus,$$ \lim _{x \rightarrow a^{+}} \frac{1}{x-a}=+\infty \quad \text { and } \quad \lim _{x \rightarrow a^{-}} \frac{1}{x-a}=-\infty$$Solution (b). In Figure 1.1.16b, the function increases without bound as $x$ approaches $a$ from both the left and right. Thus,$$ \lim _{x \rightarrow a} \frac{1}{(x-a)^{2}}=\lim _{x \rightarrow a^{+}} \frac{1}{(x-a)^{2}}=\lim _{x \rightarrow a^{-}} \frac{1}{(x-a)^{2}}=+\infty$$Solution (c). In Figure 1.1.16c, the function decreases without bound as $x$ approaches $a$ from the right and increases without bound as $x$ approaches $a$ from the left. Thus,$$ \lim _{x \rightarrow a^{+}} \frac{-1}{x-a}=-\infty \quad \text { and } \quad \lim _{x \rightarrow a^{-}} \frac{-1}{x-a}=+\infty$$Solution (d). In Figure 1.1.16d, the function decreases without bound as $x$ approaches $a$ from both the left and right. Thus,$$ \lim _{x \rightarrow a} \frac{-1}{(x-a)^{2}}=\lim _{x \rightarrow a^{+}} \frac{-1}{(x-a)^{2}}=\lim _{x \rightarrow a^{-}} \frac{-1}{(x-a)^{2}}=-\infty$$
items.raw_body:
- Example 7 For the functions in Figure 1.1.16, describe the limits at $x=a$ in appropriate limit notation.

Solution (a). In Figure 1.1.16a, the function increases without bound as $x$ approaches $a$ from the right and decreases without bound as $x$ approaches $a$ from the left. Thus,

$$
\lim _{x \rightarrow a^{+}} \frac{1}{x-a}=+\infty \quad \text { and } \quad \lim _{x \rightarrow a^{-}} \frac{1}{x-a}=-\infty
$$

Solution (b). In Figure 1.1.16b, the function increases without bound as $x$ approaches $a$ from both the left and right. Thus,

$$
\lim _{x \rightarrow a} \frac{1}{(x-a)^{2}}=\lim _{x \rightarrow a^{+}} \frac{1}{(x-a)^{2}}=\lim _{x \rightarrow a^{-}} \frac{1}{(x-a)^{2}}=+\infty
$$

Solution (c). In Figure 1.1.16c, the function decreases without bound as $x$ approaches $a$ from the right and increases without bound as $x$ approaches $a$ from the left. Thus,

$$
\lim _{x \rightarrow a^{+}} \frac{-1}{x-a}=-\infty \quad \text { and } \quad \lim _{x \rightarrow a^{-}} \frac{-1}{x-a}=+\infty
$$

Solution (d). In Figure 1.1.16d, the function decreases without bound as $x$ approaches $a$ from both the left and right. Thus,

$$
\lim _{x \rightarrow a} \frac{-1}{(x-a)^{2}}=\lim _{x \rightarrow a^{+}} \frac{-1}{(x-a)^{2}}=\lim _{x \rightarrow a^{-}} \frac{-1}{(x-a)^{2}}=-\infty
$$

items.prompt_md: 17-20 True-False Determine whether the statement is true or false. Explain your answer.

17. If $f(a)=L$, then $\lim _{x \rightarrow a} f(x)=L$.
18. If $\lim _{x \rightarrow a} f(x)$ exists, then so do $\lim _{x \rightarrow a^{-}} f(x)$ and $\lim _{x \rightarrow a^{+}} f(x)$.

20. If $\lim _{x \rightarrow a^{+}} f(x)=+\infty$, then $f(a)$ is undefined.

21-26 Sketch a possible graph for a function $f$ with the specified properties. (Many different solutions are possible.)
21. (i) the domain of $f$ is $[-1,1]$
(ii) $f(-1)=f(0)=f(1)=0$
(iii) $\lim _{x \rightarrow-1^{+}} f(x)=\lim _{x \rightarrow 0} f(x)=\lim _{x \rightarrow 1^{-}} f(x)=1$
22. (i) the domain of $f$ is $[-2,1]$
(ii) $f(-2)=f(0)=f(1)=0$
(iii) $\lim _{x \rightarrow-2^{+}} f(x)=2, \lim _{x \rightarrow 0} f(x)=0$, and $\lim _{x \rightarrow 1^{-}} f(x)=1$
23. (i) the domain of $f$ is $(-\infty, 0]$
(ii) $f(-2)=f(0)=1$
(iii) $\lim _{x \rightarrow-2} f(x)=+\infty$
24. (i) the domain of $f$ is ( $0,+\infty$ )
(ii) $f(1)=0$
(iii) the $y$-axis is a vertical asymptote for the graph of $f$
(iv) $f(x)<0$ if $0<x<1$
25. (i) $f(-3)=f(0)=f(2)=0$
(ii) $\lim _{x \rightarrow-2^{-}} f(x)=+\infty$ and $\lim _{x \rightarrow-2^{+}} f(x)=-\infty$
(iii) $\lim _{x \rightarrow 1} f(x)=+\infty$

(ii) $\lim _{x \rightarrow-1^{-}} f(x)=0$ and $\lim _{x \rightarrow-1^{+}} f(x)=+\infty$
(iii) $\lim _{x \rightarrow 1^{-}} f(x)=1$ and $\lim _{x \rightarrow 1^{+}} f(x)=+\infty$

items.title: Properties of Limits
items.prompt_md: 1.2.2 THEOREM Let a be a real number, and suppose that$$ \lim _{x \rightarrow a} f(x)=L_{1} \quad \text { and } \quad \lim _{x \rightarrow a} g(x)=L_{2} $$That is, the limits exist and have values $L_{1}$ and $L_{2}$, respectively. Then:(a) $\lim _{x \rightarrow a}[f(x)+g(x)]=\lim _{x \rightarrow a} f(x)+\lim _{x \rightarrow a} g(x)=L_{1}+L_{2}$(b) $\lim _{x \rightarrow a}[f(x)-g(x)]=\lim _{x \rightarrow a} f(x)-\lim _{x \rightarrow a} g(x)=L_{1}-L_{2}$(c) $\lim _{x \rightarrow a}[f(x) g(x)]=\left(\lim _{x \rightarrow a} f(x)\right)\left(\lim _{x \rightarrow a} g(x)\right)=L_{1} L_{2}$(d) $\lim _{x \rightarrow a} \frac{f(x)}{g(x)}=\frac{\lim _{x \rightarrow a} f(x)}{\lim _{x \rightarrow a} g(x)}=\frac{L_{1}}{L_{2}}, \quad$ provided $L_{2} \neq 0$(e) $\lim _{x \rightarrow a} \sqrt[n]{f(x)}=\sqrt[n]{\lim _{x \rightarrow a} f(x)}=\sqrt[n]{L_{1}}$, provided $L_{1}>0$ if $n$ is even.Moreover, these statements are also true for the one-sided limits as $x \rightarrow a^{-}$or as $x \rightarrow a^{+}$.This theorem can be stated informally as follows:(a) The limit of a sum is the sum of the limits.(b) The limit of a difference is the difference of the limits.(c) The limit of a product is the product of the limits.(d) The limit of a quotient is the quotient of the limits, provided the limit of the denominator is not zero.(e) The limit of an $n$th root is the $n$th root of the limit.
items.raw_body:
1.2.2 THEOREM Let a be a real number, and suppose that

$$
\lim _{x \rightarrow a} f(x)=L_{1} \quad \text { and } \quad \lim _{x \rightarrow a} g(x)=L_{2}
$$

That is, the limits exist and have values $L_{1}$ and $L_{2}$, respectively. Then:
(a) $\lim _{x \rightarrow a}[f(x)+g(x)]=\lim _{x \rightarrow a} f(x)+\lim _{x \rightarrow a} g(x)=L_{1}+L_{2}$
(b) $\lim _{x \rightarrow a}[f(x)-g(x)]=\lim _{x \rightarrow a} f(x)-\lim _{x \rightarrow a} g(x)=L_{1}-L_{2}$
(c) $\lim _{x \rightarrow a}[f(x) g(x)]=\left(\lim _{x \rightarrow a} f(x)\right)\left(\lim _{x \rightarrow a} g(x)\right)=L_{1} L_{2}$
(d) $\lim _{x \rightarrow a} \frac{f(x)}{g(x)}=\frac{\lim _{x \rightarrow a} f(x)}{\lim _{x \rightarrow a} g(x)}=\frac{L_{1}}{L_{2}}, \quad$ provided $L_{2} \neq 0$
(e) $\lim _{x \rightarrow a} \sqrt[n]{f(x)}=\sqrt[n]{\lim _{x \rightarrow a} f(x)}=\sqrt[n]{L_{1}}$, provided $L_{1}>0$ if $n$ is even.

Moreover, these statements are also true for the one-sided limits as $x \rightarrow a^{-}$or as $x \rightarrow a^{+}$.

This theorem can be stated informally as follows:
(a) The limit of a sum is the sum of the limits.
(b) The limit of a difference is the difference of the limits.
(c) The limit of a product is the product of the limits.
(d) The limit of a quotient is the quotient of the limits, provided the limit of the denominator is not zero.
(e) The limit of an $n$th root is the $n$th root of the limit.

items.title: Example 4
items.prompt_md: This example demonstrates the application of limit properties to various expressions:
items.solution_md: $$\begin{array}{lc}\lim _{x \rightarrow a}[f(x)-g(x)+2 h(x)]=\lim _{x \rightarrow a} f(x)-\lim _{x \rightarrow a} g(x)+2 \lim _{x \rightarrow a} h(x) \\ \lim _{x \rightarrow a}[f(x) g(x) h(x)]=\left(\lim _{x \rightarrow a} f(x)\right)\left(\lim _{x \rightarrow a} g(x)\right)\left(\lim _{x \rightarrow a} h(x)\right) \\ \lim _{x \rightarrow a}[f(x)]^{3}=\left(\lim _{x \rightarrow a} f(x)\right)^{3} & \text { Take } g(x)=h(x)=f(x) \text { in the last equation. } \\ \lim _{x \rightarrow a}[f(x)]^{n}=\left(\lim _{x \rightarrow a} f(x)\right)^{n} & \begin{array}{l}\text { The extension of Theorem 1.2.2(c) in which } \\ \text { there are } n \text { factors, each of which is } f(x)\end{array} \\ \lim _{x \rightarrow a} x^{n}=\left(\lim _{x \rightarrow a} x\right)^{n}=a^{n} & \text { Apply the previous result with } f(x)=x .\end{array}$$
items.raw_body:
## Example 4

$$
\begin{array}{lc}
\lim _{x \rightarrow a}[f(x)-g(x)+2 h(x)]=\lim _{x \rightarrow a} f(x)-\lim _{x \rightarrow a} g(x)+2 \lim _{x \rightarrow a} h(x) \\
\lim _{x \rightarrow a}[f(x) g(x) h(x)]=\left(\lim _{x \rightarrow a} f(x)\right)\left(\lim _{x \rightarrow a} g(x)\right)\left(\lim _{x \rightarrow a} h(x)\right) \\
\lim _{x \rightarrow a}[f(x)]^{3}=\left(\lim _{x \rightarrow a} f(x)\right)^{3} & \text { Take } g(x)=h(x)=f(x) \text { in the last equation. } \\
\lim _{x \rightarrow a}[f(x)]^{n}=\left(\lim _{x \rightarrow a} f(x)\right)^{n} & \begin{array}{l}
\text { The extension of Theorem 1.2.2(c) in which } \\
\text { there are } n \text { factors, each of which is } f(x)
\end{array} \\
\lim _{x \rightarrow a} x^{n}=\left(\lim _{x \rightarrow a} x\right)^{n}=a^{n} & \text { Apply the previous result with } f(x)=x .
\end{array}
$$

items.title: Example 5
items.prompt_md: Find $\lim _{x \rightarrow 5}\left(x^{2}-4 x+3\right)$.
items.solution_md: Solution.$$\begin{aligned}\lim _{x \rightarrow 5}\left(x^{2}-4 x+3\right) & =\lim _{x \rightarrow 5} x^{2}-\lim _{x \rightarrow 5} 4 x+\lim _{x \rightarrow 5} 3 \\ & =\lim _{x \rightarrow 5} x^{2}-4 \lim _{x \rightarrow 5} x+\lim _{x \rightarrow 5} 3 \\ & =5^{2}-4(5)+3 \\ & =8\end{aligned}$$
items.raw_body:
## Example 5 Find $\lim _{x \rightarrow 5}\left(x^{2}-4 x+3\right)$.

## Solution.

$$
\begin{aligned}
\lim _{x \rightarrow 5}\left(x^{2}-4 x+3\right) & =\lim _{x \rightarrow 5} x^{2}-\lim _{x \rightarrow 5} 4 x+\lim _{x \rightarrow 5} 3 \\
& =\lim _{x \rightarrow 5} x^{2}-4 \lim _{x \rightarrow 5} x+\lim _{x \rightarrow 5} 3 \\
& =5^{2}-4(5)+3 \\
& =8
\end{aligned}
$$

items.title: Limit of a Polynomial
items.prompt_md: ### 1.2.3 THEOREM For any polynomial$$ p(x)=c_{0}+c_{1} x+\cdots+c_{n} x^{n} $$and any real number $a$,$$ \lim _{x \rightarrow a} p(x)=c_{0}+c_{1} a+\cdots+c_{n} a^{n}=p(a) $$
items.proof_md: PROOF$$ \begin{aligned}\lim _{x \rightarrow a} p(x) & =\lim _{x \rightarrow a}\left(c_{0}+c_{1} x+\cdots+c_{n} x^{n}\right) \\ & =\lim _{x \rightarrow a} c_{0}+\lim _{x \rightarrow a} c_{1} x+\cdots+\lim _{x \rightarrow a} c_{n} x^{n} \\ & =\lim _{x \rightarrow a} c_{0}+c_{1} \lim _{x \rightarrow a} x+\cdots+c_{n} \lim _{x \rightarrow a} x^{n} \\ & =c_{0}+c_{1} a+\cdots+c_{n} a^{n}=p(a)\end{aligned} $$
items.raw_body:
### 1.2.3 THEOREM For any polynomial

$$
p(x)=c_{0}+c_{1} x+\cdots+c_{n} x^{n}
$$

and any real number $a$,

$$
\lim _{x \rightarrow a} p(x)=c_{0}+c_{1} a+\cdots+c_{n} a^{n}=p(a)
$$

PROOF

$$
\begin{aligned}
\lim _{x \rightarrow a} p(x) & =\lim _{x \rightarrow a}\left(c_{0}+c_{1} x+\cdots+c_{n} x^{n}\right) \\
& =\lim _{x \rightarrow a} c_{0}+\lim _{x \rightarrow a} c_{1} x+\cdots+\lim _{x \rightarrow a} c_{n} x^{n} \\
& =\lim _{x \rightarrow a} c_{0}+c_{1} \lim _{x \rightarrow a} x+\cdots+c_{n} \lim _{x \rightarrow a} x^{n} \\
& =c_{0}+c_{1} a+\cdots+c_{n} a^{n}=p(a)
\end{aligned}
$$

items.prompt_md: Find $\lim _{x \rightarrow 1}\left(x^{7}-2 x^{5}+1\right)^{35}$.
items.solution_md: Solution. The function involved is a polynomial (why?), so the limit can be obtained by evaluating this polynomial at $x=1$. This yields$$ \lim _{x \rightarrow 1}\left(x^{7}-2 x^{5}+1\right)^{35}=0 $$

items.title: Example 7
items.prompt_md: Find $\lim _{x \rightarrow 2} \frac{5 x^{3}+4}{x-3}$.
items.solution_md: Solution. $$\begin{aligned}\lim _{x \rightarrow 2} \frac{5 x^{3}+4}{x-3} & =\frac{\lim _{x \rightarrow 2}\left(5 x^{3}+4\right)}{\lim _{x \rightarrow 2}(x-3)} \\ & =\frac{5 \cdot 2^{3}+4}{2-3}=-44\end{aligned}$$
items.raw_body:
- Example 7 Find $\lim _{x \rightarrow 2} \frac{5 x^{3}+4}{x-3}$.

Solution.

$$
\begin{aligned}
\lim _{x \rightarrow 2} \frac{5 x^{3}+4}{x-3} & =\frac{\lim _{x \rightarrow 2}\left(5 x^{3}+4\right)}{\lim _{x \rightarrow 2}(x-3)} \\
& =\frac{5 \cdot 2^{3}+4}{2-3}=-44
\end{aligned}
$$

items.title: Example 9
items.prompt_md: Find (a) $\lim _{x \rightarrow 3} \frac{x^{2}-6 x+9}{x-3}$ (b) $\lim _{x \rightarrow-4} \frac{2 x+8}{x^{2}+x-12}$ (c) $\lim _{x \rightarrow 5} \frac{x^{2}-3 x-10}{x^{2}-10 x+25}
items.solution_md: Solution ( $\boldsymbol{a}$ ). The numerator and the denominator both have a zero at $x=3$, so there is a common factor of $x-3$. Then $$ \lim _{x \rightarrow 3} \frac{x^{2}-6 x+9}{x-3}=\lim _{x \rightarrow 3} \frac{(x-3)^{2}}{x-3}=\lim _{x \rightarrow 3}(x-3)=0 $$ Solution (b). The numerator and the denominator both have a zero at $x=-4$, so there is a common factor of $x-(-4)=x+4$. Then $$ \lim _{x \rightarrow-4} \frac{2 x+8}{x^{2}+x-12}=\lim _{x \rightarrow-4} \frac{2(x+4)}{(x+4)(x-3)}=\lim _{x \rightarrow-4} \frac{2}{x-3}=-\frac{2}{7} $$ Solution ( $\boldsymbol{c}$ ). The numerator and the denominator both have a zero at $x=5$, so there is a common factor of $x-5$. Then $$ \lim _{x \rightarrow 5} \frac{x^{2}-3 x-10}{x^{2}-10 x+25}=\lim _{x \rightarrow 5} \frac{(x-5)(x+2)}{(x-5)(x-5)}=\lim _{x \rightarrow 5} \frac{x+2}{x-5} $$ ![A number line labeled $x$ displays the sign of the expression $\frac{x+2}{x-5}$. The critical points are marked at $x=-2$ and $x=5$. For $x < -2$, the expression is positive; at $x=-2$, it is zero...](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/84333fdc-d75a-4de5-aded-d41110c1154d-019.jpg?height=195&width=461&top_left_y=456&top_left_x=216) Figure 1.2.4 Discuss the logical errors in the following statement: An indeterminate form of type $0 / 0$ must have a limit of zero because zero divided by anything is zero. However, $$ \lim _{x \rightarrow 5}(x+2)=7 \neq 0 \quad \text { and } \quad \lim _{x \rightarrow 5}(x-5)=0 $$ so $$ \lim _{x \rightarrow 5} \frac{x^{2}-3 x-10}{x^{2}-10 x+25}=\lim _{x \rightarrow 5} \frac{x+2}{x-5} $$ does not exist. More precisely, the sign analysis in Figure 1.2.4 implies that $$ \lim _{x \rightarrow 5^{+}} \frac{x^{2}-3 x-10}{x^{2}-10 x+25}=\lim _{x \rightarrow 5^{+}} \frac{x+2}{x-5}=+\infty $$ and $$ \lim _{x \rightarrow 5^{-}} \frac{x^{2}-3 x-10}{x^{2}-10 x+25}=\lim _{x \rightarrow 5^{-}} \frac{x+2}{x-5}=-\infty $$
items.answer: a) 0; b) -2/7; c) does not exist

- Example 9 Find
(a) $\lim _{x \rightarrow 3} \frac{x^{2}-6 x+9}{x-3}$
(b) $\lim _{x \rightarrow-4} \frac{2 x+8}{x^{2}+x-12}$
(c) $\lim _{x \rightarrow 5} \frac{x^{2}-3 x-10}{x^{2}-10 x+25}$

Solution ( $\boldsymbol{a}$ ). The numerator and the denominator both have a zero at $x=3$, so there is a common factor of $x-3$. Then

$$
\lim _{x \rightarrow 3} \frac{x^{2}-6 x+9}{x-3}=\lim _{x \rightarrow 3} \frac{(x-3)^{2}}{x-3}=\lim _{x \rightarrow 3}(x-3)=0
$$

Solution (b). The numerator and the denominator both have a zero at $x=-4$, so there is a common factor of $x-(-4)=x+4$. Then

$$
\lim _{x \rightarrow-4} \frac{2 x+8}{x^{2}+x-12}=\lim _{x \rightarrow-4} \frac{2(x+4)}{(x+4)(x-3)}=\lim _{x \rightarrow-4} \frac{2}{x-3}=-\frac{2}{7}
$$

Solution ( $\boldsymbol{c}$ ). The numerator and the denominator both have a zero at $x=5$, so there is a common factor of $x-5$. Then

$$
\lim _{x \rightarrow 5} \frac{x^{2}-3 x-10}{x^{2}-10 x+25}=\lim _{x \rightarrow 5} \frac{(x-5)(x+2)}{(x-5)(x-5)}=\lim _{x \rightarrow 5} \frac{x+2}{x-5}
$$

![A number line labeled $x$ displays the sign of the expression $\frac{x+2}{x-5}$. The critical points are marked at $x=-2$ and $x=5$. For $x < -2$, the expression is positive; at $x=-2$, it is zero...](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/84333fdc-d75a-4de5-aded-d41110c1154d-019.jpg?height=195&width=461&top_left_y=456&top_left_x=216)
Figure 1.2.4

Discuss the logical errors in the following statement: An indeterminate form of type $0 / 0$ must have a limit of zero because zero divided by anything is zero.

However,

$$
\lim _{x \rightarrow 5}(x+2)=7 \neq 0 \quad \text { and } \quad \lim _{x \rightarrow 5}(x-5)=0
$$

so

$$
\lim _{x \rightarrow 5} \frac{x^{2}-3 x-10}{x^{2}-10 x+25}=\lim _{x \rightarrow 5} \frac{x+2}{x-5}
$$

does not exist. More precisely, the sign analysis in Figure 1.2.4 implies that

$$
\lim _{x \rightarrow 5^{+}} \frac{x^{2}-3 x-10}{x^{2}-10 x+25}=\lim _{x \rightarrow 5^{+}} \frac{x+2}{x-5}=+\infty
$$

and

$$
\lim _{x \rightarrow 5^{-}} \frac{x^{2}-3 x-10}{x^{2}-10 x+25}=\lim _{x \rightarrow 5^{-}} \frac{x+2}{x-5}=-\infty
$$

items.title: Example 10
items.prompt_md: Find $\lim _{x \rightarrow 1} \frac{x-1}{\sqrt{x}-1}$. Confirm the limit in Example 10 by factoring the numerator.
items.solution_md: Solution. In Example 2 of Section 1.1 we used numerical evidence to conjecture that this limit is 2 . Here we will confirm this algebraically. Since this limit is an indeterminate form of type 0/0, we will need to devise some strategy for making the limit (if it exists) evident. One such strategy is to rationalize the denominator of the function. This yields $$ \frac{x-1}{\sqrt{x}-1}=\frac{(x-1)(\sqrt{x}+1)}{(\sqrt{x}-1)(\sqrt{x}+1)}=\frac{(x-1)(\sqrt{x}+1)}{x-1}=\sqrt{x}+1 \quad(x \neq 1) $$ Therefore, $$ \lim _{x \rightarrow 1} \frac{x-1}{\sqrt{x}-1}=\lim _{x \rightarrow 1}(\sqrt{x}+1)=2 $$

Example 10 Find $\lim _{x \rightarrow 1} \frac{x-1}{\sqrt{x}-1}$.

One such strategy is to rationalize the denominator of the function. This yields

$$
\frac{x-1}{\sqrt{x}-1}=\frac{(x-1)(\sqrt{x}+1)}{(\sqrt{x}-1)(\sqrt{x}+1)}=\frac{(x-1)(\sqrt{x}+1)}{x-1}=\sqrt{x}+1 \quad(x \neq 1)
$$

Confirm the limit in Example 10 by factoring the numerator.

items.title: Example 11
items.prompt_md: Let $$ f(x)=\left\{\begin{aligned} & 1 /(x+2), & x & <-2 \ & x^{2}-5, & -2 & <x \leq 3 \ & \sqrt{x+13}, & x & >3 \end{aligned}\right. $$ Find (a) $\lim _{x \rightarrow-2} f(x)$ (b) $\lim _{x \rightarrow 0} f(x)$ (c) $\lim _{x \rightarrow 3} f(x)$
items.solution_md: Solution (a). We will determine the stated two-sided limit by first considering the corresponding one-sided limits. For each one-sided limit, we must use that part of the formula that is applicable on the interval over which $x$ varies. For example, as $x$ approaches -2 from the left, the applicable part of the formula is $$ f(x)=\frac{1}{x+2} $$ and as $x$ approaches -2 from the right, the applicable part of the formula near -2 is $$ f(x)=x^{2}-5 $$ Thus, $$ \begin{aligned} \lim _{x \rightarrow-2^{-}} f(x) & =\lim _{x \rightarrow-2^{-}} \frac{1}{x+2}=-\infty \\ \lim _{x \rightarrow-2^{+}} f(x) & =\lim _{x \rightarrow-2^{+}}\left(x^{2}-5\right)=(-2)^{2}-5=-1 \end{aligned} $$ from which it follows that $\lim _{x \rightarrow-2} f(x)$ does not exist. Solution (b). The applicable part of the formula is $f(x)=x^{2}-5$ on both sides of 0 , so there is no need to consider one-sided limits here. We see directly that $$ \lim _{x \rightarrow 0} f(x)=\lim _{x \rightarrow 0}\left(x^{2}-5\right)=0^{2}-5=-5 $$ Solution (c). Using the applicable parts of the formula for $f(x)$, we obtain $$ \begin{aligned} & \lim _{x \rightarrow 3^{-}} f(x)=\lim _{x \rightarrow 3^{-}}\left(x^{2}-5\right)=3^{2}-5=4 \\ & \lim _{x \rightarrow 3^{+}} f(x)=\lim _{x \rightarrow 3^{+}} \sqrt{x+13}=\sqrt{\lim _{x \rightarrow 3^{+}}(x+13)}=\sqrt{3+13}=4 \end{aligned} $$ Since the one-sided limits are equal, we have $$ \lim _{x \rightarrow 3} f(x)=4 $$ We note that the limit calculations in parts (a), (b), and (c) are consistent with the graph of $f$ shown in Figure 1.2.5.
items.answer: a) does not exist; b) -5; c) 4

& 1 /(x+2), & x & <-2 \\
& x^{2}-5, & -2 & <x \leq 3 \\
& \sqrt{x+13}, & x & >3
\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Find
(a) $\lim _{x \rightarrow-2} f(x)$
(b) $\lim _{x \rightarrow 0} f(x)$
(c) $\lim _{x \rightarrow 3} f(x)$

Solution (a). We will determine the stated two-sided limit by first considering the corresponding one-sided limits. For each one-sided limit, we must use that part of the formula that is applicable on the interval over which $x$ varies. For example, as $x$ approaches -2 from the left, the applicable part of the formula is

$$
f(x)=\frac{1}{x+2}
$$

and as $x$ approaches -2 from the right, the applicable part of the formula near -2 is

$$
f(x)=x^{2}-5
$$

Thus,

$$
\begin{aligned}
\lim _{x \rightarrow-2^{-}} f(x) & =\lim _{x \rightarrow-2^{-}} \frac{1}{x+2}=-\infty \\
\lim _{x \rightarrow-2^{+}} f(x) & =\lim _{x \rightarrow-2^{+}}\left(x^{2}-5\right)=(-2)^{2}-5=-1
\end{aligned}
$$

from which it follows that $\lim _{x \rightarrow-2} f(x)$ does not exist.

Solution (b). The applicable part of the formula is $f(x)=x^{2}-5$ on both sides of 0 , so there is no need to consider one-sided limits here. We see directly that

$$
\lim _{x \rightarrow 0} f(x)=\lim _{x \rightarrow 0}\left(x^{2}-5\right)=0^{2}-5=-5
$$

Solution (c). Using the applicable parts of the formula for $f(x)$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \lim _{x \rightarrow 3^{-}} f(x)=\lim _{x \rightarrow 3^{-}}\left(x^{2}-5\right)=3^{2}-5=4 \\
& \lim _{x \rightarrow 3^{+}} f(x)=\lim _{x \rightarrow 3^{+}} \sqrt{x+13}=\sqrt{\lim _{x \rightarrow 3^{+}}(x+13)}=\sqrt{3+13}=4
\end{aligned}
$$

Since the one-sided limits are equal, we have

$$
\lim _{x \rightarrow 3} f(x)=4
$$

We note that the limit calculations in parts (a), (b), and (c) are consistent with the graph of $f$ shown in Figure 1.2.5.

items.title: Limits of 1/x^n and (1 + 1/(2x))^x
items.solution_md: ## Example 4(a) It follows from (1), (2), (9), and (10) that if $n$ is a positive integer, then$$\lim _{x \rightarrow+\infty} \frac{1}{x^{n}}=\left(\lim _{x \rightarrow+\infty} \frac{1}{x}\right)^{n}=0 \quad \text { and } \quad \lim _{x \rightarrow-\infty} \frac{1}{x^{n}}=\left(\lim _{x \rightarrow-\infty} \frac{1}{x}\right)^{n}=0$$(b) It follows from (7) and the extension of Theorem 1.2.2(e) to the case $x \rightarrow+\infty$ that$$\begin{aligned}\lim _{x \rightarrow+\infty}\left(1+\frac{1}{2 x}\right)^{x} & =\lim _{x \rightarrow+\infty}\left[\left(1+\frac{1}{2 x}\right)^{2 x}\right]^{1 / 2} \\& =\left[\lim _{x \rightarrow+\infty}\left(1+\frac{1}{2 x}\right)^{2 x}\right]^{1 / 2}=e^{1 / 2}=\sqrt{e}\end{aligned}$$
items.raw_body:
## Example 4

(a) It follows from (1), (2), (9), and (10) that if $n$ is a positive integer, then

$$
\lim _{x \rightarrow+\infty} \frac{1}{x^{n}}=\left(\lim _{x \rightarrow+\infty} \frac{1}{x}\right)^{n}=0 \quad \text { and } \quad \lim _{x \rightarrow-\infty} \frac{1}{x^{n}}=\left(\lim _{x \rightarrow-\infty} \frac{1}{x}\right)^{n}=0
$$

(b) It follows from (7) and the extension of Theorem 1.2.2(e) to the case $x \rightarrow+\infty$ that

$$
\begin{aligned}
\lim _{x \rightarrow+\infty}\left(1+\frac{1}{2 x}\right)^{x} & =\lim _{x \rightarrow+\infty}\left[\left(1+\frac{1}{2 x}\right)^{2 x}\right]^{1 / 2} \\
& =\left[\lim _{x \rightarrow+\infty}\left(1+\frac{1}{2 x}\right)^{2 x}\right]^{1 / 2}=e^{1 / 2}=\sqrt{e}
\end{aligned}
$$

items.title: Limit of a Rational Function using Division Method
items.prompt_md: Find $\lim _{x \rightarrow+\infty} \frac{3 x+5}{6 x-8}$.
items.solution_md: Solution. Divide each term in the numerator and denominator by the highest power of $x$ that occurs in the denominator, namely, $x^{1}=x$. We obtain$$ \begin{aligned} & \lim _{x \rightarrow+\infty} \frac{3 x+5}{6 x-8}=\lim _{x \rightarrow+\infty} \frac{3+\frac{5}{x}}{6-\frac{8}{x}} \\ &=\frac{\lim _{x \rightarrow+\infty}\left(3+\frac{5}{x}\right)}{\lim _{x \rightarrow+\infty}\left(6-\frac{8}{x}\right)} \quad \text { Divide each term by } x . \\ &=\frac{\lim _{x \rightarrow+\infty} 3+\lim _{x \rightarrow+\infty} \frac{5}{x}}{\lim _{x \rightarrow+\infty} 6-\lim _{x \rightarrow+\infty} \frac{8}{x}} \quad \text { quotient of the limits. } \\ &=\frac{\begin{array}{l} \text { Limit of a sum is the } \\ \text { sum of the limits. } \end{array}}{3+5 \lim _{x \rightarrow+\infty} \frac{1}{x}}=\frac{3+0}{6-8 \lim _{x \rightarrow+\infty} \frac{1}{x}}=\frac{1}{2} \quad \text { A constant can be moved through a } \\ & \text { limit symbol; Formulas (2) and (13). } \end{aligned} $$

items.title: Limits of Rational Functions (More Cases)
items.prompt_md: Find (a) $\lim _{x \rightarrow-\infty} \frac{4 x^{2}-x}{2 x^{3}-5}$ (b) $\lim _{x \rightarrow+\infty} \frac{5 x^{3}-2 x^{2}+1}{1-3 x}$
items.solution_md: Solution (a). Divide each term in the numerator and denominator by the highest power of $x$ that occurs in the denominator, namely, $x^{3}$. We obtain$$ \begin{aligned} \lim _{x \rightarrow-\infty} \frac{4 x^{2}-x}{2 x^{3}-5} & =\lim _{x \rightarrow-\infty} \frac{\frac{4}{x}-\frac{1}{x^{2}}}{2-\frac{5}{x^{3}}} \\ & =\frac{\lim _{x \rightarrow-\infty}\left(\frac{4}{x}-\frac{1}{x^{2}}\right)}{\lim _{x \rightarrow-\infty}\left(2-\frac{5}{x^{3}}\right)} \quad \text { Divide each term by } x^{3} . \\ & =\frac{}{\lim _{x \rightarrow-\infty} \frac{4}{x}-\lim _{x \rightarrow-\infty} \frac{1}{x^{2}}} \quad \begin{array}{l} \text { Limit of a quotient is the } \\ \text { quotient of the limits. } \end{array} \\ & \quad \lim _{x \rightarrow-\infty} 2-\lim _{x \rightarrow-\infty} \frac{5}{x^{3}} \\ & =\frac{4 \lim _{x \rightarrow-\infty} \frac{1}{x}-\lim _{x \rightarrow-\infty} \frac{1}{x^{2}}}{2-5 \lim _{x \rightarrow-\infty} \frac{1}{x^{3}}}=\frac{0-0}{2-0}=0 \quad \begin{array}{l} \text { A constant a difference is the be moved through } \\ \text { a limit symbol; Formula (14) and } \\ \text { Example 4. } \end{array} \end{aligned} $$Solution (b). Divide each term in the numerator and denominator by the highest power of $x$ that occurs in the denominator, namely, $x^{1}=x$. We obtain$$ \begin{equation*} \lim _{x \rightarrow+\infty} \frac{5 x^{3}-2 x^{2}+1}{1-3 x}=\lim _{x \rightarrow+\infty} \frac{5 x^{2}-2 x+\frac{1}{x}}{\frac{1}{x}-3} \tag{19} \end{equation*} $$In this case we cannot argue that the limit of the quotient is the quotient of the limits because the limit of the numerator does not exist. However, we have$$ \lim _{x \rightarrow+\infty} 5 x^{2}-2 x=+\infty, \quad \lim _{x \rightarrow+\infty} \frac{1}{x}=0, \quad \lim _{x \rightarrow+\infty}\left(\frac{1}{x}-3\right)=-3 $$Thus, the numerator on the right side of (19) approaches $+\infty$ and the denominator has a finite negative limit. We conclude from this that the quotient approaches $-\infty$; that is,$$ \lim _{x \rightarrow+\infty} \frac{5 x^{3}-2 x^{2}+1}{1-3 x}=\lim _{x \rightarrow+\infty} \frac{5 x^{2}-2 x+\frac{1}{x}}{\frac{1}{x}-3}=-\infty $$
items.raw_body:
Example 8 Find
(a) $\lim _{x \rightarrow-\infty} \frac{4 x^{2}-x}{2 x^{3}-5}$
(b) $\lim _{x \rightarrow+\infty} \frac{5 x^{3}-2 x^{2}+1}{1-3 x}$

Solution (a). Divide each term in the numerator and denominator by the highest power of $x$ that occurs in the denominator, namely, $x^{3}$. We obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}
\lim _{x \rightarrow-\infty} \frac{4 x^{2}-x}{2 x^{3}-5} & =\lim _{x \rightarrow-\infty} \frac{\frac{4}{x}-\frac{1}{x^{2}}}{2-\frac{5}{x^{3}}} \\
& =\frac{\lim _{x \rightarrow-\infty}\left(\frac{4}{x}-\frac{1}{x^{2}}\right)}{\lim _{x \rightarrow-\infty}\left(2-\frac{5}{x^{3}}\right)} \quad \text { Divide each term by } x^{3} . \\
& =\frac{}{\lim _{x \rightarrow-\infty} \frac{4}{x}-\lim _{x \rightarrow-\infty} \frac{1}{x^{2}}} \quad \begin{array}{l}
\text { Limit of a quotient is the } \\
\text { quotient of the limits. }
\end{array} \\
& \quad \lim _{x \rightarrow-\infty} 2-\lim _{x \rightarrow-\infty} \frac{5}{x^{3}} \\
& =\frac{4 \lim _{x \rightarrow-\infty} \frac{1}{x}-\lim _{x \rightarrow-\infty} \frac{1}{x^{2}}}{2-5 \lim _{x \rightarrow-\infty} \frac{1}{x^{3}}}=\frac{0-0}{2-0}=0 \quad \begin{array}{l}
\text { A constant a difference is the be moved through } \\
\text { a limit symbol; Formula (14) and } \\
\text { Example 4. }
\end{array}
\end{aligned}
$$

Solution (b). Divide each term in the numerator and denominator by the highest power of $x$ that occurs in the denominator, namely, $x^{1}=x$. We obtain

$$
\begin{equation*}
\lim _{x \rightarrow+\infty} \frac{5 x^{3}-2 x^{2}+1}{1-3 x}=\lim _{x \rightarrow+\infty} \frac{5 x^{2}-2 x+\frac{1}{x}}{\frac{1}{x}-3} \tag{19}
\end{equation*}
$$

In this case we cannot argue that the limit of the quotient is the quotient of the limits because the limit of the numerator does not exist. However, we have

$$
\lim _{x \rightarrow+\infty} 5 x^{2}-2 x=+\infty, \quad \lim _{x \rightarrow+\infty} \frac{1}{x}=0, \quad \lim _{x \rightarrow+\infty}\left(\frac{1}{x}-3\right)=-3
$$

Thus, the numerator on the right side of (19) approaches $+\infty$ and the denominator has a finite negative limit. We conclude from this that the quotient approaches $-\infty$; that is,

$$
\lim _{x \rightarrow+\infty} \frac{5 x^{3}-2 x^{2}+1}{1-3 x}=\lim _{x \rightarrow+\infty} \frac{5 x^{2}-2 x+\frac{1}{x}}{\frac{1}{x}-3}=-\infty
$$
